text: Foreword Prior to surgical procedures, the importance of the anatomy is often underestimated, and this despite the fact, that precise anatomical preparation during surgery is usually the safest route towards a successful outcome. There are a number of reasons that can explain the superiority of anatomical preparation in surgery. First of all, anatomical preparation per definition respects the grown structures in specific spaces with determined borders, thus permitting the definition of specific landmarks, more noble structures, and dependant territories. Respecting these known anatomical boundaries allows to avoid unnecessary tissue damage during and/or after the procedure and thus, impacts directly short and long term outcome. Nowadays it is a routine to check prior to a surgical procedure, whether the anatomy of a specific location or a patient respectively is normal, or if there are anomalies, and/or pathological structures. However, in order to assess the anatomy in a specific case, one has to know what the most frequent anatomical landscape looks like, and whether, effectively in a given situation the anatomy is standard or different. For a better understanding of the issues raised here, we like the wording “functional anatomy”, a term reminding us, that for most anatomical structures there is a reason to be there, to construct there, to connect there, to resist there, to move there, to pass there, and so forth... As a matter of fact numerous anatomists not only tried to identify specific bodily structures, but even more so worked on their interconnection in order to understand their function. Many of these efforts were made not that a long time ago by Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564) and his successors. Interestingly enough, it was very difficult in those days to have access to cadavers for dissection, which may explain why mainly the bodies of executed criminals were used in those days. Already Vesalius had already described that the human heart had four chambers and that the blood vessels originated in the heart and not the liver. Of prime importance for cardio-vascular surgery was however the discovery of the circulation by William Harvey (1578–1657), and the proof of the capillary connection between the right heart and the left heart by Marcello Malpighi (1628–1694), a discovery only possible by a microscope as described by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1632–1723). Not all anatomists received for their discoveries the recognition they deserved. As a matter of fact, Michael Servetus (1509–1553) who was probably the first to describe the pulmonary circulation was burned for heresy together with his works in Geneva in 1553, and the later confirmation of his anatomical findings by Realdo Colombo (1516–1559) and Andrea Cesalpina (1519–1603) was not exactly helpful for him.

text: Another interesting observation can be made on the quite recent attempts to protect the brain during circulatory arrest by retrograde superior vena caval perfusion, which gave and still gives matter for endless controversies about its usefulness. Many of these discussions might have been shortened by a thorough analysis of the literature, because it appears, that already in the 16th century Hieronymus Fabrizio ab Aquapendente described in his book ”De Venarum Ostiolis” published in 1603, a valve at the origin of the jugular vein (Tabula prima: A), a fact which indeed does not allow to perfuse the brain in retrograde fashion through the veins. It has been confirmed more than 400 years later, that the human species has not evolved in this respect, that the valves in the venous system draining the blood from the head towards the heart are still there, and that therefore retrograde cerebral perfusion remains an unreliable thing with, unfortunately, unpredictable outcome! Of course, there are other examples for “new” therapeutic proposals, which are often not so new, not so useful, and often also not so true. Most such proposals are not really helpful as already suggested by Socrates (469 BC–399 BC). With the “Operative Anatomy of the Heart” Denis Berdajs and Marko I. Turina have realized a detailed documentation with splendid illustrations of the anatomy of the heart which can be recommended to anybody interested in the heart and its structures. Furthermore the surgeons should look-up “Operative Anatomy of the Heart” before they find themselves in the unfriendly waters of the unknown during surgery. “Operative Anatomy of the Heart” is a reference for all procedures within and around the heart. “Operative anatomy of the Heart” not only provides minute details about what is where for the heart and its interiors, but also demonstrates how to get there... Lausanne, May 8, 2010 Ludwig K. von Segesser VI Foreword

text: Preface Only those who dare to fail greatly can ever achieve greatly Robert Kennedy 1925–1968 Books and articles on techniques in cardiac surgery date back to 1952, when the first successful closure of an atrial septal defect was performed. In all surgical disciplines, but particularly in cardiac surgery, success is greatly dependent upon the use of appropriate operative techniques. In one of the first textbooks on operative surgery, Kirschner remarked that a good operative technique requires a detailed knowledge of the underlying morphology. This rule has gained further importance since the introduction of minimally invasive techniques, which have highlighted the necessity of a perfect knowledge of the underlying cardiac and thoracic morphology. A precise knowledge of the anatomy of not only the valvular structures, but also the coronary vessels and the conducting system has become essential for procedures involving the mitral or tricuspid valves. Similarly, new reconstructive procedures relating to the aortic and pulmonary root require not only detailed knowledge of the macroscopic anatomy, but also a thorough understanding of the spatial relationships between these complex physiological and morphological units. The first chapter of this book describes the detailed topographical anatomy of the human thorax. The morphological regions are illustrated using preserved human specimens, which were dissected from skin level to the bony skeleton of the thorax. The most important regions are presented from the ventral and dorsal aspects. The second chapter discusses the approaches used in standard cardiac surgery, including a detailed step-by-step presentation of the standard sternotomy and right anterolateral thoracotomy. Special attention is devoted to minimally invasive approaches to the heart, such as limited sternotomies and thoracotomies, as well as the transdiaphragmatic approach to the inferior aspect of the heart. Furthermore, other approaches to the thoracic aorta, such as posterolateral thoracotomy and thoracoabdominal incision, are visualized. The chapter on coronary surgery (Chap. 3) emphasizes the arterial coronary conduits. Normal coronary morphology and their anatomical variants, as well as surgical approaches are described. This chapter is divided into two major parts, the first dealing with the general anatomy of the coronary vasculature, from descriptions of their orifices to an analysis of arterial dominance. The second part is devoted to a description of the venous drainage of the heart and to the surgical exposure of target coronary vessels Chapter 4 describes the heart valves. As in previous chapters, the general morphology and their variations are detailed together with the topography and histology, and a description of related structures. This is followed by the surgical section, wherein the valves are exposed and shown from the view-

The remaining chapters deal with the morphology of the interventricular septum, with special attention paid to the variations in its blood supply, the heart conduction system, and exposure of the thoracic and abdominal aorta. We have chosen photographs that depict the structures as they appear to the surgeon in the operating theater. In order to clarify surgical procedures and anatomical structures, some photographs have been supplemented with drawings to provide better orientation. We trust this new book will be of interest not only to the cardiac surgeon, but also to the cardiologist, surgical pathologist, and anesthesiologist, all of whom should profit from the detailed descriptions of the cardiac structures provided in this work. In the second section of this chapter we focus on a detailed discussion of the deeper structures. The morphology of the thorax is defined and influenced mainly by the bony elements such as the ribs, the thoracic vertebra, and the bones of the shoulder, and by the muscular layer. Although individual variations can influence the relief and fine form of the thorax, there are fundamental characteristics that are true of all individuals. The superficial relief, which is defined by the bony skeleton and the borders of the visceral thorax cavity, do not correspond to each other. In the ventral aspect, the superficial border Fig. 1.1. Ventral thorax regions of the thorax is defined by the clavicle; on the dorsal side, there is a virtual line between the acromioclavicular joint and the seventh thoracic vertebra. The muscular layer at the visceral border at the superior thorax aperture is about two fingers over the superior edge of the clavicle. The same phenomenon is seen at the inferior border of the thoracic cage. The ventral inferior border is defined by the xiphoid process and anterior rib arch, and the dorsal border is defined by a virtual line between the 12th thoracic vertebra and the most inferior arch of the 12th rib. At this point it should be remembered that the diaphragm reaches up to the fifth thoracic vertebra. The part of the axillary artery inferior to the pectoralis minor is also known as the distal or the third segment of the artery. Topography of the lateral thoracic artery in the axillary fossa, inferior view The pectoralis major was removed next and the entire length of the pectoralis minor was exposed. The tendinous attachment of the pectoralis minor was dissected; the medial edge was lifted away, as shown in Fig. 1.13 and the corresponding schematic drawing in Fig. 1.14. Note that during this maneuver the second segment of the axillary artery was exposed. The lateral thoracic artery arises just inferior to the retracted pectoralis minor. After branching, this artery traverses superiorly, crossing the axillary vein and running along the lateral chest wall just underneath the pectoralis minor, as shown in the Figs. 1.13 and 1.14. After a short run off, the artery gives off medial and lateral branches. The medial segment runs toward the sternocostal junction, where it merges with the intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery. The clinical importance of this anastomosis is discussed further in Chap. 3. The lateral branch of the lateral thoracic artery runs over the serratus anterior. Note that the opening of the thoracoepigastric vein into the axillary vein can be seen just inferior to the run off of the lateral thoracic artery. The small segmental branches arise perpendicularly from the artery and run into the pectoralis minor. The brachial plexus wraps around the superior and posterior walls of the axillary artery; the inferior wall is in contact with the axillary vein, and the posterior wall is positioned on the first rib. It is thus clear that only the superior wall may be considered as a free segment, being covered only by the pectoralis minor, an anatomical fact that should be heeded. This segment of the subclavian artery may be used as the arterial site at which to establish a cardiopulmonary bypass. The anatomical segments of the axillary artery will now be discussed. The first portion of the axillary artery is covered anteriorly by the clavicular portion of the pectoralis major and the coracoclavicular fascia. The detailed anatomy of this segment and of the associated structures will be discussed later on in this chapter. The axillary artery, together with the axillary vein and the brachial plexus, is enclosed within a fibrous sheath, the axillary sheath, which is continuous with the deep cervical fascia above. The second portion of the axillary artery is covered anteriorly by the pectorales major and minor. The posterior cord of the brachial plexus is found posterior to this artery (Fig. 1.13). The axillary vein is found medially and is separated from the artery by the medial cord of the brachial plexus and the medial anterior thoracic nerve; the lateral cord of the brachial plexus is seen lateral to the second portion of the axillary artery. 12 1 Thorax Regions

Topography of the subclavian artery and vein (modified from [1]) The third portion of the axillary artery extends from the lower border of the pectoralis minor to the lower border of the tendon of the teres major (Fig. 1.15). Anteriorly, it is covered by the lower part of the pectoralis major, and inferiorly only by the integument and fascia below; it is associated with the lower part of the subscapularis, and the tendons of the latissimus dorsi and teres major behind. The coracobrachialis is found lateral to this part of the axillary artery, and the axillary vein can be seen laterally, on its medial or thoracic side. Removal of the pectoralis major opens up the deltoideopectoral sulcus. Note that the base of the sulcus is made distally by the biceps muscle and proximally, just near to the clavicle, by the tendinous part of the pectoralis minor. The pectoralis minor, which is a thin structure that is positioned under the pectoralis major, arises from the upper margins and outer surfaces of the third, fourth, and fifth ribs, near their cartilage (Fig. 1.15). The fibers pass upward and laterally, and converge to form a flat tendon, which inserts into the medial border and upper surface of the coracoid process of the scapula. This tendon creates the proximal base of the deltoideopectoral sulcus. The cephalic vein, which has also been exposed, turns downward and medially at the superior edge of the pectoralis minor, where it crosses the subclavian artery and opens into the subclavian vein (Fig. 1.15). The subclavius can be seen superior to the attachment of the cephalic and the subclavian veins. This is a very thin muscle that is positioned between the first rib and the clavicle (Fig. 1.15). It arises from the first rib and its cartilage, proceeding obliquely upward and laterally, to insert into the groove on the under surface of the clavicle between the costoclavicular and conoid ligaments. At this point we should briefly mention the coracoclavicular fascia, which is a strong fascia that is situated under the clavicular portion of the pectoralis major. It occupies the interval between the pectoralis minor and the subclavius. Note that before opening into the axillary vein, the cephalic vein perforates this fascia (Fig. 1.15); however, on the presented specimen the fascia was removed in order to expose the subclavian vessels positioned between the pectoralis minor and the subclavius. 1.2 Deep Thorax Regions 13

Laterally, it is very thick and dense, and is attached to the coracoid process, below which it is thin. At the upper border of the pectoralis minor it splits into two layers to envelop the muscle. From the lower border of the pectoralis minor it continues downward to join the axillary fascia, and laterally to join the fascia over the short head of the biceps brachii. The so-called little supraclavicular triangle may be found between the sternal and clavicular parts of the muscular attachment. Here, the segmental arterial branches exit the deeper layers in order to provide a blood supply to the skin. On the dissected specimen only the sternal segment of the attachment may be seen. Of note, the line connecting the little supraclavicular triangle and the auricle of the ear describes the course of the internal jugular vein, and is hence a good reference for puncture of that vessel. text: The subclavian vein is in front of and slightly lower than the subclavian artery. The artery is positioned on the lowest trunk of the brachial plexus, which intervenes between it and the scalenus medius (Fig. 1.18). Above and lateral to it are the upper trunks of the brachial plexus. At the beginning of its route the subclavian artery rests on the pleura, and later on the upper surface of the first rib (Fig. 1.18). The origin of the lateral thoracic artery is seen at the lateral segment of the subclavian artery, which crosses the subclavian vein soon after it arises. The subclavian vein was resected to allow examination of the second portion of the subclavian artery (Figs. 1.19 and 1.20). Furthermore, the scalenus anterior was removed from the first rib to allow investigation of that part of the artery that lies behind the muscle. Note that this part of the artery forms the highest part of the arch described by the vessel. On the right side of the neck, the phrenic nerve is separated from the second part of the subclavian artery by the scalenus anterior, while on the left side it crosses the first part of the artery close to the medial edge of the muscle. Behind the vessel are the pleura and the scalenus medius (Figs. 1.19 and 1.20). The apical part of the pleura was exposed by retracting the scalenus anterior. At this level the artery does not have any contact with the first rib. On the dry-dissected specimen (Fig. 1.19) the pleura is seen between the inferior border of the artery and the first rib. The attachment of the scalenus anterior is seen on the superior surface of the first rib. Retraction of the scalenus anterior also exposed the costocervical trunk (Figs. 1.19 and 1.20), which arises from the upper and back part of the subclavian artery, behind the scalenus anterior. Passing backward, it gives off the profunda cervicalis and, continuing as the intercostalis suprema (highest intercostal) artery, it later descends behind the pleura in front of the necks of the first and second ribs, and anastomoses with the first aortic intercostal artery, as seen in Figs. 1.19 and 1.20. The superficial cervical artery, which originates from the thyrocervical trunk, is seen in front of the scalenus anterior. The artery crosses the phrenic nerve on the medial edge of the scalenus anterior. After leaving the lateral edge of the scalenus anterior, the artery runs toward the lateral neck triangle (Figs. 1.19 and 1.20). In the following we will discuss the anatomy of the suprajugular space, which is a very complex structure that extends from the jugular notch up to the hyoid bone. The dry-dissected specimen (Fig. 1.21) shows the jugular venous arch, which is supplied by the superficial dorsal jugular veins, which join laterally. Superficially, the arch connects to the ventral superficial jugular vein, which drains directly into the internal jugular vein (Fig. 1.22). The suprajugular notch has a triangular shape. The posterior wall is composed of the median neck fascia and the anterior wall is created by the superficial neck fascia. Both connective tissue layers run toward the hyoid bone and join the common fascia at the level of the thyroid gland. The space is bordered on the left and the right by the left and the right sternocleidomastoid muscles, respectively. Note that the suprajugular notch is covered by a ligament that spans between the left and right sternoclavicular articulations. This ligament was dissected and demonstrated on the drydissected specimen (Fig. 1.21). Deep muscles of thoracoabdominal transition, lateral view The rectus abdominis is a long flat muscle that extends along the entire length of the front of the abdomen (Fig. 1.37). It arises from two tendons, the lateral or larger one of which is attached to the crest of the pubis, and the medial is interlaced with its counterpart on the opposite side and is connected with the ligaments covering the front of the symphysis pubis. The muscle is inserted by three portions of unequal size into the cartilages of the fifth, sixth, and seventh ribs (Fig. 1.37). The upper portion, which is attached principally to the cartilage of the fifth rib, usually has some insertion fibers into the anterior extremity of the rib itself. Some fibers are occasionally connected to the costoxiphoid ligaments and the side of the xiphoid process. Release of the xiphoid process by median sternotomy requires dissection of the aforementioned attachment of the rectus abdominis away from this part of the sternum. It is therefore suggested that young surgeons have a clear picture of the muscular attachments in this region. The external oblique muscle is situated on the lateral and anterior parts of the abdomen, and originates as eight fleshy digitations from the external surfaces and inferior borders of the lower eight ribs (Fig. 1.37). The five superior serrations increase in size from above downward, and are received between corresponding processes of the serratus anterior. From their attachments, the fleshy fibers proceed in various directions. Those from the lowest ribs pass nearly vertically downward and insert into the anterior half of the outer lip of the iliac crest; the middle and upper fibers are directed downward and forward, ending in an aponeurosis opposite a line drawn from the prominence of the ninth costal cartilage to the anterior superior iliac spine. 1.2 Deep Thorax Regions 31

The rhomboideus major converges into a narrow tendinous arch that is attached above to the lower part the rhomboideus minor and to the base of the triangular smooth surface at the root of the spine of the scapula. It is usually separated from the rhomboideus major by a slight interval, but the adjacent margins of the two muscles occasionally unite (Figs. 1.42 and 1.43). The levator scapulae is situated superior to both rhomboideus muscles at the back and side of the neck, originating via tendinous slips from the transverse processes of the atlas and axis and from the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the third and fourth cervical vertebrae. It runs diagonally toward the vertebral border of the scapula, where it is also attached. Note that the serratus lateralis may be found lateral to the attachment of the levator scapulae, and is attached to the medial angle of the scapula. The omohyoid muscle is found between the levator scapulae and serratus lateralis (Figs. 1.42 and 1.43). The suprascapular artery and vein enter in this region. Both structures run just superior to the transverse ligament of the scapula, and the suprascapular nerve is found inferior to it (Figs. 1.42 and 1.43). The muscle is situated at the junction of the thoracic and lumbar regions; it originates via a thin aponeurosis from the spinous processes of the lower two thoracic and upper two or three lumbar vertebrae, and from the supraspinal ligament (Figs. 1.46 and 1.48). Passing obliquely upward and laterally, it becomes fleshy and divides into four flat digitations, which insert into the inferior borders of the lower four ribs. The serratus superior posterior (Fig. 1.47) is a thin, quadrilateral muscle that is situated at the upper and back part of the thorax. It arises via a thin and broad aponeurosis from the lower part of the ligamentum nuchae, from the spinous processes of the seventh cervical and upper two or three thoracic vertebrae. Inclining downward and laterally, it becomes muscular and inserts via four fleshy digitations into the upper borders of the second, third, fourth, and fifth ribs just beyond their angles. 1.2 Deep Thorax Regions 39

Intrajugular space; example of a dilated intrajugular vein In the jugular notch, one should pay close attention to the intrajugular vein and ligament (Figs. 2.7 and 2.8). Very important landmarks of this region are the bilateral insertions of the sternocleidomastoid muscle on the sternoclavicular joint. Lateral and cranial to the articulation is the clavicular part of the pectoralis major (Figs. 2.7 and 2.8). The intrajugular ligament is located between the insertions of the left and right sternocleidomastoid muscles. This ligament is an extension of the fibrous sternoclavicular joint capsule, and is located in the jugular notch, medial to the sternoclavicular joint. Inferiorly, it inserts directly onto the sternal periosteum. The topographical location of the intrajugular ligament shows that its incision is necessary for a successful sternal division. 2.1 Sternotomy 45

Incision of the linea alba over the xiphoid process In some cases, a large intrajugular vein may be found the jugular notch (Fig. 2.8), especially in congestive heart disease. This vein is sometimes a source of unsolicited hemorrhaging, especially after a cardiopulmonary bypass is established. We suggest ligating the vein after its exposure (Fig. 2.9). A vein may occasionally be found at the subiculum cordis in the adipose tissue, on the border between the sternal body and the xiphoid process. This vein is an anastomosis between the left and right internal thoracic veins (Fig. 2.10), and in some cases may be a source of unfavorable hemorrhaging, especially in a patient with congestive heart disease. As indicated, the incision of the linea alba extends two finger-breadths under the xiphoid process (Figs. 2.4 and 2.5). The medial attachment of the rectus abdominis and the interdigitation of the rectus sheath and pectoral fascia in the sternocostal angle are dissected to release the process (Fig. 2.5 and 2.10). In the next step, the xiphoid process is split along its midline; the artery supplying the process may be easily damaged during this process. The xiphoid branch is an end-branching of the internal thoracic artery and, in 7% of cases, supplies the xiphoid process directly (Fig. 2.10). 46 2 Surgical Approaches

Jugular area as seen following sternotomy 2.1.1.2 The Sternal Incision A vertical sternal incision should be made deep to the periosteum of the sternum (Fig. 2.11). Advancing the sternal incision, the posterior sternal wall should be released from the sternopericardial ligament. After the xiphoid process has been divided, the dissection is continued retrosternally either digitally or with a short-tipped, rightangled clamp. During this procedure, the pericardium and the parietal pleura are released from the posterior wall of the sternum. The retrosternal space is entered and the sternum is divided along its midline from the sternocostal angle toward the jugular notch (Figs. 2.12, 2.13, and 2.14). Hemostasis is accomplished using cauterization to control hemorrhaging vessels at the sternal periosteum. After placement of a sternal spreader, the thymic adipose tissue (Fig. 2.15), which is crossed by a few thymic veins, is incised up to the plane of the brachiocephalic vein (Fig. 2.16). The veins are then separated and clipped; the pericardium is reached just inferiorly to the thymic veins. Any of the heart chambers or the surface of the heart can be manipulated through this incision, making possible surgery of the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk and their primary branches. 2.1 Sternotomy 47

Skin incision for inverse “T” sternotomy 2.2 Partial Sternotomy 2.2.1 Superior Partial “Inverse T” Sternotomy 2.2.1.1 Patient Position and Skin Incision The patient is in the supine position (Fig. 2.17). The skin incision is made in the presternal region over the superior two-thirds of the sternum (Figs. 2.17 and 2.18). It commences two finger-breadths under the jugular notch and extends to the fourth intercostal space. The anterior sternal surface can be identified deep to the dissected subcutaneous adipose tissue. The sternal parts of the left and right pectoralis major are found on the lateral sternal edges, inserting on the sternocostal junctions (Fig. 2.19). The intrajugular ligament is divided in the jugular notch. Dissection and partial release of the sternum from the retrosternal tissue is performed digitally (Fig. 2.20). The insertion of the pectoral fascia to the surface of the sternum is dissected from the fourth intercostal space to the level of the sternal notch, exposing the insertion of the sternal part of the pectoralis major. To perform the superior partial “T” sternotomy, the left and right pectorales major must be horizontally incised just superior to the fourth intercostal space (Fig. 2.21). Division of the intercostal muscles is then performed. Prior to the incision, the intercostal fascia and the internal intercostal muscle are identified. 49

Incision of the external intercostal muscle 2.3.1.2 The Thoracic Incision The thoracic cavity is opened at the fourth intercostal space. There are three well-known and commonly used surgical procedures for achieving this. 1. Incising the intercostal muscles in the intercostal space, with the opening cut beginning at the superior edge of the inferior rib of the corresponding intercostal space. Note that the external and internal intercostal muscles run in opposite directions (Figs. 2.60 and 2.61). The internal intercostal muscles are oriented in the ventrodorsal direction, from the inferior to the superior edge of the rib (Fig. 2.62). The external intercostal muscle does not reach the lateral edge of the sternum and the sternocostal junction; instead, it ends at the parasternal line. Thereafter, the internal intercostal muscle is covered by the external intercostal membrane. Using this approach, the supracostal structures such as the supracostal arteries, veins, and nerves (which are branches of the intercostal arteries, veins, and nerves) can be easily damaged (Fig. 2.63). However, this does not influence any segmental innervations or blood supply. After the segmental branches are coagulated and the parietal pleura is exposed (Fig. 2.64), the thoracic spreader may be inserted (Fig. 2.65 and 2.66). 68 2 Surgical Approaches

Exposure of the thorax incision 2.3.2.2 The Thoracic Incision The thoracic cavity can be opened at the level of the fifth or fourth intercostal spaces. The incision should begin at the level of the fourth intercostal space if the target structures are the aortic arch, the patent arterial duct, or the aortic isthmus. If the entire length of the thoracic aorta must be seen, the incision should be made at the level of the fifth intercostal space. To identify the correct rib, one must palpate the space between the lateral chest wall and the latissimus dorsi until the second rib is identified. This is the landmark that enables counting the ribs inferiorly/ caudally to identify the correct intercostal space. The thoracic incision is then executed above the superior edge of the corresponding rib. To avoid damage to the intercostal structures, the intercostal muscle must be incised immediately superior to the rib (Fig. 2.98). To also prevent injury to the lung, the pleura should be punctured to ensure free space. The lung is then gently retracted from the chest wall and the incision is widened (Figs. 2.98 and 2.99). 80 2 Surgical Approaches

text: Vagal nerve Phrenic nerve I Superior cervical artery Ascending cervical artery Suprascapular artery Brachial plexus Internal thoracic artery Subclavian artery Insertion of scalenus anterior Pleural cupule Clavicle Subclavian vein Scalenus anterior Jugular vein 3.1 Internal Thoracic Artery 3.1.1 General Anatomy of the Internal Thoracic Artery 3.1.1.1 Origin and Course of the Internal Thoracic Artery The thoracic part of the right subclavian artery originates from the brachiocephalic trunk, just behind the sternoclavicular joint, and passes upward in the scalenotracheal fossa to the medial margin of the scalenus anterior. The left subclavian artery arises directly from the aortic arch, just behind the left common carotid artery at the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra. In its initial run off, the artery ascends in the superior mediastinal cavity to the root of the neck. From the sternoclavicular articulation, the topographies of the left and right subclavian arteries are similar. In the scalenotracheal fossa, the artery winds around the pleural cupule toward the medial border of the scalenus anterior. The muscular part lies in the subclavian groove of the first rib. Its boundary is formed by the scaleni anterior and medius. This part of the artery forms the highest part of the arch described by the vessel. In some rare variants, the artery passes in front of the scalenus anteFig. 3.1. Origin of the internal thoracic artery rior; in these cases, a vascular ring sometimes surrounds the muscle. In the case of a rudimentary first rib, the artery always is seen above the uppermost rib. The cervical part is contained in the omoclavicular triangle. The artery runs downward and laterally from the lateral margin of the scalenus anterior to the outer border of the first rib. This is the most superficial segment. The internal thoracic artery arises from the thoracic part of the subclavian artery, just opposite to the thyrocervical trunk and medial to the scalenus anterior. In its initial run off, the artery descends on the pleural cupule to cross, after a short course, the sternal third of the clavicle and the first rib cartilage, in order to enter the thoracic cavity. Before reaching the first rib, the artery is crossed by the brachiocephalic vein. Shortly after its origin, the phrenic nerve joins the artery from its lateral aspect. After a short run off, the nerve runs medial and ventral to the artery, behind the subclavian vein (Fig. 3.1 and 3.2). On the dry-dissected specimen, the right internal thoracic artery is inspected from the omoclavicular triangle. The right clavicle has been removed and the scalenus anterior detached from the first rib. For better interpretation of the topographical relationships, the subclavian vein has also been removed. One can see that the artery originates just behind the venous angle and runs on the pleural cupule toward the first rib. The phrenic nerve is presented as a white cord running along the ventral aspect of the brachiocephalic trunk and, in this way, crosses the internal thoracic artery (Figs. 3.1 and 3.2). The internal thoracic artery may branch off from the cervical part of the subclavian artery (with an incidence of 1.4%, as postulated by Adachi); in this rare instance, the artery can be identified on the lateral edge of the scalenus anterior. 110 3 Coronary Bypass Grafts

Variants of the origin of the internal thoracic artery Morphological variants of the origin of the internal thoracic artery cannot be discussed without emphasizing its relationships with the vertebral artery, and the costocervical and thyrocervical trunks. Adachi’s classification scheme distinguishes several frequently occurring anatomical types with respect to origin from the subclavian artery. In the most common (normal) type (45.5%), the vertebral and the internal thoracic arteries, and the costocervical and thyrocervical trunks arise as separate branches (Fig. 3.5a). In the second variant (19%), the internal thoracic artery and the transverse cervical artery arise from a common trunk, and the others likewise together (Fig. 3.5b). In the third variant (8.3%), the internal thoracic artery and the suprascapular artery share a common origin (Fig. 3.5c). In the fourth variant (4.1%), the transverse cervical artery originates separately and the other arteries branch off together (Fig. 3.5d). All of the vessels may arise from a common trunk (3.3%; Fig. 3.5e). The internal thoracic, suprascapular, and transverse cervical arteries can arise separately, the others having a common origin (3.3%; Fig. 3.5f). Thymus, anterior view, schematic drawing In most cases, the right lobe is bigger than the left, and sometimes the right and left are separated by an intermediate lobe (Figs. 3.10 and 3.11). Venous drainage of the gland is carried out by the thymic vein, which collects the venous blood from both thymic lobes; after fusion of both branches, the main stem runs straight to the brachiocephalic vein. In contrast to the artery, the vein is still present in adults. Thus, the topographical position of the vein indicates the position of the aorta, and so the pericardial cover of the aorta may be reached by downward dissection just inferior to the thymic veins. The thymus gland is positioned partly in the thorax and partly in the neck. It extends from the fourth costal cartilage upward, as high as the inferior border of the thyroid gland. In the thorax, it is covered by the sternum, where it rests on the pericardium, being separated from the aorta and big vessels by fascia. When it reaches the neck, the superior part of the gland is directly in front of the left brachiocephalic vein. In the neck, the gland is in front of the trachea and behind the sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles. 3.1 Internal Thoracic Artery 117

Intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery Anterior intercostal branches arise in the uppermost five intercostal spaces. After the initial run off in the intercostal space within the internal intercostal muscle, the artery branches off to form the anterior intercostal and supracostal arteries. Initially, both branches run between the pleura and the intercostal muscles; later on in their course, they travel in the subcostal space and anastomose with the posterior intercostal arteries. Before entering the subcostal sulcus, a small component branches off as the supracostal artery (Fig. 3.16). The mediastinal branches of the internal thoracic artery are small and supply the retrosternal fatty tissue, the mediastinal lymph nodes, and the muscles of the chest wall (Fig. 3.14 and 3.16). 120 3 Coronary Bypass Grafts

The superior epigastric artery is the medial terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery. It runs thought the sternocostal triangle, which is a fibrous structure between the sternal and costal part of the diaphragm, and enters the sheath of the rectus abdominis (Fig. 3.16). Morphological variants of the sternal blood supply space. In its run off, this branch communicates with the anterior and posterior intercostal arteries. As noted previously, the main sources of the sternal blood supply are the sternal branches. These branches are positioned in the intercostal spaces, the positioning of which corresponds to the embryologic development of the sternum. The corresponding sternal part is supplied by an arcade-like anastomosis. The morphological variants of these anastomoses will be discussed later. The increased incidence of sternal complications after internal thoracic artery grafting is believed to be caused by damage to the sternal blood supply. To avoid these complications, it has been suggested that surgeons strive to preserve the collaterals so that they can provide perfusion to the sternum after mobilization of the internal thoracic artery. In this regard, it is recommended that the artery is mobilized in a skeletonized fashion. In light of this recommendation, it is evident that it is essential to describe the detailed anatomy of the sternum’s blood supply. Based on our data, we can state that not only the sternal branches, but also the perforating branches contribute to the sternal blood supply. According to their topographical relationship with each other and with the anterior septal artery, several variants have been identified (Fig. 3.19a–d). A representative view of these branching patterns is shown in the angiogram presented in Fig. 3.20. 122 3 Coronary Bypass Grafts

Angiogram of the internal thoracic artery In type I (Fig. 3.19a), all three arteries (sternal, perforating, intercostal branche) arise from the common main stem. After a short run off, this common artery branches off into the sternal, perforating, and anterior intercostal arteries. The collateral blood supply may reach the sternum via the anterior intercostal artery. As such, the branching point of the main artery must be protected from surgical manipulation. In type II (Fig. 3.19b), the sternal artery arises as an independent branch from the medial aspect of the internal thoracic artery. The perforating and anterior intercostal arteries arise from a common branch. After harvesting the internal thoracic artery, the collateral blood flow reaches the sternum via the perforating branch. In other words, the perforating branch is connected directly to the anterior intercostal artery. As such, the branching point of the sternocostal artery must remain intact. In the sternoperforating branch (type III), the sternal and perforating arteries from a common stem. There is no morphological communication between the sternoperforating and the anterior intercostal arteries (Fig. 3.19c); however, retrograde blood flow may theoretically reach the sternum by way of the perforating branches. It is well known that the perforating branches are connected to the vascular system of the lateral thoracic artery. As such, the branching point must be protected from manipulation. In the fourth morphological variant, all three arteries arise as independent branches (Fig. 3.19d). 3.1 Internal Thoracic Artery 123

Types A and B arcades, schematic drawing 3.1.1.3 Arcade Types As mentioned previously, the main sources of the sternal blood supply are the sternal and, in some instances, the perforating branches. The sternal branches are positioned in the intercostal spaces and supply the corresponding part of the sternum. This topographical position corresponds to the sternal ossification zones. The sternal blood supply shows an arcade arrangement of sternal arteries; however, the perforating branches also create arcades to contribute to this blood supply. The perforating arteries give off small branches to the sternum that form an arcade-pattern blood supply. These vascular rings of the perforating branches are positioned betweentheexternalintercostaland pectoralis muscles. In some instances, a vascularconnectionbetweenthe superficial and deep arcades exists. In our dissected specimens, we identified eight arcade blood supply types. In type A, the arcade anastomosis is formed by two neighboring sternal arteries (Figs. 3.21 and 3.22). In type B, a single sternal artery supplies the corresponding part of the sternum (Figs. 3.21 and 3.22). In type C, three sternal branches supply the intercostal part of the sternum (Figs. 3.23 and 3.24). All three arteries arise from the medial surface of the internal thoracic artery; two of them are arranged as an arcade anastomosis, and the third branch conjoins with this formation superiorly. 124 3 Coronary Bypass Grafts

However, this specimen is presented in order to demonstrate that arcades of one intercostal area are connected to the neighboring vascular ring. These interconnecting branches are positioned over the sternocostal joints (Figs. 3.33 and 3.34). Clinical Implications Vessels supplying the sternum are prone to damage, not only when the internal thoracic artery is being harvested, but also when the sternum is being closed. In particular, the use of sternal wires may occlude the sternal and perFig. 3.34. Type H arcade, schematic drawing forating branches, which are the functional units of the sternal blood supply. These arteries may be damaged mechanically, especially if the cerclage wires are positioned around the bone in the intercostal space. Furthermore, not only may damage occur to the sternal and perforating branches, but also the wires may harm the sternal blood supply by interrupting the vertical flow of the arcade anastomosis in each interspace. These arcades play an important role in sustaining viability, particularly in those segments wherein the adjoining interspaces have lost their blood supply. The logical recommendation is to place the wires in front of the sternocostal joint, as close as possible to the sternal edge. 128 3 Coronary Bypass Grafts

Mediastinal branch, schematic drawing 3.1.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Internal Thoracic Artery After the sternotomy is performed in a standard fashion, mobilization of the artery is performed prior to exposure of the heart and institution of a cardiopulmonary bypass. All of the precardial dissection is completed and the retrosternal fatty tissue is divided down to the pericardium. An asymmetric sternal retractor is then used to elevate the hemisternum. The table should be turned away from the surgeon and elevated to an appropriate level (Fig. 3.35). Once the sternum has been lifted, the pleural reflection may be dissected from the anterior chest wall. Following that, the pleural space may be opened widely, from the apex near the subclavian vein down to the diaphragm; the opening incision should be performed just two finger-breadths under the sternal edge. In some cases, the large mediastinal branch of the internal thoracic artery may be detected (Fig. 3.36) running from the artery toward the precardial fat tissue (Fig. 3.37). In order to avoid excessive bleeding, the mediastinal branch should be secured with clips. 3.1 Internal Thoracic Artery 129

Run-off of the internal thoracic artery, schematic drawing Some surgeons advocate leaving the pleura intact, simply pushing the pleura away from the endothoracic fascia, to reduce the incidence of postoperative pleural effusion and hemidiaphragm impairment. Furthermore, intraoperatively the intact pleura may retract the lung away from the operating area. However, this technique tends to displace the internal thoracic artery pedicle and may result in undesirable angulations by inflation of the upper lobe of the lung. Prior to dissection, one should identify the artery on the internal chest wall. The artery runs approximately 1.5 cm lateral to the sternal edge, between two veins (Fig. 3.38). Pulsation of the artery, which generally distinguishes arteries from veins, may be visualized or manually palpated. However, the artery may be visually identified quite well between the first rib and the third intercostal space. Along this distance, the artery runs on the parietal pleura; from the level of the third rib to its bifurcation, the artery runs between the chest wall and transversus thoracis. Here, the artery and the veins cannot be visualized very well and the only way to identify the run off is by manual palpation (Fig. 3.39). The medial aspect of the endothoracic fascia is then incised at most accessible portion of the internal thoracic artery, usually at the level of the middle or inferior third. Internal thoracic artery, as seen after harvesting, schematic drawing 3.1.2.1 Skeletonized Harvesting Prior to the incision, the artery has to be identified at the point where it crosses the costal cartilage. The fascia is incised at the superiormost level of the artery near the internal thoracic vein. Downward traction of the fascia with the arteriovenous pedicle, combined with cold dissection, permits separation of the artery from the anterior chest wall. The cold dissection should separate the artery from the surrounding muscle, fascia, and fatty tissue. We suggest beginning with isolation on the medial aspect of the artery, between the thoracic wall and the artery, and then progressing over the superficial surface of the artery toward the lateral side of the graft. In this way, the sternal, perforating, and intercostal branches are isolated (Fig. 3.40). In order to preserve the sternal blood supply after mobilization of the internal thoracic artery, the branches must be secured with metal clips just over the internal thoracic artery (Fig. 3.41; also see Sect. 3.1.1.2). Dissection in this manner is carried out along the entire course of the artery. 3.1.2.2 Pedicle Harvesting A longitudinal fascial incision is made approximately 1 cm lateral and medial to the artery. The artery is harvested as a pedicle including the fascia, muscle, connective tissue, and both veins. The incision is made on the cartilage, since there are no branches of the artery. An appropriate level can be identified and the entire pedicle can be detached from the chest wall. The same maneuver is repeated at each rib following exposure of the intercostal segments of the artery. In the intercostal spaces, the sternal perforating and anterior intercostal arteries are electrocauterized or secured with metal clips, depending upon their size (Fig. 3.41). The pedicle is drawn away with smooth-tipped forceps and peeled down from the chest wall by gentle cold preparation with the electrocautery blade. By a combination of traction and cold preparation, the perforating branches may be identified and secured; permanent downward traction facilitates the distal dissection. Finally, the pedicle has been separated from the chest wall. 3.1 Internal Thoracic Artery 131

Morphological variants of the radial artery Morphologic Variants of the Radial Artery Under normal conditions, the radial artery branches off from the brachial artery at the level of the radial neck (Fig. 3.53 and 3.55a). The run off of the artery may be described as a straight line placed from the radial neck and the direction and the styloid process. In some cases, the artery has a highly placed origin (Fig. 3.55b); in the presented schematic drawing, the radial artery arises from the brachial artery. High division of the brachial artery occurs mostly in the inferior or in the proximal third of the arm. In cases of a high division of the radial artery, the distant part of the brachial artery branches off into the ulnar and interosseus arteries. On rare occasions, the radial artery branches off together with the interosseus artery (Fig. 3.55c). High division of the radial artery is without surgical importance and does not influence the harvesting of the graft from a technical point of view. Note that approximately 75% of radial arteries have a high division. Insufficient collateral flow between the ulnar and radial arteries is the definitive contraindication for harvesting of the radial artery. The Allen test was proposed to prove this; however, in 15% of cases this was found to give a false-positive result. In this situation, the patency of the ulnar artery must be proved with the aid of pulse palpation. The superficial arch is a source of the blood supply to the fingers. In light of the aforementioned morphological evidence, it is imperative to discuss the morphological variants of the superficial palmar arch. In particular, in the case of insufficient anastomosis between the radial and ulnar arteries, harvesting of the radial artery may result in ischemic damage to the hand. The radioulnar type of superficial palmar arch corresponds to the classical morphological description of the superficial arch formed by the ulnar and radial arteries (Fig. 3.56, labels 1 and 2). However, only approximately 25% of the normal types are created by the ulnar and radial arteries (Fig. 3.56a), and in another 25% is the radial artery very small (Fig. 3.56b). In this case, the ulnar artery alone creates the complete superficial arch and supplies the first and second fingers. In the medianoulnar type (Fig. 3.56c), the median artery replaces the radial artery in the formation of the superficial arch (6% of cases). In 16.5% of cases the superficial arch is not developed (Fig. 3.56e, f). It should be noted that harvesting of the radial artery may be performed without any risk of ischemic injury only in the radioulnar and medianoulnar morphological variants of the superficial palmar arch. 3.2 Radial Artery 141

Exposure of the antebrachial fascia 3.2.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Radial Artery 3.2.2.1 Skin Incision The left radial artery is harvested in right-handed individuals and vice versa. The patient is positioned with the arm at a 90° angle with longitudinal axis of the body. The following superficial landmarks define the extent of the required skin incision: the brachioradialis, the biceps tendon at the proximal end of the forearm, the radial styloid, and the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis at the distal end of the forearm (Fig. 3.57). A groove between the medial side of the brachioradialis muscle and the biceps tendon can be palpated at the proximal part of the forearm. The skin incision extends from a point about one finger-breadth lateral to the palpable biceps tendon, and continues down the length of the forearm to a point midway between the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis and the radial styloid at the wrist crease (Fig. 3.57). It is performed as a slightly curved line that follows the rounded belly of the brachioradialis. Note that at the distal third of the forearm the artery is not covered by fascia. At this level, it is covered by skin; thus, careful dissection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue is advisable at this point (Fig. 3.58 and 3.59). 142 3 Coronary Bypass Grafts

Exposure of the radial artery origin 3.2.2.3 Surgical Harvesting The artery is most easily visualized in the middle zone, as it emerges underneath the cover of the belly of the brachioradialis (Fig. 3.63). Initial dissection should begin here. The artery is mobilized minimally so that a vessel loop can be placed around it. Elevation of the radial artery reveals the perforating branches that exit the main trunk (Figs. 3.64 and 3.65). Continuous delicate upward traction is applied to the vessel loop as these branches are divided. The perforating branches that supply the surrounding muscles tend to be longer, sturdier, and more prominent than those in the distal third of the forearm. The risk of damage to the superficial radial nerve is greatest along this section of the arterial run off. At the distal part of the artery, first a suture is placed at the level of the radial styloid. When the distal suture is secured, the artery is divided. One must be particularly careful at this point because isolation of the perforating branches here is very difficult. The branches are shorter, finer, and more delicate than along the proximal two-thirds of the artery’s length. These perforating branches exit the artery at irregular points along the dorsomedial and dorsolateral aspects (Figs. 3.65 and 3.66). 3.2 Radial Artery 145

Origin of the gastroepiploic artery Fig. 3.68. Branches of the gastroepiploic artery The right gastroepiploic artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery. The gastroduodenal artery is a short but wide branch of the hepatic artery. The artery descends between the superior part of the duodenum and the neck of the pancreas, and divides at the lower border of the duodenum into the right gastroepiploic and the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery. Branches of the gastroepiploic artery along the greater curvature The gastroepiploic artery runs between the pancreas and the posterior wall of the duodenum, toward the pylorus. After reaching the pylorus it runs along the greater curvature of the stomach, between the layers of the greater omentum. Except at the pylorus, where it is in contact with the stomach, it lies about one finger-breadth from the greater curvature (Figs. 3.69 and 3.70). At its termination, the right gastroepiploic artery is connected to the left gastroepiploic artery, which is a branch of the splenic artery that supplies the rest of the greater curvature. The anastomosis of the left and right gastroepiploic arteries is also known as the inferior arterial gastric arch. In most cases, the right gastroepiploic artery supplies the right twothirds of the greater curvature (Figs. 3.69 and 3.71a). In cases where the majority of the great curvature is supplied by the right gastroepiploic artery, there is no detectable connection to its left counterpart. The anastomosis of the left and right gastroepiploic arteries may be found at the midpoint of the greater curvature (Fig. 7.71b). The vascular connection sometimes presents as a common branch that reaches up to the gastrosplenic ligament (Fig. 7.71c). 148 3 Coronary Bypass Grafts

Gastroepiploic artery in the greater omentum 3.3.2 Surgical Anatomy An extension of a median sternotomy into a superior median laparotomy is usually used to approach the right gastroepiploic artery. After dissection of the subcutaneous fatty tissue and achieving hemostasis, the linea alba is reached. This fibrous structure is dissected and the parietal part of the peritoneum is opened. The structures of the epigastrium are retracted into the operating field (Fig. 3.73). The liver (segments IVb and V) is seen on the upper right side, and on the left, the entire left lobe is visible. The gallbladder is seen inferior to the liver on the right, and the stomach and pylorus on the left. The left and right segments are separated by the falciform ligament. The gastroepiploic artery is usually buried within the fatty tissue that is part of the greater omentum (Figs. 3.73 and 3.74). After its origin, the artery passes behind the duodenum, where it crosses the posterior wall of the duodenum and enters the greater omentum (Figs. 3.75, 3.76, and 3.77). 150 3 Coronary Bypass Grafts

In 28% of cases, it arises inferior to the inguinal ligament, and in 15% of cases from the femoral artery. Adachi described its common origin with the medial circumflex femoral artery, the deep femoral proprial artery, or the medial profundocircumflex trunk. These common trunks may take their origin from either the external iliac artery or the femoral artery. In very rare cases, the artery originates from the internal iliac artery together with the obturator artery. Fig. 3.78. Origin of the inferior epigastric artery When originating superior to the inguinal ligament, the artery runs medially, toward the medial edge of the deep inguinal ring. At this level, the artery crosses the ductus deferens or, in females, the round ligament of the uterus. Here, there are two readily observed branches: the pubic branch and the cremasteric artery (in females, the artery of the round ligament of the uterus). The pubic branch runs toward the symphysis and anastomoses with the obturator artery. In some cases, the latter may also arise from the inferior epigastric artery. The cremasteric branch enters the inguinal canal and divides in the skin of the scrotum (Fig. 3.78). 153

A midline incision can be used to harvest both the left and right inferior epigastric arteries. The paramedian incision starts from the level of the umbilicus in the medioclavicular line. It first follows the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis, and then continues, to reach the inferior third of the muscle, where the skin incision is slightly angled down toward the femoral artery, ending approximately 3 cm above the inguinal ligament. Origin of the inferior epigastric artery, schematic drawing After anticoagulation and preparation of the subcutaneous tissue, the linea alba and rectus sheath are reached (Fig. 3.84). The rectus sheath is entered only by division of the anterior rectus sheath (Figs. 3.85 and 3.86). The medial edge of the muscle and the rectus sheath should be retracted laterally to expose the artery. The inferior epigastric artery can be readily isolated at the level corresponding to the lateral border of the rectus abdominis. Upward dissection under appropriate retraction conditions is possible until the level of the terminal branching of the artery, superior to the linea arcuata (Figs. 3.87 and 3.88). Inferiorly, the artery must be isolated until its branching point. At this stage, the iliohypogastric nerve must be identified and preserved using a no-touch technique. To expose the origin, the transverse fascia must be opened at the pubic insertion of the rectus sheath. At the level of the arterial origin, it is necessary to identify and isolate the external spermatic and pubic arteries (Figs. 3.88 and 3.89). 3.4 Inferior Epigastric Artery 157

text: 4.1 General Anatomy 4.1.1 Positions of the Coronary Artery Ostia In this chapter, we describe the anatomy of the left and right coronary ostia. The classical anatomical literature describes the origins of the left and right coronary arteries (LCA and RCA, respectively) as being positioned centrally in the middle of the left and the right coronary sinuses, respectively. Considering the blood supply area of the LCA, which in most cases includes the sternocostal surface and left lateral surface of the heart, one would expect that the artery would take its origin from the anterior or left lateral part of the left coronary sinus, and not from the central part of the coronary sinus, as it is present in most cases. Taking its origin from the left coronary sinus, the left main branch (LMB) of the LCA runs in its initial phase behind the pulmonary trunk. The direction of the LMB is straightforward, toward the sternocostal surface of the heart. According to its course, the LMB may be divided into following parts. The first segment is found in the left coronary groove and is positioned just behind the posterior wall of the pulmonary root; this is the retropulmonary segment. Note that the left coronary groove is bordered anteriorly by the pulmonary root and posteriorly by the left atrium. The second segment of the LMB may be identified leaving the posterior wall of the pulmonary root. This segment is still positioned in the left coronary groove and may stretch between the pulmonary root and the anterior interventricular sulcus. This second segment is also known as the sternocostal segment of the LMB. The length of this segment varies widely. Normally, the LMB branches just behind of the pulmonary trunk so that the sternocostal segment is absent. If the LMB reaches the sternocostal surface of the heart and runs, without branching, into the left anterior descending artery (LAD) and the circumflex artery (Cx), into the anterior interventricular sulcus, we call this the long LMB. On the other hand, the RCA, after its origin from the right coronary sinus, initially passes through the groove, which is bordered anteriorly by the posterior wall of the infundibulum and posteriorly by the right atrium. This groove is also known as the right coronary groove. Leaving this area, the RCA enters the right coronary sulcus, where it initially runs around the anterior part of the tricuspid valve toward the acute margin of the right ventricle. Considering the blood supply area of the RCA, which in normal cases includes the right side of the heart, it would be appropriate for its origin to be positioned on the right side of the right coronary sinus. For better understanding of the positions of the left and right coronary ostia in the wall of sinuses of Valsalva, the positions of the coronary artery ostia were investigated in the horizontal and vertical planes. 4.1.1.1 Horizontal Plane To describe the position of the coronary ostia in the horizontal plane, the circumference of the aortic root was divided in a clockwise direction into three areas corresponding to the position of the left, right, and noncoronary sinuses, respectively. The three main marking lines, which also indicate the coaptation of the leaflets, were positioned at 0, 120, and 360° (Fig. 4.1a, b). Note that these reference lines also indicate the borders between the three sinuses, see the corresponding drydissected specimen (Fig. 4.1c). The aortic root is viewed from the superior view. The noncoronary sinus is positioned posteriorly; left coronary sinus is seen on the left, and the right coronary sinus on the right (Fig. 4.1c). The drawing of the heart (Fig. 4.1a) shows the situation schematically. At this point of the discussion, we must note that this arrangement, as seen on the presented schematic drawing, does not correspond 100% to the situation in the native aortic root, in that in native hearts the three sinuses do not show symmetrical morphology. The right coronary sinus is the largest, followed by the noncoronary sinus and the left coronary sinus. As such, the aforementioned divisions between the sinuses are not precisely at 0, 120, and 360°. See also the dry-dissected specimen (Fig. 4.1c), where the asymmetry of the three sinuses is presented clearly. However, from the didactic point of view, we will describe these three sinuses as symmetrical structures (Fig. 4.1a, b; the left side of the heart is marked in red and the right side in blue). Moreover, each sinus is divided into three parts, as depicted in the schematic drawing of the aortic root, viewed form the superior aspect; note that the left coronary sinus is shown in red, the right in blue, and the noncoronary sinus in gray (Fig. 4.1b). The three aforementioned areas in each sinus are also defined by three reference lines. Central position of the right coronary artery (RCA) ostium 4.1.1.2 Vertical Plane To facilitate the discussion of the coronary ostium in the vertical plane, the sinus wall was divided into the superior, middle, and inferior thirds. This division is presented on the schematic drawing shown in Fig. 4.4. Here, the aortic root wall was dissected in the vertical plane, and the wall of the sinus is inspected from a lateral view. The wall of the sinus of Valsalva was divided in a vertical direction into superior, inferior, and middle levels. The superior level is beyond the sinotubular junction, the inferior third includes the base of the aortic root, and the middle part is positioned between the superior and inferior levels (Fig. 4.4). In cases where the coronary ostium is positioned in the superior third, we describe it as being a high-positioned ostium. In the middle third, the coronary ostium is described as normal and in the inferior third as a deep-positioned ostium (Fig. 4.4). The position of the coronary artery origin in the vertical plane influences the anatomy of the ostium, such that if the origin of the coronary artery is positioned in the middle of the sinus wall, the opening of the coronary artery meets the wall of the aortic root, in most cases at 90°. This results in a smooth, round ostium, without any sharp incisures (see Fig. 4.5). On the specimen shown (Fig. 4.5a), we present an isolated aortic root that was transected in a vertical direction. The dissection plane runs through the middle of the noncoronary sinus and the anterior intervalvular triangle. Note the small labeled drawing on Fig. 4.4, where the dashed line indicates the run off of the dissection plane (Fig. 4.5b). The noncoronary sinus and the right coronary sinus are inspected from the left lateral view (see the arrow on Fig. 4.5b). The single ostium of the RCA emerges centrally from the sinus wall; a smooth round ostium is the result (Fig. 4.5). Where the origin of the RCA is positioned at the inferior third, special care must be taken during the implantation of an artificial prosthesis; after the placement of the prosthesis, the sewing ring or the placing pledget may occlude the ostium. In our series we found no such deeply positioned coronary ostia; however, McAlpine did report a case of a deep right coronary ostium. 4.1 General Anatomy 165

An anterolateral view of the left coronary sinus presented in Fig. 4.7; note that the opening of the LCA is positioned in the superior third of the aortic root wall. The dissection plane of the aortic root passes thought the middle of the LMB and the right intervalvular triangle. The LMB is inspected from the lateral aspect. Note that the LMB subtends a sharp angle with the lateral wall of the left coronary sinus; consequently, the main axis of the artery is directed inferiorly and closes during its run off at an angle of 45° with the aortic wall. Furthermore, the opening of the LCA has a high position in the frontal plane. Both aforementioned morphological situations result in an incisure at the inferior margin of the left coronary ostium. Note also that at the aortic root base, at the level of the hinge area of the aortic valve leaflets part of the left fibrous trigone is easy to identify. In this case, the very prominent structure contains some cartilage elements. This is an exception for the human heart, and it is well known that the cartilage tissue cannot be identified even with histological methods. However, in this case the cartilage tissue can be seen with the unaided eye (Fig. 4.7). 166 4 Coronary Arteries

text: a b c d e f g The ostium of the RCA is in most cases positioned in the middle of the right sinus wall The origin of the RCA, which is positioned in the superior third of the right sinus wall, was a very rare finding in our series. In the case presented, the RCA originates from the level of the sinotubular junction (Fig. 4.8). An inferior incisure can be seen at the ostium of the right coronary sinus. Note that discrete calcification plaques are present at the inferior part of the ostium; this phenomenon may be a result of the impaired flow through the elevated coronary ostia and consequent generation of the additional turbulence. The generation of turbulence downstream may result in atherosclerosis, which is registered at the opening of the coronary artery (Fig. 4.8). However, the presence of this morphological variation has further clinical significance. The superiorly positioned ostium may be injured during cross-clamping of the aorta or during dissection, by an inferiorly positioned aortotomy. 4.1.1.3 Ectopic Location of the Coronary Ostia In this part of the chapter we will describe the ectopic origins of the LCA and the RCA. Corresponding schematic drawings are presented in Fig. 4.9. The LAD may arise from the initial part of the RCA. After its origin, the artery crosses the anterior wall of the infundibulum, running toward the interventricular sulcus (Fig. 4.9a). On reaching the sternocostal surface and the anterior interventricular sulcus, the LAD runs as seen in normal cases. The course of the artery on the pulmonary trunk may follow varying courses from the very high position to a very deep placing. In the very high position, the LAD crosses the pulmonary root base, and in very deep position it crosses the lower part of the right ventricular outflow tract. These morphological variants are shown in Fig. 4.9a. It has been postulated that this variant is found more frequently in tetralogy of Fallot than in normal hearts. Note that the relationship between the LAD and the infundibulum is important when performing reconstruction of a pulmonary stenosis. There is always a risk of damaging this vessel when performing a right ventriculotomy, especially if the LAD runs beyond the pulmonary root. The RCA may take its origin from the left coronary sinus just lateral to the origin of the LCA (Fig. 4.9b). In this morphological variant, the ostium of the RCA is in most cases positioned in the right third of the left coronary sinus. The LCA runs out from the left part of the coronary sinus. To reach the right ventricle, the RCA runs between the pulmonary and aortic roots (Fig. 4.9b). Fig. 4.8. High-positioned RCA ostium Fig. 4.9. text: The LCA may also have an ectopic origin. Its origin from the right coronary sinus is seen in Fig. 4.9c. In this morphological variant, the LCA originates from the right coronary sinus. As compared to the RCA, the origin of the LCA is usually positioned just superior and to the left part of the right coronary sinus. Note that the LMB is relatively long, and after its origin runs between the pulmonary and aortic roots. On reaching the sternocostal surface of the left ventricle, the LMB divides into the LAD and the Cx. The supply areas of the LAD and Cx are not different from that of an LCA with a normal origin. Note that with this kind of morphological variant, damage to the LCA during a low-positioned aortotomy may have lethal consequences. In the following case there is no effective LCA (Fig. 4.9d) and the LAD and the Cx take their origins from different morphological structures. The LAD arises directly from the left coronary sinus. It runs straight from its origin toward the anterior interventricular sulcus. The Cx takes its origin from the initial part of the RCA. The RCA originates from the right coronary sinus, as in the normal case. The Cx, which actually has an ectopic origin in this case, initially runs just around the attachment of the tricuspid valve; more specifically, between the right coronary sinus and the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve (Fig. 4.9d). On reaching the level of the noncoronary sinus, the Cx encircles the whole aortic root from behind and runs between the attachment of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve and the non- and left coronary sinuses, in front of the right and left atria. On reaching the left fibrous trigone, the artery turns into the left part of the coronary sinus on the lateral wall of the left ventricle toward the posterior interventricular groove. In the following case (Fig. 4.9e), the Cx takes its origin from the initial part of the RCA and then has a course similar to that described in the previous case. The LAD arises directly from the right coronary sinus (Fig. 4.9e). The LAD in its initial course crosses the infundibulum anteriorly, and then runs toward the interventricular groove. On reaching the anterior interventricular groove, the artery runs in a standard manner toward the apex of the heart. In this morphological variant, the entire sternocostal surface of the heart is supplied by the LAD, including both the left and right ventricles. Note that the diagonal branch, which supplies the lateral surface of the left ventricle, takes its origin directly from the left coronary sinus. The septal branch takes its origin from the diagonal branch; on Fig. 4.9e, the septal branch is depicted as the first large branch of the diagonal branch. In the following case the Cx and the LAD take their origin from the LMB (Fig. 4.9f). The large LMB takes its origin from the right coronary sinus, initially running between the aortic root and the tricuspid valve in front of the left and right atria. Finally, the LMB reaches the sternocostal surface of the heart, where it branches into the LAD and Cx (Fig. 4.9f). In the final case, the LAD and the Cx originate separately from the right coronary sinus, and the course of the Cx is similar to that of the LMB described in the previous case (Fig. 4.9g). Note that the in the retroaortal position of the Cx, as described for the cases shown in Fig. 4.9d–g, it runs between the mitral and aortic wall annuli. This special position of the artery means that it may be damaged during the implantation of a mitral or aortic valve, due to the deeply positioned sutures. This is especially true for mitral valve implantation; it is well known that the origin of the left atrium and the course of the artery in such cases are coterminous. To avoid damage to the Cx, coronary angiograms must be performed and investigated just prior to the surgical intervention. Thus, the position of the retroaortal Cx may be identified, especially in the right anterior oblique (RAO) view of the left ventriculogram. As described previously, the coronary arteries may exhibit three separate origins. In the normal anatomical case, there may also be a third coronary artery beneath the RCA and LCA that originates separately from the aortic root. This third additional coronary artery is positioned mostly in the right coronary sinus. In our series, the left coronary sinus did not possess an additional ostium; an additional ostium was observed in 55% of the 200 investigated hearts. Of these 110 cases, the second ostium belonged to the conus artery in 99 (90%). According to the definition, the conus artery is a supernumerary artery that originates from the right coronary sinus as an independent artery and runs toward the pulmonary conus. Hadziselimovic found this artery in 62% of investigated cases; he reported that the artery in most cases takes its origin just in front of the opening of the RCA, as shown in Fig. 4.10. On the demonstrated specimen, the heart is transected in the oblique plane and the right sinus is viewed from the left lateral side. Note the large origin of the RCA; the conus artery is in front of the RCA origin. The dissection line is through the anterolateral and posterolateral commissures of the tricuspid valve, running in the oblique direction, separating the right coronary sinus from the rest of the aortic root. The musculature seen beyond the aortic and pulmonary roots belongs to the interventricular septum. Note that the first septal artery and its origin from the LAD have been exposed in an oblique plane. The initial part of the LAD was brought into view in its frontal plane. The origin of the first septal artery is also exposed in its frontal axis. Note that it is very important to differentiate between the conus artery and the conus branch, which takes its origin from the RCA. In the following specimen (Fig. 4.11), the initial part of the RCA and the right coronary sinus are exposed. The RCA was filled with the red-colored gelatin. Note that in this case three separate arteries take their origin from the right coronary sinus. The conus artery originates from the left lateral part of the right coronary sinus. The conus artery runs along the border between the pulmonary root and muscular part of the infundibulum on its convex surface. Near to the conus artery, the first preventricular artery takes its origin from the right coronary sinus; this artery is medial to the conus artery and runs along the surface of the infundibulum toward the sternocostal area of the right ventricle. After its origin, the artery passes just inferior to the left atrial appendage, entering the left anterior segment of the coronary sulcus. On the presented specimen, the origin of the Cx is seen from left lateral view (Figs. 4.28 and 4.29). The Cx is divided along its course into three segments: proximal, middle, and distal (Fig. 4.29). Note that the anterior interventricular branch continues in the direction of the LMB and the Cx runs to the left; its origin is almost under 90°. Immediately after its origin, the Cx artery gives off a large branch, which supplies the anterolateral aspect of the left ventricle. In cardiosurgical nomenclature, the branches of the Cx that supply the anterolateral aspect of the left ventricle are labeled “obtuse marginal branches” (OMBs). If the OMB arises from the proximal segment of the Cx, we refer to the first OMB. Note that on the presented case there is a large first OMD. The third OMB originates from the posterior segment of the Cx (see also Fig. 4.28). Thus, when this artery is positioned at the level of the left ventricular margin, it is also known as the marginal branch of the Cx. Note that in the presented specimen a large atrial branch originates from the proximal part of the Cx. This branch runs along the anterior wall of the left atrium, crossing the origin of the left appendage. The left conus branch, which is a very rare morphological entity that arises from the superior third of the LAD, is identified here (Fig. 4.28). After reaching the margin of the infundibulum, the left conus branch divides into two arteries, the anterior and posterior branches. This topographical situation will be discussed later. In some case, the first OMB runs diagonally, toward the posterior wall of the left ventricle. In this case, the artery supplies the diaphragmal surface of the left ventricle. 178 4 Coronary Arteries
