Circumflex artery as a branch of the RCA Morphological Variant of the Cx Originating from the RCA This variant is shown on Fig. 4.40, in which the specimen is viewed from the superior anterior direction to expose the course of the Cx; the pulmonary root has been retracted away from the aortic root. The anomalous Cx arises from the initial part of the RCA. At first the artery courses just above the attachment of the tricuspid valve and the right atrium to the membranous part of the septum. This part is just in front and to the right of the intervalvular triangle. The artery then winds around the bottom of the aortic root; this corresponds to the noncoronary sinus segment, crosses the right fibrous trigone, and continues across the left fibrous trigone to terminate on the left lateral wall of the left ventricle. The relationship between the artery and the tricuspid valve, mitral valve, and aortic root is very clear. Note that the vessel may be injured by a deeply placed suture during valve placement or in the placement of a patch to close a primary septum defect. Due to its position between the mitral and aortic annuli, the artery may be entrapped following dual valve replacement. The incidence of this type of arterial variation has been reported to be as high as 0.07–0.35%. This relatively high rate of occurrence is an additional reason why coronary arteriography should be undertaken just prior to the operation. 4.1.3.2 Branches of the LAD The LAD is a branch of the LMB. In some special cases the artery may arise from the RCA or directly from the left coronary sinus. In most cases, the bifurcation of the LMB is posterior to the pulmonary trunk; in this case, the part of the LAD that originates from the LMB is positioned posterior to the pulmonary trunk and is termed the retropulmonary segment. In the case of a direct origin from the left coronary sinus or a short LMB, the LAD may even be traced to the left coronary sinus. In the case of a very long LAD, the proximal third of the artery runs between the pulmonary trunk and the anterior wall of the left atrium. In the anterior interventricular sulcus, the artery courses downward toward the apex, as described for classic cases. In most cases the artery reaches the apex and then courses beyond the apex of the heart, terminating on the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle. For a better morphological understanding of the arterial course and its relationship to the left and right heart, the artery was divided into three segments: the superior, middle, and inferior thirds. This division corresponds to the segments of the anterior interventricular sulcus. In the retropulmonary position, the LAD in most cases does not have branches. In the anterior interventricular sulcus, the LAD gives off superficial and deep branches. The superficial branches run toward the sternocostal surface of the left and/or right ventricles. The branches to the sternocostal surface of the left ventricle are termed diagonal branches. The deep branches run in the interventricular septum and are termed septal perforating branches. The course of the LAD is presented on the presented dry-dissected specimen in Fig. 4.41, in which the heart is viewed from the left anterolateral aspect. The LMB is very short and divides into three vessels, the LAD, the Cx, and the first diagonal branch (D1). A relatively short LMB results in a long LAD. In Fig. 4.42 LAD gives of three diagonal branches, which run along the sternocostal surface of the left ventricle. D3 originates from the inferior third of the LAD and D2 originates from the superior third of the LAD and may be termed a high diagonal branch. Note that D2 and D3 run laterally on the anterolateral aspect of the left ventricle. D1 originates from the fork between the LAD and Cx, as the third branch of the LMB. According to the classical anatomical nomenclature, the diagonal branch is defined as a branch of the main LCA that arises from the fork formed by the Cx and the LAD. In anatomical reports, it has been postulated that the artery is the third branch of the LMB. Trifurcation of the LCA was postulated to occur in 58–60% of cases. However, the surgical nomenclature also uses the term diagonal branch for the lateral branches of the LAD running to the anterior aspect of the left ventricle (Fig. 4.42). We have also followed this rule; however, in a strictly anatomical manner, the diagonal arteries should be directed anteroinferiorly or posteroinferiorly. The branches that descend in the lateral or the posterolateral direction should be labeled the anterolateral branches. However, for a better and clearer understanding of the nomenclature, the lateral branches of the LAD and the third artery of the LMB have been labeled diagonal branches. Furthermore, we classified these arteries according to their origin and course. D1 is used to describe the third branch of the LMB or the artery arising from the LAD; D2 refers to the arteries arising from the middle part, and D3 to those arising from the inferior third of the LAD. One should also note that the Cx in some cases gives off arteries to the anterolateral surface of the left ventricle. If they arise just in front of the left marginal branch in terms of crossing to the left margin, these arteries are labeled OMBs (Fig. 4.43). 4.1 General Anatomy 185

The artery is vulnerable to damage during mobilization of the pulmonary root. 4.1.4 Branches of the RCA The RCA in normal anatomical cases originates from the right coronary sinus. The relationship between the sinus and the initial part of the coronary artery has already been discussed. The initial part of the RCA is positioned just behind the pulmonary trunk, in the space between the right atrium, the right coronary sinus, and the pulmonary trunk. This virtual cavity is also known as the right coronary fossa. After a short course in the right coronary fossa, the artery reaches the right distal segment of the coronary sulcus, where it runs toward the right margin of the right ventricle to reach the posterior interventricular sulcus. According to its position, the RCA may be divided into three segments. The first, or initial segment is positioned in the right coronary fossa. The next part is termed the anterior segment of the RCA; it begins at the point where the RCA enters the coronary sinus and courses to the right acute margin. Note that this anterior segment enters the coronary sinus just in front of the anterolateral leaflet of the tricuspid valve, and is thus in very close contact with the annulus fibrosus. As it continues, when the anterior segment approaches the marginal area, it is even further displaced away from the annulus. Finally, at the right margin it is just superior and anterior to the tricuspid valve. The third part of the RCA is to be found between the acute margin and the posterior descending sulcus. This part of the coronary artery is not so closely related to the annulus fibrosus of the tricuspid valve; in most cases it is just inferior to the tricuspid valve. The anterior segment of the RCA is presented in the specimen shown in Fig. 4.52, which shows an anterior view of the heart. Note a very small right conus branch, which runs at the border between the pulmonary artery and the conal part of the right ventricle. This is at the junction between the musculature and the arterial substance. This right conus artery is connected directly to the left conus artery, and as such they create an anastomosis ring surrounding the pulmonary root (Fig. 4.52). The conus branch must be differentiated from the conus artery. The artery originates as an independent artery from the right coronary sinus; by contrast, the conus branch originates directly from the initial part of the RCA. A large preventricular branch may be seen on the presented specimen (Fig. 4.52). This branch supplies the anterior wall of the right ventricular outflow tract. In most cases the branch originates from the initial part of the RCA. In the presented specimen, the preventricular branch divides into one major and one smaller artery (Fig. 4.52). The superior branch with its two subdivisions delivers the blood to the outflow part of the right ventricle. The main larger branch, which is an extension of the preventricular branch, runs toward the apex. Note that during its course, the artery penetrates the musculature of the infundibulum (Fig. 4.52). At the level of the right acute margin, a large acute marginal branch arises from the RCA. In classical anatomical nomenclature, this artery is also known as the right marginal branch. The morphology of the termination is very important because, in the case of proximal obstruction of the RCA, for example, the surgeons brings the graft to the RCA on the crux or just to the right of the crux. However in some cases, to achieve optimal revascularization, it is advisable to bring the anastomosis on the posterior descending artery (PDA) or to the left ventricular posterolateral branches of the RCA. This is especially true if multiple small, nongraftable distal branches of the RCA are present, if the PDA is large, or in the case when the posterolateral branch of the RCA on the left ventricle is larger then the PDA. We will first discuss the relative size of the PDA and of the right posterolateral branch (Fig. 4.56, part 1). As presented in Fig. 4.56, part 1a, the RCA terminates in multiple small arteries. Note that there is no graftable large branch. The PDA is also presented as a small branch that supplies just the superior third of the fourth groove. text: Great cardiac vein Great cardiac vein Left marginal vein 4.1.6 Coronary Veins 4.1.6.1 Anatomy of the Coronary Veins The cardiac veins may be divided into three groups. The largest system, which collects a major amount of venous blood from the left ventricle and ends with the coronary sinus, opens into the right atrium. The second system of cardiac veins gathers venous blood from the right twothirds of the right ventricle and ends in the right atrium. The third is the system of the Thebessian veins, and comprises small veins that drain different portions of the right atrium and ventricle and empty directly and individually into these chambers. The internal openings, the foramina venarum minimarum, are best seen at the atrial septal wall. The anterior view of a dry-dissected specimen seen in Fig. 4.65 presents the course of the great cardiac vein. The vein emerges from the inferior third of the anterior interventricular sulcus and runs toward the left coronary fossa. Note that a large branch from the anterolateral surface of the left ventricle provides venous drainage. This is the so-called anterolateral vein, which opens into the great cardiac vein. On reaching the lateral wall of the pulmonary trunk, the great cardiac vein turns to the left and enters the left lateral extremity of the coronary sulcus. This is presented in Fig. 4.66, wherein the specimen is inspected from the left lateral view; note that the left auricle covers the vein. Running beyond the left auricle, the vein reaches the margin of the left ventricle, and just beyond the obtuse margin the great cardiac vein opens into the coronary sinus. This transition is seen in the dry-dissected specimen in Fig. 4.66 and on the corresponding schematic drawing in Fig. 4.67. Fig. 4.65. The great cardiac vein Fig. 4.66. Embryologically, the vein develops from the left superior cardinal vein, and in some cases persists in adults as the left superior vena cava. The latter is commonly associated with congenital defects such as tetralogy of Fallot (with an incidence of 20%) and Eisenmenger’s syndrome (with an incidence of 8.3%), and is frequently an isolated malformation that receives the hemi-azygos vein. In the dry-dissected hearts shown in Figs. 4.66 and 4.68, the relatively large marginal vein is seen; this vessel collects the venous drainage from the lateral left ventricular wall, running at the obtuse margin and finally opening into the coronary sinus. 200 4 Coronary Arteries

Angiogram of the heart veins According to the literature, the right marginal vein is also connected to the small cardiac veins, as demonstrated on the schematic drawing in Fig. 4.75. However, we were unable to find this kind of connection in our series. The importance of the conus vein must be discussed relative to the conus artery (see Fig. 4.75). It has been postulated that these two vessels play an important role in the development of the arteriovenous collaterals. This is especially true in the case of occlusive vascular diseases. These veins may be misinterpreted as arterial branches in coronary angiograms of the arteriovenous anastomosis in such cases (Fig. 4.75). Furthermore, when properly developed this vein can communicate with the anterior large vein. The same can be postulated for the small cardiac veins, which can create the anastomosis between the coronary sinus and the venous drainage of the right heart (see Fig. 4.75). A venous angiogram was made by injection of contrast material into the coronary sinus. The coronary sinus collects the entire venous drainage from the left ventricle via the great and middle cardiac veins (Fig. 4.76). In addition, the left marginal and posterolateral veins contribute to the left ventricular venous drainage. The small cardiac vein is present as a small vein that opens into the terminal part of the coronary sinus. Note the anatomy of the large marginal coronary vein. This anatomical situation may be of clinical importance. With the aid of retrograde cardioplegia, the injected fluid only provides protection to the left ventricular muscles. Thus, the veins of the right ventricle do not communicate with the coronary sinus, and so the cardioplegia can not reach the right half of the heart. This may be related to the variable venous anatomy of the heart; because the anterior region of the right ventricle is not drained by the coronary sinus, and it is not uncommon for the heart to have several coronary sinus anomalies, there may be a heterogeneous distribution of cardioplegic solutions, thus limiting myocardial protection. As a consequence, a technique for simultaneously delivering cardioplegia both antegradely and retrogradely has been developed. 204 4 Coronary Arteries

It should be noted that the small venous branches providing the drainage of the right and left ventricles may cross the LAD anteriorly before joining the great vein. This may have some clinical consequences; namely, during surgical exposure of the LAD, the small branches may be a source of annoying bleeding. However, it has been postulated that in most cases the great cardiac vein runs on the right side of the artery, or in some cases there may even be two venous branches commencing from the left and right sides of the LAD. In other cases, the course of the anterior great cardiac vein lies over the LAD, as seen in Fig. 4.78. This morphological situation may be annoying during exposure of the artery. This is especially true when the epicardium is covered by a large amount of fat tissue, in which case the surgeon may mistake the vein for the artery and bypass the conduit graft to the vein. However, such a misinterpretation may also be the result of the intramural position of the LAD, as presented on the in situ dry-dissected specimen in Fig. 4.78, wherein the proximal part of the LAD is covered by the musculature of the left ventricle. The great cardiac vein runs on the left side of the retropulmonary part of the LAD; on reaching the termination of the anterior sulcus, the vein turns to the left toward the coronary sulcus. In most cases, the vein crosses the Cx superiorly in the left coronary fossa. This situation is seen in Figs. 4.79 and 4.80. Note that at the initial part of the coronary sinus, the vein has a very close relationship with both the left atrium and the mitral valve. Here, the Cx is positioned under the great cardiac vein, on edge of the left ventricular ostium (Figs. 4.79 and 4.80). In this morphological situation, the artery cannot be identified at this level. However, on reaching the area of the obtuse margin, the vein runs smoothly from the level of the ventricular wall to the wall of the left atrium. As a consequence, the Cx becomes superficial and may be easily identified just inferior to the coronary sinus. This anatomical situation is seen in Fig. 4.80. Note that the aforementioned anatomical relationships may be particularly important clinically; the great vein reaches the ostium of the left ventricle at the level of the left fibrous trigone, thus the vein is prone to injury during mitral or aortic valve surgery. In the presented drawing, the vein runs just lateral to the LAD and superficial to the Cx. In some cases the vein may interdigitate with both the LAD and the Cx. Intraoperative identification of the loop formation in this area obviously discourages cardiac surgeons from performing bypass surgery at the initial part of the LAD and Cx. 206 4 Coronary Arteries

The position of the coronary sinus ostium also influences the course of the posterior coronary vein. Namely, a right-sided ostium results in a right-sided posterior cardiac vein, and vice versa, relative to the posterior interventricular sulcus. Venous system of the heart, overview A summary of the main venous branches of the heart is given schematically in Fig. 4.83, in which the heart is inspected from a superior view; the left and right atria have been removed and the coronary sinus retracted. The small cardiac and posterior cardiac veins empty into the terminal part of the coronary sinus. The coronary sinus is the most constant feature of the cardiac veins, and on average measures 40 mm in length and 10 mm in diameter. The posterior part of the left ventricular ostium is most clearly observed in the venous phase of the coronary angiogram. Vieussens’ valve is present in most cases, but is incompetent. The posterior vein of the left ventricle is positioned at the diaphragmal surface of the left ventricle and is present in 75% of cases. This vein empties into the coronary sinus in 95% of cases. The oblique vein of the left atrium terminates at the junction of the great cardiac vein and the coronary sinus. This vein is found posterior to the left auricle and anterior to the left inferior pulmonary vein. The left marginal vein is positioned at the obtuse margin and is often parallel to the left marginal branch. The great cardiac vein is positioned in the anterior interventricular groove. This part is also called the vertical part of the great cardiac vein. On reaching the left coronary fossa, the vein turns toward the coronary sulcus and takes off in a horizontal direction, passing the left auricle and then continuing into the coronary sinus. The anterior and posterior interventricular veins are positioned at the interventricular grooves; at the apex, both are connected to the left marginal and left posterior coronary veins, and in some cases with the right marginal vein. Finally, the anterior venous drainage of the right heart comprises three to six veins that transport the venous blood of the anterior wall of the right ventricle. The anterior cardiac veins cross the coronary sulcus, and any of them may empty as separate vessels into the right atrium. The veins may empty into a common venous lake, which definitively opens into the anterior aspect of the right atrium. The conus vein is very important and is one of the small cardiac veins, which open directly into the coronary sinus. Bibliography 1. Adachi S (1928) Das Arteriensystem der Japaner. In this section we interpret the most commonly used radiographic views in coronary angiography. Parallel to the native coronary angiogram, special three-dimensional drawings are presented. Each drawing views the corresponding heart from the same perspective as that seen on the coronary angiogram. In addition, the topography of the counterpart coronary artery will be discussed. The relationships between the vessels and the positions of the mitral and tricuspid valves are also discussed. Fig. 4.84. Anteroposterior projection of LCA 4.1.7.1 Left Coronary Artery Anteroposterior Projection An anteroposterior (AP) view of the LCA is presented on a coronary angiogram in Fig. 4.84; a corresponding schematic drawing is given in Fig. 4.85. This view is not commonly obtained because the spine sits in the middle of the cineangiographic picture. In this particular view, the LCA lies directly in front of the spinal column. The similarities in radiographic density between the spine and the contrast-filled coronary vessels interfere with the quality of the images. However, it is obtained occasionally when the location and severity of a stenosis cannot be clearly defined using conventional views. The AP view may be of particular value in evaluating the ostium of the main LCA and the shaft of the medial part of the LAD. In other words, the X-ray camera is directly above the patient’s chest, with the beam coming straight up from the X-ray tube and perpendicular to the patient. The LMB and the ostium of the LCA are best seen in this view. Main branch stenoses in particular are in some cases detectable only in this projection; this is especially true for LMBs with a horizontal axis (see Fig. 4.84). The schematic drawing in Fig. 4.85 presents an AP projection of the heart, and will be used to discuss the topography of the LCA as compared to the other important landmarks of the heart. Note that the RCA is also depicted on Fig. 4.85a. In the AP projection, the LMB travels in a horizontal direction and is posterior to the pulmonary root, and later to the left and superior to the aortic root (Fig. 4.85). The LAD runs in its superior segment in a diagonal direction, to the left and inferior. In its distal segment, the artery is almost parallel to the vertebral column (Figs. 4.84 and 4.85). Note that the obtuse margin and the left marginal branch are lateral to the aorta and are positioned to the left relative to the LAD and the anterior interventricular groove (Figs. 4.84 and 4.85). The marginal branch runs in the same direction as the initial part of the LAD (Figs. 4.84 and 4.85). The initial part of the Cx is directed to the left and posteroinferiorly to the LAD; it is seen running straight down in this plane (Figs. 4.84 and 4.85). On reaching the obtuse margin, the posterior part of the Cx turns to the right and runs in a diagonal direction toward the posterior interventricular groove (Fig. 4.85). This segment of the Cx indicates the position of the posterior mitral valve annulus. The branches running to the posterior wall of the left ventricle are best seen here (Figs. 4.84 and 4.85). The posterior descending artery, which indicates the position of the posterior interventricular groove, is to the right and inferior to the anterior interventricular groove. Its course is parallel to the obtuse margin of the left ventricle, which means that the artery travels in the same direction as the OMB. Note that the tricuspid ostium is superior to the mitral valve. Straight LAO Projection In the LAO position, the camera of the X-ray tube is to the left of the patient. The “straight” LAO view of the LCA is limited by overlap and foreshortening of the proximal vessels, particularly the Cx system. However, a steep (50–60°) view may be of value in studying the middle and distal parts of the LAD and the diagonal arteries. To facilitate further investigation of the other vessels, the camera may also be pivoted toward or away from the patient’s head, a position that is described as cranial or caudal, respectively. 4.1 General Anatomy 211

text: 4.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Coronary Arteries 4.2.1 Median Sternotomy for Exposure of the Coronary Arteries A median sternotomy is performed following the technique described in Chap. 2, exposing the anterior layer of the pericardium. Initially the prepericardial fat tissue, which is an embryological remnant of the thymus, must be dissected down to the fibrous layer of the pericardium. The thymus vein, which is almost always found in this tissue, drains into the left brachiocephalic vein. This small vein is a good indicator of the border between the left and right thymus lobes. We suggest ligation of the small vein so that the prepericardial fat tissue can be pushed aside and the anterior layer of the pericardium may be reached without any annoying bleeding. The exposed anterior layer of the pericardium is presented in Fig. 4.100. In the standard approach pericardium is exposed up from the brachiocephalic vein down to the diaphragm. In the presented situation (Fig. 4.100), the whole anterior sheet of the pericardium is exposed to allow a more descriptive view. Note the position of the left brachiocephalic vein. The pericardial incision should be initiated at the inferior part of the pericardium, approximately two finger-breadths over the diaphragm. Using electrocauterization, the incision is extended cranially toward the Fig. 4.100. Exposure of the pericardium (the dashed line indicates the pericardial incision) left brachiocephalic vein (see Fig. 4.101). The surgeon must be aware that by reaching the base of the heart, the incision must continue over the groove positioned between the aorta and the pulmonary root. At this stage, two very important structures of the heart are vulnerable to damage. In the case of an ascending aorta aneurysm, the aorta may be incised as a result of extreme anterior bulging or due to extensive adhesions to the pericardium. On the other hand, the right auricle in some cases reaches over the sternocostal surface and may even cover the pulmonary root. The last case is especially true in the case of tricuspid insufficiency, where extensive dilatation of the right atrium may be present. The pericardial incision terminates at the level of the aortic arch, just inferior to the origin of the brachiocephalic artery. Following termination of the vertical pericardial incision, two horizontal extensions at the inferior level of the vertical incision just over the diaphragm must be performed. The right-side incision is extended in a diagonal manner to the right, toward the inferior vena cava, and the left-side incision is extended left toward the apex of the heart (Fig. 4.101). 220 4 Coronary Arteries

At the ventricular part of the heart, almost the whole sternocostal aspect is represented by the right ventricle; the left ventricle is seen only in the area near to the apex. In this superior view, the anterior segment of the LAD and the anterior part of the RCA may be identified. The anterior part of the RCA appears in the right part of the coronary sulcus just inferior to the right atrium. Note that the direction of the RCA identified in the initial part of the coronary sulk also indicates the course of the RCA in the right coronary fossa. It is not always very easy to identify the artery, as the extensive collection of epicardial fat tissue in the coronary sulk may cover its course. In the majority of cases, a large branch of the RCA may be found among the right acute margine. The artery runs along the right margin just parallel to the diaphragm, toward the apex. On passing the acute margin, the RCA enters the posterior part of the coronary sulcus. Note that the ostium and the initial part of the RCA may be found by lifting up the right auricle and retracting the infundibulum. Because of the physiological left rotation of the whole heart in this aspect, only the middle and distal segments of the LAD can be seen (Fig. 4.102; only the part of the Fig. 4.103. Exposure of right coronary artery and crux cordis LAD near to the apex is visible here). However, by lifting the left heart, half of the entire course of the LAD and the proximal part of the Cx may be seen. This maneuver may be achieved by placing a coiled operating cloth into the left pericardial hemicavity. The LAD runs just over the anterior interventricular groove on the left side of the anterior cardiac vein. In cases where there is an extensive epicardial fat collection, the position of the artery may be difficult to identify. A smooth groove in the fat tissue just over the artery may indicate its position. However, it should be pointed out that this groove is not an absolute landmark; finding the artery may be particularly difficult when it is in the intramural position. Furthermore, the surgeon must be aware that the concomitant vein in some cases runs just over the artery, mimicking the course of the LAD. In addition, if the intramural course of the artery is present, the anterior cardiac vein may be bypassed as a target artery. The heart is then rotated to the left side, exposing the posterior part of the RCA (including the PDA), as shown in Figs. 4.103 and 4.104. This may be achieved by placing pure string sutures or with the aid of special socalled suction devices. Exposure of the RCA and the posterolateral descending artery, right lateral view are thus explored. In addition, the part of the left ventricle just near to the posterior interventricular sulcus is also visible Fig. 4.104. The vessels of the aforementioned surface are thus excellently brought into view as target vessels; this exposition of the heart is in most cases appropriate for revascularization of the proximal part of the RCA, the right marginal artery, and the PDA. The right marginal branch runs along the acute margin of the right ventricle, toward the apex of the left ventricle. In most cases the artery runs alone and without the concomitant vein (Fig. 4.104), and is easy to verify. The part of the RCA, which is positioned in the diaphragmal part of the coronary sinus, is identified by searching the border between the epicardial fat tissue and the inferior border of the right atrium. The RCA is identified as an artery with a large diameter that runs in the epicardial fat tissue underneath the edge of the right atrium. In most cases, the artery may be traced down to the crux, where it turns into the posterior descending sulcus. Bear in mind the different variations of PDA origin from the RCA, as described earlier (see Sect. 4.1.4). In the case when the PDA branches off proximal to the crux, the artery is not always to be found in the posterior descending sulcus. In some cases, the PDA runs to the left or to the right of the posterior sulcus. As mentioned previously, the middle cardiac vein is found just lateral to the PDA, and in most cases on the left side and superficial to it. Note that the inferior vena cava is found entering the right atrium just anterior and inferior to the diaphragmal surface of the heart (Figs. 4.103 and 4.104). In order to expose completely all vessels on the diaphragmal surface of the left and right ventricles, the apex must be lifted from the pericardium caudally and to the right. This maneuver may be completed without problem by using an apical suction device. Furthermore, the Trendelenburg position and/or positioning the surgical towel just deep to the oblique pericardial sinus facilitates elevation of the apex out of the chest. The exposure of the diaphragmal surface of the heart is presented on Figs. 4.105–4.107, and schematically in Fig. 4.108. 4.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Coronary Arteries 223

Pericardial incision 4.2.2 Left Anterolateral Thoracotomy for Exposure of the LAD This approach has been described in Chap. 2, and as such the description here will be limited to the left anterolateral part of the thorax. The patient’s left chest wall is tilted by approximately 30° to the right. Following the chest-wall incision, the left lung is retracted, exposing the left mediastinal sheet of the pericardium (Fig. 4.109). Note that the phrenic nerve and its corresponding vessels run superiorly to the hilum of the left lung. Because of the left rotation of the heart and the left inferior position of the apex, the left phrenic nerve runs downward after passing the left hilum. The nerve is no longer superficially placed at the level of the apex, as seen clearly in Fig. 4.109. However, it can be said that the left phrenic nerve exhibits a relatively deeper course on the pericardium than the right phrenic nerve, possibly as a result of the aforementioned left rotation of the heart. The pericardial incision must be positioned approximately two finger-breadths superior to the phrenic nerve, as depicted schematically in Fig. 4.110. The pericardium must be incised widely in order to secure optimal exposure of the target vessels. It is advisable to begin with an incision over the distal end of the lung hilum, with extension just over the apex. A caudal extension of the incision must then be performed, over the left auricle and pulmonary trunk (Fig. 4.110) 226 4 Coronary Arteries

Sternocostal surface of the heart, left lateral view It is very important to remember that exposing the coronary arteries via a left anterior thoracotomy limits bypass surgery only to the coronary vessels of the anterolateral and marginal surfaces of the left ventricle. After the pericardial incision is completed, the exposure may be facilitated by positioning stay sutures and retracting the edges of the pericardium (Figs. 4.111 and 4.112). The first thing to be noted is the course of the LAD and the diagonal arteries. The LAD runs almost horizontally in the anterior interventricular sulcus. The great cardiac vein is positioned on the left side of the artery. The D2 runs approximately parallel to the artery toward the apex, and supplies the sternocostal and apical areas of the left ventricle. D1 run vertically and supply the superolateral part of the left ventricle. Note that the diagonal branches are not conjoined to the cardiac veins (Figs. 4.111 and 4.112). The proximal edge of the retracted pericardium is positioned just over the pulmonary trunk, and inferior to the greater vessel, the left appendage covers the bifurcation of the LCA (Fig. 4.112). 4.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Coronary Arteries 227

Left coronary fossa with the LAD, left main branch (LMB), and circumflex branch (Cx) Fig. 4.116. Left coronary fossa with the LAD, LMB, and Cx, schematic drawing Furthermore, instigation of an anterolateral thoracotomy provides the opportunity to inspect the LMB, the superior third of the LAD, and the initial part of the Cx (Figs. 4.115 and 4.116). The LMB is positioned in the left coronary fossa, the space between the posterior wall of the pulmonary artery, and the anterior wall of the left atrium. In the in situ situation, this area is mostly covered by the left auricle. Retraction of the left atrium exposes the left coronary fossa (Figs. 1.115 and 1.116). One should be aware that dissection and identification of the LMB in this area may be made difficult due to the positioning of the great cardiac vein, which in some cases may even be found to the left of the coronary sinus wall. However, it is always inferior to the LMB, and as such, care should be taken not to injure it during dissection of the LMB. The exposed left coronary fossa is seen in Fig. 4.115; an explanation of the morphological situation is presented in Fig. 4.116. Note that the LMB branches off into the LAD and the Cx. After passing the lateral wall of the pulmonary root, the LAD runs in the anterior interventricular sulcus. At the beginning of the sulcus, the great cardiac vein crosses the LAD as a superficial structure and is thus very hard to identify. Furthermore, the vein is often present as a double vessel, crossing the artery superiorly and inferiorly. However in this exposure, the proximal branches of the LAD and D1 may be clearly identified; consequently, this exposure helps in the localization of the anastomosis on the initial part of D1. After its origin in the left coronary fossa, the Cx continues its course in the coronary sulcus, initially covered by the great coronary vein (Fig. 4.116). This morphological condition renders dissection of the artery inadvisable in practice. 4.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Coronary Arteries 229

Pericardial incision 4.2.3 Left Anterior Thoracotomy for Exposure of the LCA Exposure of the coronary arteries using a left anterior thoracotomy limits bypass surgery to the LAD and its branches. This is a minimally invasive approach and exposure that is limited to the anterior chest wall. The left sternocostal surface of the left ventricle may be exposed by tilting the chest wall into the right side. After the thorax wall incision and insertion of the appropriate spreader, the left mediastinal sheet of the pericardium can be reached (Fig. 4.119). Due to the small incision, only a very limited segment of the pericardium is brought into view, as well as the superior part of the mediastinal pericardium (Fig. 4.119). The left phrenic nerve must be identified before making an incision into the pericardium. Compare this exposure to that described in Sect. 4.2.2, and note here that the apex and the hilum of the lung may not be visualized completely. Thus, the pericardial incision is not performed on the mediastinal sheath of the pericardium; rather, it is done on the sternocostal surface of the pericardium (Fig. 4.119 and Fig. 4.120, dashed line). Due to this limited access, only the middle and the upper parts of the sternocostal surface with their arteries are brought into view (see Figs. 4.121, 4.122, and 4.123). 4.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Coronary Arteries 231

Course of the right phrenic nerve 4.2.4 Right Anterolateral Thoracotomy for Exposure of the RCA The chest wall is opened between the sternal and anterior axillary lines with the aid of a right anterolateral incision, as described in Chap. 2; the heart is approached from the right side, exposing the right lateral surface of the right ventricle. After the thorax spreader is inserted and the right lung retracted, the right mediastinal sheet of the pericardium is reached (Figs. 4.127 and 4.128). Note the bulging of the superior vena cava visible on the cranial side of the pericardium, in most cases appearing as a transparent blue structure. The pericardial impression of the ascending aorta may be identified superior, and in some instances deep to the superior vena cava. Note that after entering the chest cavity, the right phrenic nerve runs along the pericardial surface covering the superior vena cava (Fig. 4.127). On reaching the area where the vein enters the right atrium, the nerve turns inferiorly toward the right hilum of the lung. This change of direction is seen in Fig. 4.127. Then, on reaching the superior layer of the hilum, the nerve continues its course on the right mediastinal sheet of the pericardium, running toward the diaphragm (Fig. 4.128). When it reaches the right cupule of the diaphragm, the nerve and its conjoined vessels divide into branches in the fat tissue between the pericardium and the diaphragm (Fig. 4.128). These branches run in a radial direction on the surface of the diaphragm, toward its attachment. 4.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Coronary Arteries 235

text: Left ventricle Noncoronary sinus Left coronary sinus Right ventricle Interatrial septum Tricuspid valve Right ventricle Aortic root Pulmonary root Mitral valve Left ventricle 5.1 General Anatomy of the Aortic Valve 5.1.1 Definition of the Aortic Root The aortic root is a morphological physiological unit that is composed of the sinuses of Valsalva, three leaflets, and both coronary ostia, as well the three intervalvular triangles. From a strictly morphological point of view, the intervalvular triangles belong to the outflow tract of the left ventricle; however, from a functional point of view they belong to the aortic root. Thus, the aortic root structure is a compound of two morphological parts, namely the proximal part of the ascending aorta, including the area of the three leaflets, and the terminal part of the left ventricular outflow tract. In light of this morphophysiological definition, in this chapter we will describe the detailed anatomy of aortic root. In the presented dry-dissected specimen (Fig. 5.1), the great vessels and the left and right atria have been removed and the aortic root is inspected from posterior aspect. In this view, it is clear that the non coronary sinus is in direct contact with the left and right atria. The interatrial septum in this case indicates the middle of the noncoronary sinus, and as such, it is a landmark that separates the left and right halves of the noncoronary sinus (Fig. 5.1). Note that the aortic root is positioned in the anterior half of the left ventricular ostium, and the posterior half is occupied by the opening of the mitral valve. Fig. 5.1. Posterior view of the aortic root Fig. 5.2. Posterolateral view of the aortic root, schematic drawing A posterolateral view of the aortic root is presented on the schematic drawing in Fig. 5.2, in which, for didactic reasons, the noncoronary sinus is colored in green, the right coronary sinus in blue, the left coronary sinus in red, and the interventricular triangles in yellow. This coloring of the corresponding sinuses will be used throughout this chapter. The left and right atria have been removed, and only the position of the attachments is indicated. The right coronary sinus is positioned just over the posterolateral wall of the right ventricle. The right coronary sinus may also be divided into anterior and posterior segments. The posterior segment, which is near to the noncoronary sinus, is connected directly to the anterolateral commissure of the tricuspid valve. This right half of the noncoronary sinus is positioned just over the septal leaflet and membraneus septum. The left segment is conjoined to the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. As mentioned previously the interatrial septum separates the noncoronary sinus into right and left parts. The right/anterior half of the noncoronary sinus is attached to the posterior superior area of the interventricular septum. Sinotubular junction as a superior border of the aortic root Fig. 5.4. Sinotubular junction as a superior border of the aortic root, schematic drawing mal part of the aforementioned septum. The left/posterior part of the noncoronary sinus is placed over the posterolateral commissure of the mitral valve. The right half of the left coronary sinus is anterior to the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve; only the left part of the sinus is connected directly to the left ventricular muscle (Fig. 5.2). The superior border of the aortic root is known as the sinotubular junction. This ring-like structure is positioned on the transition between the sinuses and the tubular part of the ascending aorta. A cross-section of the sinotubular junction in a dry-dissected specimen is shown in Fig. 5.3, and on the corresponding drawing (Fig. 5.4). The aortic root was transected in the frontal direction, the transection plane running through both coronary arteries. The left and right coronary sinuses have been partially removed, but the attachments of the right and left coronary arteries remain. Note that the right coronary artery has a superior horizontal axis, and the left has an inferior axis. The noncoronary sinus is viewed in the frontal direction (Fig. 5.3). The sinotubular junction is positioned at the level of the commissures, although in some cases it may be placed just beyond the three commissures. Note that the left coronary artery is placed almost at the level of the sinotubular junction, and as such, the opening of the artery may be described as having a high-positioned ostium. 5.1 General Anatomy of the Aortic Valve 247

Inferior border of the aortic root, at the level of the mitral valve attachment Fig. 5.6. Topography of the intervalvular triangles and run-off of the aortic root base The inferior border of the aortic root is defined as the aortic root base. This is also a circular structure; however, unlike the sinotubular junction, the anatomy of the aortic root base is not unique. This circular line is a combination of the intervalvular triangles (Fig. 5.5) and the nadirs of the leaflet attachments (Fig. 5.6). The posterior part of the left ventricle has been removed in the dry-dissected specimen in Fig. 5.5, in which the area of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve is inspected from the posterior aspect. The noncoronary and left coronary sinuses are seen superior to the mitral valve. The leaflets of the corresponding sinuses have been removed. The nadirs of the leaflets and the intervalvular triangle over the mitral valve together create the aortic root base (see dashed line). The intervalvular triangles are structures belonging to the left ventricle and are positioned between the attachments of the leaflets. The classical anatomical literature describes the three intervalvular triangles as left, right, and posterior. The left intervalvular triangle is positioned between the left and right coronary sinuses, just over the left ventricular musculature. The posterior intervalvular triangle is found between the left and noncoronary sinuses, and is positioned over the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. From the ventricular aspect, the border between the anterior leaflet and the intervalvular triangle is defined by the line that connects the deepest points of the noncoronary and left coronary sinuses (Fig. 5.5 dashed line). From the atrial aspect, the inferior border of the triangle is connected directly to the left atrial attachment and to the hinge line of the anterior leaflet. The right intervalvular triangle is located just over the membranous septum, between the right and noncoronary sinuses. A schematic drawing of the aortic root with special focus on the aortic root base is shown in Fig. 5.6. The line connecting the interventricular triangles and the leaflet attachments represents the virtual course of the aortic root base (Fig. 5.6). 248 5 Aortic Valve

Note that this structure was also described previously by McAlpine, and that in our series we also investigated this membranous structure in 10 hearts. Removal of the posterior intervalvular triangle and the adjacent parts of the left and noncoronary sinuses exposes the large ostium of the left ventricle; this is the so-called muscular opening of the left ventricle, and is presented in Fig. 5.11. This is the same specimen as seen on Fig. 5.9, wherein the opening of the left ventricle is inspected from the left lateral superior view. The attachment of the left and right coronary sinuses to the left ventricle has been exposed. The anterior mitral valve was excised along with the conjoined part of the aortic root, leaving only the left half of the left coronary sinus and the right half of the noncoronary sinus. Note that the entire right coronary sinus is attached to the anterior superior part of the interventricular septum. Both of these structures are connected directly to the left ventricle (Fig. 5.11). Note that the left fibrous trigone is found at the cross-section of the left coronary sinus, the right fibrous trigone is found at the cross-section of the non coronary sinus, the membranous septum and the attachment of the septal leaflet may be identified inferior to the right trigone (Fig. 5.11). It should be noted that the posterior intervalvular triangle and the adjacent parts of the left and noncoronary sinuses are not directly attached to the left ventricle in this situation (see Fig. 5.10). They are positioned between the left and right fibrous trigones, an area in which there is no solid structure to support the attachment of the aortic root. Indeed, the transition between the mitral valve and the aortic root seems to be without any macroscopically visible borders. However, the superior border of the mitral valve hinge area may be interpreted as being the only fibrous structure providing any attachment to the left atrium and aortic root. Furthermore, the left and right fibrous trigones serve as anchoring structures, providing the fixation for the mitral valve hinge region. Left posterior view of the aortic root 5.1.2 Relationship Between the Aortic Root and the Left Heart The special relationship between the root components and all four chambers of the heart will be discussed now. To achieve that, we believe it is essential to provide a detailed description of the root components and their relationship to the left and/or right halves of the heart. In this chapter, we will describe the relationship between the aortic root and the left heart, and in particular its relationship to the left ventricle and left atrium. In Fig. 5.16, the aortic root is inspected from the left posterior view. The left atrium has been removed, leaving only the part creating the left wall of the interatrial septum. Here, one can observe the left side of the oval fossa. Posterior bulging of the left and noncoronary sinuses toward the anterior wall of the left atrium is a characteristic of this specimen. The left coronary artery was dissected at the level of the left main branch. Its origin and position definitively indicate the position of the left coronary sinus. Note that the right part of the left coronary sinus and the left part of the noncoronary sinus are positioned in front and to the anterior wall of the left atrium. The posterior intervalvular triangle is positioned between two sinuses just over the middle of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. At this point we should call to mind the relationship between the noncoronary sinus and the interatrial septum, whereby the wall of the interatrial septum is positioned at the middle of the noncoronary sinus, thus indicating the middle of the sinus (Fig. 5.16). However, the atrial septum is not always placed at the middle of the noncoronary sinus, and so it may be used as a landmark between the left and right halves of the noncoronary sinus. In the case where the atrial septum is positioned behind the left half of the noncoronary sinus, or as seen in very rare cases behind the posterior interventricular triangle, the aortic root has been recorded as being left rotated. In addition, if the aortic root is right rotated, the interatrial septum is found just behind the right half of the noncoronary sinus. A smooth groove may be found just inferior to the anterior inferior part of the interatrial septum at the level of the mitral valve annulus, in front and superior to the posterolateral commissure of the mitral valve. This intussusception in the area of the annulus indicates the position of the right fibrous trigone (Fig. 5.16). Note that the fibrous trigone is placed in front of the posterior commissure of the mitral valve. Here one can see very clearly that the fibrous trigone is not in contact with the posterolateral commissure. The average distance between these two structures is about 11 mm, and they come directly into contact with the annulus only at the place where the anterior wall of the left and right atria meets and creates the anterior edge-line of the interatrial septum. Analogous to the right fibrous trigone, the incisure of the left fibrous trigone may also be found at the left side of the mitral valve annulus, in front of the anterolateral commissure (see Fig. 5.16). Note that the point at which the left fibrous trigone is attached to the left ventricular muscle corresponds to that where the left coronary sinus of the aorta very nearly approaches the mitral valve. This situation must be considered strongly when placing suture stitches during mitral valve surgery. This area of the left fibrous trigone also represents a very complex morphological entity; this is also where the left lateral ventricular muscle attaches to the interventricular septum. 254 5 Aortic Valve

Right lateral view of the aortic root 5.1.3 Relationship Between the Aortic Root and the Right Heart We will now discuss the relationship between the aortic root and the right part of the heart. To facilitate this discussion, the lateral anterior and posterior walls of the right atrium in the dry-dissected specimen have been removed (Fig. 5.21; inspected from the right lateral perspective). The septal wall and the area of the anterior interatrial sulcus have been left in situ, and so the shape and position of the right atrium may be imagined. The right and noncoronary sinuses are thus visible. The right coronary sinus is identified by the right coronary ostium and is anterior to the noncoronary sinus. The right intervalvular triangle is positioned between them. From this perspective, it is clear that the right ventricle is directly related to the right coronary sinus and to the right intervalvular triangle. Note that the posterior wall of the infundibulum is positioned in front of the right coronary sinus and in front of the anterior intervalvular triangle (Fig. 5.21). The part of the right ventricle that acts as an anchor for the right coronary sinus and the right intervalvular triangle is known as the posterolateral wall of the right ventricle (see also Fig. 5.22, dashed line). This part of the right ventricle is positioned between the infundibulum and the tricuspid valve. The morphology of the posterolateral wall of the right ventricle will be discussed later. Note that in this case the noncoronary sinus is placed in front of the interatrial sulcus (Fig. 5.21). In most cases, the attachment between the atria is positioned at the midpoint of the noncoronary sinus. If the interatrial septum is shifted to the right of the noncoronary sinus midpoint, the left coronary sinus is turned anteriorly. In this situation, the left coronary sinus has almost no contact with the left atrium; this is a right-rotated aortic root. If the interatrial septum is shifted to the left of the midline of the noncoronary sinus, the term left-rotated aortic root is used. In this case, the right coronary sinus has lost its contact to the right atrium. The left coronary sinus is rotated to the right and posteriorly, and the right coronary sinus is placed almost in a frontal direction. A superior view of the right coronary sinus and its relationship to the right ventricle is presented on the drydissected specimen in Fig. 5.22 and on the corresponding schematic drawing (Fig. 5.23). Note that the left ventricle and the left atrium have been removed. Only the anterior part of the mitral valve remains, with the corresponding attachments of the left atrium (marked as a red line posterior to the aortic root in Fig. 5.23a). The right atrium has been left in situ, and the walls of the aortic root sinuses have been removed (Fig. 5.22). The attachments of the leaflets and the commissures remain; in this way only the fibrous skeleton of the aortic root is intact. In this view, the pulmonary root and the infundibulum are anterior to the aortic root. The noncoronary sinus is marked as green, the right as blue and the left coronary sinus as red (Fig. 5.23). The posterolateral wall of the right ventricle is colored in blue (Fig. 5.23b) and, as seen here, is positioned inferior to the right coronary sinus. This segment of the right ventricle stretches from the right surface of the pulmonary root to the anterolateral wall of the right atrium (Fig. 5.23). The anterior wall of the right atrium is apposed to the right intervalvular triangle, and in part to the noncoronary sinus. The interatrial septum is viewed from the left superior aspect and, because the left atrium has been removed, it represents only the right side of the septum (Fig. 5.23). text: 5.1.4 Apposition of the Aortic Leaflets The aortic leaflets of the noncoronary sinus and of the right coronary sinus are shown in Fig. 5.27 and the corresponding drawing (Fig. 5.28). The demonstrated aortic root has been dissected in the anteroposterior plane, the dissection plane running through the middle of the noncoronary sinus and the anterior intervalvular triangle. This specimen is seen from the left lateral view. The right coronary sinus, with its leaflet, is thus exposed in the frontal direction; note that the ostium of the right coronary artery is positioned centrally. The noncoronary sinus is viewed laterally, allowing visualization of the whole structure of the coronary sinus. The structure of the leaflets is seen in both frontal and lateral aspects. Note that the aortic leaflet has two structural parts (Fig. 5.27; the drawing in Fig. 5.28 is intended for orientation). The anterior leaflet of the mitral valve is seen inferior to the noncoronary sinus. This is marked in orange, as are the walls of the sinuses, in Fig. 5.28; the superior third of the leaflet is yellow, the border between the superior and inferior parts of the leaflets is marked with a dashed line, and the left ventricular musculature underneath the right coronary sinus is marked in brown. The basal, denser part of the leaflet represents the inferior two-thirds of the leaflet length, as seen on the dry-dissected specimen (Fig. 5.27). The less dense, superior third of the leaflet is also termed the lunula and is responsible for the coaptation of the leaflets (see Fig. 5.28). The morphology of the lunula is highly variable; however, in all variants the area of the lunula is commonly reinforced by a nodule found in the middle of this loose area. This nodule is termed the nodulus Aranti, and was first described by Arantius in the 16th century. Developmental abnormalities of the lunula are common, fenestrations being the most common morphological deviations. These often occur in the area of the commissure; however, large extended fenestrations may Fig. 5.27. Apposition of the right and noncoronary leaflets Fig. 5.28. Apposition of the right and noncoronary leaflets, schematic drawing Fig. 5.29. Nodulus Aranti I Fig. 5.30. Nodulus Aranti II also be present in the inferior part of the leaflet. These may result in inadequate coaptation of the leaflets during diastole and may result regurgitation. In Fig. 5.29, the noncoronary sinus is inspected in the frontal direction. Note that the nodulus Aranti is represented here as a triangular shape. However, the node has four surfaces, one of which serves as attachment to the lunula, two serve as contact surfaces for the neighboring leaflets (these are also called ventricular surfaces), and the fourth is superior and is directed toward the ascending aorta (Fig. 5.29). In some cases these nodules may be absent, but this does not reduce the congruence of the leaflets. A magnified view of the transition between the sinus walls, the aortic leaflet, the left atrium, and the mitral valve is shown in Figs. 5.35 and 5.36. The connective tissue is mostly in the form of collagen fibers on the aortic side of the mitral valve. This tissue is a direct continuation of the collagen fibers of the left coronary sinus wall. This extension of the collagen is clearly demonstrated in Fig. 5.35. The ventricular part of the aortic leaflet is covered with a thick layer of elastic fibers, which are themselves covered with endothelium. This is seen as a loose tissue just beneath the endothelium (Fig. 5.35). This relatively thick layer continues directly into the ventricular layer of the mitral valve, which is shown here as a relatively thin elastic tissue component. The muscles arising from the left atrium are positioned over the collagen layer of the mitral valve and are found only in the superior part of the leaflet. The atrial surface of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve is a direct continuation of the atrial tissue (Figs. 5.35 and 5.36). The core of the mitral valve is collagenous tissue, which is conjoined to the collagen in the sinus wall of the aortic root. Fig. 5.36. The left part is positioned over the mitral valve and exhibits a similar structure to the left coronary sinus; the segment over the right ventricle also has the same morphology as the right coronary sinus, and this will be demonstrated later on. The middle part of the coronary sinus, which is apposed to the membranous septum, will be discussed here. The lateral view of the specimen demonstrates the noncoronary sinus and its transition into the membranous septum of the interventricular wall. The wall of the coronary sinus has already been discussed. Note that the sinotubular junction is not as prominent as in Fig. 5.33, and that the transition between the muscular and fibrous part is also positioned in the inferior third of the sinus wall. The aortic leaflet is attached at the base of the sinus wall. From here on, the membranous septum takes its origin and is anchored between the muscular septum and the noncoronary sinus (Figs. 5.37 and 5.38). On reaching the anterior segment of the right coronary sinus, the incision turns downward toward the middle point of the noncoronary sinus. The incision ends at the base of the noncoronary sinus, thus exposing the entire aortic leaflet. Incision of the pericardium 5.2.2 “J” Sternotomy for Aortic Valve Exposure The “ J” sternal incision is an alternative to total sternal splitting. It is a minimally invasive surgical approach and as such, is indicated in the majority of cases for esthetic reasons. This incision opens the sternum between the second and fourth intercostal spaces, thus exposing the superior mediastinum. However, the level superior to the left brachiocephalic vein is not exposed. The skin incision and the sternotomy are described in detail in Chap. 2. The retrosternal fatty tissue is dissected away and the anterior sheath of the pericardium is reached (Fig. 5.53). Using this exposure, the left brachiocephalic vein cannot be seen because in normal cases the vein is found at the level of the first rib. Thus, during dissection of the prepericardial fat, only the remnants of the thymic veins may be found. From the morphological standpoint, these veins cannot be traced up to the brachiocephalic vein. After the pericardium is exposed, the position of the ascending aorta may be clearly identified (Fig. 5.53). The pericardial incision is made over the ascending aorta and must be positioned slightly to the left of the aorta, almost over the sulcus between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk. This is demonstrated on the schematic drawing in Fig. 5.54. The incision is extended over the infundibulum, crossing the interventricular septum, and ends over the upper part of the border between the left ventricle and the infundibulum. From this end point, the incision is extended to the right and to the left side. The exposed ascending aorta is presented in Fig. 5.55. Fig. 5.55. The right auricle can be seen inferior and to the right of the ascending aorta. The infundibulum initially covers the aortic root from anterior; due to the left and superior axis, it may finally may be located to the left of the ascending aorta (Fig. 5.55). Note that by using this approach, the surgeon can also establish a cardiopulmonary bypass by central cannulation. The right auricle is exposed for the venous line, and the ascending aorta may be used for the aortic line. The superior vena cava may be also exposed by retracting the ascending aorta on the left lateral side, as presented in Fig. 5.56, thus enabling bicaval venous cannulation. In the presented exposure, the superior vena cava is positioned to the right of the ascending aorta. The aorta has been dissected away from its surrounding tissue and mobilized away from the anterior walls of the left and right atria. The mobilized aorta may be pulled to the left, thus revealing the entire course of the superior vena cava. The aortic incision is performed as described previously, and is demonstrated on the schematic drawing in Fig. 5.57. The “S”- shaped incision is initiated over the left coronary sinus. The aorta is incised approximately two fingerbreaths over the sinotubular junction at the left lateral surface of the aorta. On reaching the anterior surface of the aorta, the incision takes a horizontal direction. This horizontal part of the incision lies over the left and right coronary sinuses. On reaching the right convex surface of the aorta, the incision turns into the descending part. The details of this technique are described in Chap. 2. Note that the skin is incised over the superior two-thirds of the sternum, and is therefore also acceptable from the esthetic point of view. The sternotomy is performed between the jugulum and the fourth sternocostal area. From here on, the sternotomy is performed in an oblique manner toward the fourth intercostal spaces on the left and the right sides. After the sternum is split and the retrosternal space exposed, the thymic vein must be found. The case presented exhibits extensive retrosternal fat-tissue condensation (Fig. 5.70). In such cases, the orientation and identification of the left brachiocephalic vein may be very difficult. It may be easier if the thymic veins are found and traced up to their opening into the brachiocephalic vein. After the brachiocephalic vein is secured, a deeper dissection of the fat tissue may be performed in order to locate the anterior pericardial sheath. After exposure of the anterior pericardial sheath, the pericardial incision is performed in an inverse “T” fashion (as presented in Fig. 5.71). The edges of the incised pericardium are then lifted and fixed to the sternal spreader, exposing the anterior surface of the heart (Fig. 5.72). Note that the elongated ascending aorta fills almost the entire superior mediastinum. In such an elongated ascending aorta, the aortic root is normally located very deep behind the infundibulum Fig. 5.70. Exposure of the right lateral pericardial sheath following right thoracotomy 5.2.5 Anterior Thoracotomy for Aortic Valve Exposure Up to now, we have described methods in which the aortic valve and ascending aorta are approached via a sternotomy. However, the anterior thoracotomy is a very good alternative to the median approach when performing a reoperation of the aortic root or ascending aorta. The superior mediastinum is in this case exposed via a right-sided anterior thoracotomy, which is performed in the fourth intercostal space. After the skin incision is completed and the intercostal muscles are split, the right thoracic cavity is exposed. The surgical technique required to achieve this exposure is described in detail in Chap. 2. An intercostal spreader is inserted and the superior lobe of the right lung is retracted away. In this way, the right lateral sheath of the pericardium laying over the right atrium and the lateral aspect of the right ventricle may be exposed. This situation is seen on Fig. 5.77. With the consequent retraction of the right lung, the anterior part of the right hilus may also be exposed inferiorly. At first inspection, the large right atrium may be identified as it bulges out of the pericardium. The superior vena cava is found superior to the right atrium, and in normal cases also appears through the pericardial sheath. In the presented case, the fat tissue covers the area of the superior vena cava, and as such it cannot be identified as easily as the right atrium (Fig. 5.77). The course of the right phrenic nerve should be mentioned at this point; this nerve must be identified before carrying out the pericardial incision. The phrenic nerve initially runs over the right lateral surface of the superior vena cava and cannot be identified here because of fat-tissue condensation (Fig. 5.77). After the nerve leaves the area of the superior vena cava, it runs inferior to the right atrium. The pericardiacophrenic artery and vein, which accompany the nerve, must also be identified. The nerve runs straight toward to the right phrenicopericardial angle, which in the presented case is marked by an extensive accumulation of fat tissue (Fig. 5.77). 284 5 Aortic Valve

The mitral valve and the subvalvular apparatus are very important morphological and functional units, and as such are an integral part of the left ventricle. Both play an important role in left-ventricular geometry and systolic function. The details of the functional interactions between the mitral valve, the subvalvular apparatus, and the function of the left ventricle are not understood in all details. However, it appears that the annulopapillary continuity is the most important factor in this relationship. In this chapter, we will discuss the anatomy of the subvalvular apparatus, and provide a detailed description of the anatomy of the papillary muscles, chordae tendineae, and the mitral valve leaflets. The position of the papillary muscles and their relationship to the left ventricular wall is shown in a cross section of the left ventricle in Fig. 6.1, wherein the section plane is positioned at the border of the superior and the middle thirds of the left ventricular walls, and in the corresponding drawing in Fig. 6.2. The specimen is inspected from a superior view. For didactical reasons, we have divided the left ventricular musculature into three parts: the septal wall, the anterolateral wall, and the posterolateral wall. The borders between the three walls are indicated by the coronary arteries. The Fig. 6.1. Position of the papillary muscles, superior view anterior interventricular branch runs between the left and right ventricles in the anterior descending groove. This groove may also be interpreted as the anterior edge of the interventricular septum muscular part, and indicates the meeting point of the anterolateral and septal left ventricular segments. Note that at this level the muscular septum also meets the anterior wall of the right ventricles (Figs. 6.1 and 6.2). The marginal branch is positioned at the left obtuse margin, marking the border between the anterior and posterior walls. The posterior interventricular artery is positioned in the posterior interventricular sulcus, and represents the connection between the muscular septum and the posterolateral wall. However, one should be aware that the aforementioned division of the left ventricle on the septal anterior and posterior walls is only acceptable from a morphological point of view. From a mechanical point of view, the left ventricular musculature is a single functional unit. From the superior view, note that the anterior papillary muscle is positioned at the junction of the anterolateral and posterolateral walls of the left ventricle (Figs. 6.1 and 6.2). This corresponds to the left obtuse margin, which is identified by the left marginal artery. In this view, the posterior papillary muscle is found at the junction of the posterior and septal walls. The heart is viewed from the posterior superior view. The aortic root wall has been removed, leaving only the intervalvular triangles and the leaflet attachment in situ. The pulmonary root has been given the same treatment. Furthermore, the left and right atria have been removed at the level of their attachment to the right and left ventricles, respectively. The left and right fibrous trigone are part of a greater morphological structure called the subvalvular membrane, which will be discussed later in this chapter (Sect. 6.1.4). The right fibrous trigone is positioned between the mitral valve ostium, the left ventricular opening, and the annulus of the noncoronary sinus (dashed triangle Fig. 6.8). It is triangular in shape and attaches via its right lateral side directly to the opening of the left ventricle. Its left lateral side is conjoined to the annulus of the anterior leaflet. The superior line of the triangle provides the attachment to the noncoronary sinus (Figs. 6.8 and 6.9). Note that the left segment of noncoronary sinus is attached only by the intermediation of the triangle to the left ventricle. Given the imposed forces during the cardiac cycle, it is not surprising that this part of the subvalvular membrane exhibits a triangularshaped thickening. Note that the atrioventricular node (AVN) is just distal to the right fibrous trigone. 294 6 Mitral Valve

Morphological variants of the left ventricular papillary muscles Table 6.1 Distribution of papillary muscle types (our own results) Group Anterior papillary muscle (n=100) Posterior papillary muscle (n=100) I 65 25 II/A 11 26 II/B 14 22 III/A 2 5 III/B 4 7 III/C 4 15 6.1.2 Chordae Tendineae of the Mitral Valve The chordae tendineae are fibrous cord-like structures that connect the mitral valve leaflets and the papillary muscle. They originate from the apex of the papillary muscle and are attached either to the anterior, posterior, or commissural parts of the mitral leaflet. The chordae proved the vital part of the papillary annular integrity; rupture of the chordae results in acute insufficiency of the leaflet. Furthermore, it is thought that the integrity of the papillary annulus serves as an anchor for the left ventricle, preventing extreme dilatation of the ventricular cavity. In this part of the chapter, we will discuss the morphological properties of the chordae tendineae, focusing on their origin, number, and attachments to the mitral valve. First, a brief description of the main types of papillary muscle (types I–III) will be given, to allow a better understanding of the chordae tendineae origins and their morphological arrangement. The classification of these muscles is based on the morphology and origin of the papillary muscle head (Fig. 6.16). Type I papillary muscles have one head and one origin (Fig. 6.16a). In type II papillary muscles, the head area is split in two; if the two heads have one common origin, it is termed type II/A (Fig. 6.16b), and if each of the two heads has its own origin, this morphological variant is termed type II/B (Fig. 16.6c). The third morphological variant of papillary muscles, type III, has three heads. Those type III variants for which the three heads have one common origin are termed type III/A (Fig. 16.6d). Those for which two heads originate from the same base and the third head presents as an individual papillary muscle with its own origin are termed type III/B (Fig. 6.16e). And finally, those for which each of the three heads has its own origin are termed type III/C (Fig. 6.16f). This classification is based on an investigation of 100 human hearts, and the distribution of types is given in Table 6.1. In Fig. 6.17, a dry-dissected specimen is presented showing a left lateral view of the mitral vale and its subvalvular apparatus. The lateral musculature of the left ventricle has been removed; the annulus of the mitral valve remains in situ. The investigation plane is that of the mitral valve leaflets. The papillary muscle has one origin and one head, and would thus be classified as group I (see also Fig. 6.16). The chordae tendineae that originate from the anterior segment of the papillary muscle head run to the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve (Fig. 6.17). The chordae that originate from the posterior part of the papillary muscle head are attached to the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve, and those that run from the middle segment of the papillary 298 6 Mitral Valve

Figure 6.19 shows a left lateral view of the mitral valve and the posterior papillary muscle; the investigation plane is that of the posterior commissure. The structure of the chordae tendineae that run to the posterior leaflet exhibit muscular structural changes. The papillary muscle is type II/B, having two heads with two origins. Note that on the posterior segment of the papillary muscle, one of the chordae tendineae exhibits muscular transformation. The muscular part of the chordae reaches almost to the attachment of the chordae to the posterior leaflet. This phenomenon is defined as muscularization of the chordae tendineae, and is demonstrated on the schematic drawing in Fig. 6.20, wherein the anterior part of the right ventricle has been removed. The mitral valve is inspected in the frontal plane; the anterior papillary muscle is on the right and the posterior papillary muscle on the left. Muscularization of the chordae is observed at the anterior papillary muscle. Here, a large mass of muscle extends from the lateral wall of the left ventricle to the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve (Fig. 6.20). The chordae tendineae may be classified according to their origin, and their insertion. The origin of the chordae tendineae may be from the papillary muscle or from the wall of the left ventricle. The insertion may be to the free margin of the leaflet, or to the ventricular surface of the appositional or nonappositional division of the leaflet. Accordingly, the chordae are designated either marginal appositional or nonappositional. As a rule, a stepwise increase in diameter occurs as we pass along the length of the chordae from mural to nonappositional chordae. text: Left coronary sinus Anterior leaflet Coronary sinus Coronary artery Posterolateral commissure Anterolateral commissure Posterior leaflet 6.1.3 Attachment of the Mitral Valve to the Left Ventricle In this part of the morphological description of the mitral valve, we explain the relationship between the mitral valve leaflets and the ostium of the left ventricle, and in particular the anatomy of the mitral valve attachment. In general, we can state that the posterior leaflet is attached directly to the musculature of the left ventricle; this statement describes the situation well, and one might think that it therefore needs no further discussion. However, more detailed investigation, including preparation of histological specimens, reveals a more complex morphological relationship. In addition, the attachment of the anterior leaflet and the commissural zones of the mitral valve attachment exhibit a very complex anatomy. These morphological situations will be discussed herein, incorporating the term “subvalvular membrane” to describe each facet of the mitral valve. The detailed topography of this membranous structure Fig. 6.23. Attachment of the chordae tendineae to the anterior leaflet will be discussed in Sect. 6.1.4. We must first describe the very complex attachment of the borders of the mitral valve. This may be divided into three segments: attached, commissural, and free. Note that from a physiological viewpoint, the commissural zones are integral parts of the leaflet (Figs. 6.23 and 6.24). The free border of the anterior and posterior leaflets is divided into three parts. The classification of Carpentier recognizes three major scallops in the posterior leaflet (P1–P3), and names the facing segments of the anterior leaflet, where P1 is near to the anterior commissure, P3 is a neighbor to the posterior commissure, and P2 is located in the middle of the posterior leaflet. These parts of the mitral valve are presented on the drydissected specimen and its corresponding drawing (Figs. 6.25 and 6.26, respectively), in which the left atrium has been removed and the dissection carried out at the level Fig. 6.24.
