The coronary arteries on the dry-dissected specimen have been filled with white contrast material, but left in situ. The mitral valve is inspected from the posterior superior view. The attachment of the left atrium is colored red and the subvalvular membrane is orange (Fig. 6.26). The leaflets are seen in the closed position, as they might be seen by the surgeon in theater. The closure line is semicircular and is located at the rough zone of the leaflet. The smooth part faces the left atrium in the diastolic part of the heart cycle. The anterior leaflet takes up approximately two-thirds of the entire annular circumference, and the posterior leaflet, which is rectangular, is attached to the remaining one-third of the annulus. There are numerous slits in the posterior leaflet; these acts as pleats so that the valve can close. Consequently, the surgeon sees these segments as almost completely separate structures, producing the so-called scallops of the valve. There are numerous texts in which these scallops are described as four separate leaflets (Yacoub), or even six if the commissures are also taken into account (Carpentier). More commonly, however, surgeons adopt the suggestion of Kumar et al., who labeled the functional components of the valve in alphanumeric fashion. However, in the setting of a prolapse, these individual components may be deformed in isolation and must be recognized as such. 6.1 General Anatomy of the Mitral Valve 303

Attachment of the anterior leaflet, posterior view, schematic drawing The attached part does not use the aforementioned classification for free segments of the valve. The anterior leaflet is thus divided into four parts. The anterior leaflet and its attachment area is inspected from the left lateral view on the dry-dissected specimen in Fig. 6.27. In this specimen the left atrium has been removed and the right atrium left in situ, to allow the interatrial septum to be viewed. The mitral valve is in a closed position. The attachment of the anterior leaflet is positioned in the left lateral projection. The small invagination in the area of the anterior leaflet indicates the position of the left and right fibrous trigones. On the corresponding schematic drawing in Fig. 6.28, the closed mitral valve is inspected from the posterior superior view. The left atrium has also been removed in this figure, and the different parts of the attachments of the anterior leaflet are indicated with different colors: the attachment of the left atrium is presented in red. The intervalvular part of the attachment of the anterior leaflet is located between the aortic and mitral valves, and measures on average 2.7 cm. This segment is found at the site of the anterior-superior part of the subvalvular membrane and is located between the deepest points of the left and noncoronary sinuses (Figs. 6.27 and 6.28). On the schematic drawing (Fig. 6.28), this part is indicated as a red line. Later on, we will see that this part of the leaflet is relatively immobile and it has been postulated to be an anchoring area for the anterior leaflet. The intervalvular part of the annulus is inferior and posterior to the posterior fibrous trigone of the aortic root. The junction zone on the left and right is placed between the deepest points of the noncoronary and left coronary sinuses, and corresponds to the left and the right fibrous trigones, respectively (indicated by a small, dark line in Fig. 6.28). These areas measure on average 0.7 cm in length. The right junctional zone is the site where the left and right atria are attached to the right fibrous trigone (Fig. 6.27). The commissural areas are indicated as green areas of the mitral valve in Figs. 6.27 and 6.28. The posterior leaflet is located on the posterior circumference of the mitral valve, measuring approximately 7.0 cm in length and occupying an area almost equal to that of the anterior leaflet. The importance of identifying the precise attachments of the leaflets is not debatable. In procedures such as manipulations of the posterior leaflet annulus, it is of particular importance because of the danger of periprosthetic leak in relation to the anterior leaflet. This may be because the attachment of the anterior leaflet is tougher and has fewer calcifications than that of the posterior leaflet (Figs. 6.27 and 6.28). To understand the morphology of the mitral valve attachment to the left ventricle, it is essential to discuss, if only briefly, the morphology of the left ventricular ostium. This opening of the left ventricle may be exposed if the aortic root and the mitral are removed. The opening may then be observed bordered by the left ventricular musculature and remaining part of the aortic root (Figs. 6.29 and 6.30). As mentioned, the left atrium, the whole mitral valve and a part of the aortic root have been removed, thus exposing the entire opening of the left ventricle. The left ventricular ostium is seen from the posterior superior view in Figs. 6.29 and 6.30. The posterior twothirds of this opening correspond to the opening of the mitral valve, and the anterior one-third to the aortic root. Note that the right coronary sinus remains intact and is attached to the anterior part of the ostium. The parts of the left and noncoronary sinuses that are conjoined to the right coronary sinus have also been left in situ. This shows very clearly that the aforementioned segments of the aortic root are attached to the septal wall of the left ventricle. The walls of the sinuses have been removed so that only the semicircular leaflet attachments and the commissural zones remain (Fig. 6.29). In the schematic drawing, the left coronary sinus is red, and the noncoronary sinus is green. The membrane providing the attachment of the aortic root to the left ventricle is indicated as a thin yellow strip (Fig. 6.30). 6.1 General Anatomy of the Mitral Valve 305

Posterior leaflet and circumflex branch, lateral view The posterior leaflet of the mitral valve extends between the anterolateral and posterolateral commissures. It seems that the leaflets are not directly attached to the left ventricular musculature. In the cross section of the posterior leaflet and the left ventricle presented in Fig. 6.40, one can see that a membranous structure provides anchorage to the left ventricle at the area of the posterior leaflet attachment. The detailed anatomy of this membrane and its relationship to the left ventricular ostium will be discussed later in this chapter. The dissection plane on the presented specimen (Fig. 6.40) runs thought the middle of the posterior leaflet; the attachment is inspected from the lateral direction. Note that the posterior leaflet is very closely apposed to the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery, which runs on average 0.5 cm above the attachment of the posterior leaflet. This morphological situation is very important, especially during mitral valve replacement and annulus implantation, but also for all those procedures in which manipulation of the posterior leaflet has to be taken into account. However, the circumflex branch may be found over the posterior leaflet only in the case of left and intermediate dominance. In the right-dominant heart, the left circumflex artery terminates as a left marginal branch and does not run near to the annulus of the posterior leaflet. In this case, the right posterior branch may be positioned in the left posterior coronary sulcus. As mentioned previously, the mitral valve leaflets appear not to be directly attached to the left ventricular musculature. In preparing the specimens for this chapter, we noted a membranous structure positioned between the posterior leaflets and the left ventricle. This membranous structure appears to provide the attachment between the atrial musculature and the left ventricle. As it was positioned inferior to the mitral valve, the membranous structure was identified as the subvalvular membrane. Herein, specimens will be presented in which the aorta has been dissected superior to the sinotubular junction; the left atrium has also been removed, except for a narrow rim at the site of the membrane. The detailed anatomy of the membrane will be discussed in Sect. 6.1.4. 6.1 General Anatomy of the Mitral Valve 311

Left lateral view of the subvalvular membrane 6.1.4 Subvalvular Membrane of the Mitral Valve The membrane-like structure at the edge of the left ventricular ostium is known as the subvalvular membrane. This membranous structure provides the attachment of the aortic root and of the mitral valve to the ostium of the left ventricle. Furthermore, the left atrium is attached to the outer surface of this membrane, and the conjoined attachment of the right and left atria to this membrane in front of the noncoronary sinus indicates the junctional zone of the anterior leaflet annulus. The conjoined attachment of both atria is in front and medial of the right fibrous trigone. The line between the left and right junctional attachment divides the membrane into anterior and posterior segments. The anterior segment of the membrane is divided into three parts determined by the attachments of the tricuspid leaflet, the right ventricle, and the right atrium to the membrane. The anterior-most part is that joined to the right ventricle; this part of the anterior segment also provides the attachment of the right coronary sinus. The posterior part is divided into three segments. The mitral valve, which attaches to the posterior part of the membrane, actually defines these areas. The left and right ostial zones are attached to the membrane part, which is posterior to the fibrous trigone. The left and right commissural zones represent the second zone, and the entire posterior leaflet is interpreted as the third part of the posterior segment. Figure 6.43 shows a left lateral view of a specimen that has been subjected to interior lighting to clarify the anatomy and positions of the subvalvular membrane. The corresponding drawing is seen in Fig. 6.44. The aorta has been dissected at the level of the sinotubular junction, and the left atrium has been removed just over its attachment to the subvalvular membrane (Figs. 6.43 and 6.44). In the schematic drawing (Fig. 6.44), the membrane is presented in yellow, and the attachment of the left atrium as a brown line. The mitral valve is central relative to the attachment of the left atrium (Figs. 6.43 and 6.44). With transillumination, the attachment of the left atrium appears as a dark strip; the translucent band of the subvalvular membrane is seen inferior to the atrial attachment. The left fibrous trigone appears as a Fig. 6.44. Left lateral view of the subvalvular membrane, schematic drawing less translucent triangular structure, with the apex directed toward the posterior intervalvular triangle. Anterior to the left fibrous trigone, the membrane runs inferior to the left coronary sinus and provides the attachment of the left coronary sinus to the left ventricle. Note that the membrane at this location is in some instances thinner than the part found at the area of the mitral valve (Figs. 6.43 and 6.44). Medially from the left fibrous trigone, the membrane runs between the right part of the left coronary sinus and the anterior attachment of the left atrium. The membrane is connected directly to the posterior intervalvular triangle of the aortic root. From this lateral view, one can see that the axis of the posterior intervalvular triangle corresponds to the axis of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. 6.1 General Anatomy of the Mitral Valve 313

Left posterior superior view of the subvalvular membrane The same specimen from a more posterior left lateral view is shown in Fig. 6.45. From this perspective, the relationship between the subvalvular membrane and the left coronary sinus may be observed in more detail. The subvalvular membrane appears as a transilluminated membrane located inferior to the left coronary sinus. Note that the membrane continues between the aortic root and the attachment of the anterior wall of the left atrium, toward the posterior intervalvular triangle. Just before the membrane reaches the posterior intervalvular triangle, it serves as an attachment for the right half of the left coronary sinus. This morphological situation is seen clearly in Fig. 6.45. However, at this area there is no direct connection to the left ventricle. Anchorage of this part of the left sinus to the left ventricle is only provided by the subvalvular membrane (Fig. 6.45). As mentioned earlier in this chapter, given the great forces experienced during the cardiac cycle, it is not surprising to find that the trigone membrane is thickened at this area (left fibrous trigone). Figure 6.46 shows a posterior superior view of the subvalvular membrane in a transilluminated specimen; the corresponding schematic drawing is shown in Fig. 6.47. The specimen shown in the previous figures was turned about 45° to the left. The attachment of the left atrium is presented as a dark strip (Fig. 6.46); on the schematic drawing, the same structure is brown. The subvalvular membrane can be found inferior to the atrial attachment; this appears as a translucent structure inferior to the dark strip (Fig. 6.46). The mitral valve leaflets are central to the atrial attachment. The segment of the subvalvular membrane that runs around the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve will now be discussed. Note that the translucent membrane in principle sur rounds the entire posterior segment of the mitral valve from the left fibrous trigone to the right (see Figs. 6.46 and 6.47). Thus, given that the membrane represents the sole structure providing the attachment of the valve, which is exposed to extreme hemodynamic conditions, again it is not surprising that some fibrous thickening may be found here. Henle described the membrane as extending from the left and right fibrous trigones and running around the posterior segment of the mitral valve (Fig. 6.47). Subvalvular membrane and its attachment to the left ventricle, histological specimen muscular structure (Figs. 6.51a and 6.51b). In our series, we found a case of a 28-year-old male in whom the attachment of the posterolateral part of the right ventricle to the membrane contained a membrane at the proximal part of the muscle. A schematic drawing of this situation is presented in Fig. 6.51c, in which the musculature is given in blue and the membranous part is indicated with brown. The extension of the membrane part is different; in normal cases, these may have no influence on the hemodynamics of the right ventricle. However, during pressure overload of the right ventricle, the membranous part may develop an aneurysmatic deformation. To prove the existence of the subvalvular membrane, histological specimens were taken from the area of the mitral valve attachment where the membrane was found in almost every dry-dissected heart. The posterior attachment was dissected in the axial direction. The precise relationship between the membrane and the mitral valve and the attachment of the left atrium was thus investigated histologically. The specimens were stained using the periodic acid-Schiff technique. The translucent membrane was identified as a fibrous band that is directly connected to the left ventricular muscle (Fig. 6.52). This band is colored blue in the figure, and the muscle is represented as a red structure positioned inferior to the membrane. The mural leaflet and the left atrium are attached to the central part of the membrane. The outermost part of the membrane is connected to the left ventricular musculature. The hinge line of the valve is defined by the attachment of the left atrium to the membrane. The ventricular surface of the leaflet appears as a continuation of the fibrous membrane, and the atrial surface as a continuation of the left atrium. Note that the atrial muscles are present at the proximal half of the mural leaflet. We assume that the sphincter function of the annulus is an active contraction provided by the atrial musculature present in the proximal part of the posterior leaflet. This suggestion is supported by the fact that the absence of properly timed atrial contractions, as during ventricular pacing or atrial fibrillation, abolishes the presystolic annular area reduction. 6.1 General Anatomy of the Mitral Valve 317

After the skin incision, the sternal bone is split in the middle a standard sternal spreader is inserted. The retrosternal fat tissue is prepared down to the anterior sheath of the pericardium, as shown in Fig. 6.57. The fat tissue is dissected up to the brachiocephalic vein. In most cases, the thymic vein is present as an open vessel, which should be ligated during this step of the procedure. The pericardium is incised in an inversed “T” shape. To find the middle of the anterior pericardial sheath, the groove between the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk must be identified. The border between the two great vessels may be seen on the anterior sheath of the pericardium as a shallow invagination of the pericardium. The incision is made over this border, with the distal extension toward the diaphragm. The distal end point of the vertical incision is performed just superior to the diaphragm. A horizontal incision is then performed to the left and right (Figs. 6.57 and 6.58). After the pericardial incision is completed, a sternal spreader is inserted; the edges of pericardium are lifted and fixed to the skin (Fig. 6.58). The anterior surface of the heart is thus exposed. The great vessel must now be inspected and exposed. Following exposure of the heart and the great vessels, a cardiopulmonary bypass is established with the aid of venous and arterial cannulations, and the heart is arrested using antegrade or retrograde Fig. 6.57. The posterior papillary muscle in this case presents two heads, one anterior and one posterior. The chordae that originate from the anterior head run to the anterior leaflet, and those from the posterior head anchor the posterior leaflet. The commissural zone is anchored to the medial parts of the anterior and posterior leaflets (Figs. 6.65 and 6.66). Although mitral pathology is usually obvious, it is important to perform a complete assessment. The annulus is evaluated systematically for dilatation and/or deformity. Leaflets and leaflet motion are examined next. Nerve hooks are used to assess leaflet pliability and leaflet prolapse or restriction. Lesions that produce regurgitation with prolapse include chordal rupture, chordal elongation, papillary muscle rupture, and papillary muscle elongation. After assessing the leaflets, the chordae are examined to evaluate their length, thickening, fusion, or rupture. Finally, the papillary muscles are assessed for elongation or rupture secondary to infarction. Fig. 6.65. Exposure of the posterior papillary muscle Fig. 6.66. Pericardial incision 6.2.1.2 “J” Sternotomy for Mitral Valve Surgery Nowadays, a variety of less invasive approaches have been developed to perform isolated mitral valve surgery. Chest wall incisions include lower sternotomy, partial upper sternotomy, right parasternal thoracotomy, and right thoracotomy. Excellent results have been reported with each of these approaches. The “J” sternotomy is also called the lower sternotomy. After completion of the skin incision between the second and fourth intercostal spaces and exposure of the appropriate part of the sternum, a sternotomy is performed. A specially designed sternum spreader is inserted and the retrosternal space is exposed, as shown in Fig. 6.67. The fat tissue is dissected down to the pericardium, exposing the anterior pericardial sheath, and then up to the left brachiocephalic vein (Fig. 6.67). The thymic veins must be ligated during the dissection of the fat tissue. Note that only the middle of the cardiac mediastinum is exposed. However, this is not obvious while the pericardium remains closed, especially to one who does not routinely perform this minimally invasive procedure. The pericardial incision is performed at the middle of the anterior pericardial sheath, which lies over the sulcus and between the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk (Figs. 6.67 and 6.68). In most cases, the pericardium is grasped with two forceps and lifted away from the heart. The incision is performed using electrocautery; scissors are then used to extend the pericardial incision. The superior vena cava is exposed immediately lateral to the ascending aorta; however, exposure of the inferior vena cava requires some effort. To achieve optimal exposure of the inferior vein, the right atrium must be lifted and pulled caudally (Fig. 6.70). A tourniquet is placed around the inferior vena cava, with traction directed toward the patient’s feet; this further elevates the right side of the heart. The entire length of the posterior interatrial sulcus may thus be exposed, and is a very important landmark. The procedure is described in detail in Chap. 2. The skin incision is performed between the sternal notch and the fourth sternocostal junction. The subcutaneous fat tissue is subsequently dissected and the anterior level of the bone is exposed. An oscillating saw is used for the partial superior “j” sternotomy. A sternal spreader designed specifically for minimally invasive surgery is then inserted. The prepericardial fat tissue is dissected down to the pericardium, and after identification of the anterior sheath of the pericardium, the dissection is carried out caudally to identify the left innominate vein (Fig. 6.74). Normally, the thymic veins are identified and ligated at this level; the left brachiocephalic vein is found easily by tracing the thymic vein. Note that in this approach, structures belonging to the superior mediastinum may also be exposed. The brachiocephalic vein is identified, dissected, and slightly elevated from the aortic arch with aid of purse strings. Note that the left brachiocephalic vein is positioned just behind the sternal notch and in front of the aortic arch and the right brachiocephalic trunk (Fig. 6.74). The incision details are described in Chap. 2. The patient is in the left lateral supine position and the skin incision is performed on the right lateral chest wall. After the subcutaneous fat tissue is dissected and the appropriate intercostal space is opened, the thorax spreader is inserted. The left lung is retracted, bringing the right lateral surface of the pericardium into the view (Fig. 6.81). Note that the right phrenic nerve, which runs on the pericardium and down to the diaphragm, is in front of the right pulmonary root (Fig. 6.81). The nerve is conjoined with the pericardiacophrenic artery and vein. The artery branches off from the right internal thoracic artery. When it reaches the angle between the pericardium and the diaphragm, the nerve divides of into branches that pierce the muscle, and are distributed under its surface. The area of this division normally covers the extensive region of the fat-tissue condensation (Fig. 6.81). The nerve enters the thoracic cavity in front of the subclavian artery and behind the subclavian vein. Initially, the nerve then crosses the internal mammary artery, near its origin. From here on, the nerve runs along the lateral aspect of the superior vena cava. The course of the nerve is presented herein from the inferior view (Fig. 6.82). Note that the azygos vein arches forward over the root of the right lung, and ends in the superior vena cava, just before it penetrates the pericardium. Fig. 6.81. Exposure of the right heart as seen following the lateral thoracotomy 6.2.1.5 Lateral Thoracotomy for the Mitral Valve Surgery This minimally invasive approach is discussed in Chap. 2, Sect. 2.2.1. Many surgeons prefer the hemisternotomy approach for mitral valve exposure; however, the right minithoracotomy yields excellent direct vision in videoscopic or direct mitral valve access. To access the left atrium directly, while maintaining a limited-access minithoracotomy, a 10- to 12-cm incision should be placed in the submammary fold along the anterior axillary line. The skin incision is performed on the right lateral thorax wall. To facilitate the exposure, the right chest wall may be elevated by approximately 30°. In most cases, the thorax cavity is opened at the fourth intercostal space. The fourth and fifth ribs are retracted using a special minimally invasive spreader. If the skin incision is 10–12 cm longer, the procedure may be performed without using a videoassisted technique. However, this incision may be combined with either port-access methods or with modified standard perfusion techniques. A smaller 4- to 5-cm incision with minimal rib retraction can be used in video-assisted cases and is large enough for the passage of a prosthesis. After the insertion of the spreader, the right superior lobe of the right lung is retracted. The right lateral sheath of the pericardium is exposed, as seen on the Fig. 6.88. The phrenic nerve and the conjoined vessels must be identified. Note that the right phrenic nerve runs in front of the pulmonary root. The pericardium is incised in a horizontal direction. text: Left brachiocephalic vein Pericardium Ascending aorta Pulmonary trunk Right ventricle Right atrium Superior vena cava Left brachiocephalic vein Sinoatrial node 6.2.2 Superior Transseptal Approach to the Mitral Valve 6.2.2.1 Median Sternotomy for the Superior Transseptal Approach The skin incision and median sternotomy are performed as described previously. The sternum spreader is inserted and the retrosternal space is exposed (Fig. 6.94). The fat tissue is dissected down to the anterior sheath of the pericardium; subsequently, the thymic veins are traced up to the left brachiocephalic vein. After dissection of the left brachiocephalic vein away from the surrounding fat tissue, the pericardium may be opened (see Fig. 6.94). The pericardium is opened in the inverse “T” fashion, the vertical incision beginning just inferior to the brachiocephalic vein, over the sulcus between the pulmonary and aortic roots. It is extended down to the diaphragm, from which point a horizontal pericardial incision is made. After the pericardium is opened, the sternocostal surface of the heart is exposed. The cardiopulmonary bypass can now be established between the bicaval venous cannulation and cannulation of the ascending aorta. At this point, the operating table is rotated to the left, facilitating exposure of the anterior interatrial sulcus and the anterior wall of the left atrium. The right atrium is then incised, beginning inferior to the terminal sulcus. This part of the incision is particularly important because the sinoatrial node is found at the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrium in the terminal sulcus. To avoid the damage to this very important structure, and the genesis of the postoperative rhythm disturbances, the right atrial incision must be performed distally from the terminal sulcus. The opening incision is extended in a diagonal direction toward the opening of the inferior vena cava. The opening cut of the right atrium is about 5–7 cm long (see Fig. 6.95 dashed line). Before proceeding further, the most important structures in the right atrium must be identified: the opening of the coronary sinus, the oval fossa, and the tricuspid leaflet. Note that the opening of the coronary sinus is in this case covered by its leaflet. The leaflet of the coronary sinus ostium in the right atrium may exhibit several morphological variants, such as membranous structures that may close off Fig. 6.94. text: Posterior leaflet Anterior leaflet Posterior commissure Anterior commissure Anterior papillary muscle Anterior leaflet Posterior leaflet The mitral leaflet is seen from the right superior view in Fig. 6.102, wherein the annulus fibrosus lies almost in a vertical position. This exposure and anatomical situation is very comfortable for the operating surgeon. Not only is the entire circumference of the annulus fibrosus visible, but also both leaflets and the commissural zones are brought very clearly into view. The anterior leaflet is in this projection superior to the posterior leaflets. Both commissures lie in a horizontal plane (Fig. 6.102). Two slight depressions in the tissue may be found at the level of the annulus fibrosus, on the left and right sides of the anterior leaflet. These smooth recesses, which are located slightly superior to the posterior leaflet, indicate the position of the left and right fibrous trigones. Note the right fibrous trigone is a very good indicator for the position of the AVN; this will be discussed in detail in Chap. 10. This exposure allows the morphology of the subvalvular apparatus to be examined. The anterolateral commissure is lifted, revealing the anterior papillary muscle and the chordae tendineae (Fig. 6.103). Note that in this case, the papillary muscle has only one head, and that the chordae originating from the anterior part of the head are connected to the anterior leaflet. The course of the anterior chordae may be identified clearly. The chordae from the middle part of the papillary muscle head run to the commissural zone, and those originating from the posterior part of the papillary muscle run to the posterior leaflet (Fig. 6.103). The skin incision is performed between the second and fourth intercostal spaces and the sternotomy is achieved using an oscillating bone saw. A special sternum spreader is inserted and the retrosternal fat is dissected down to the anterior fibrous sheet of the pericardium. The thymic veins are ligated. The upper border of the sternal incision is at the level of the second intercostal space, and so the left brachiocephalic vein cannot be exposed. Note that the left brachiocephalic vein is located behind the jugulum, and in this exposure is positioned just behind the superior part of the sternum (which has not been split; Fig. 6.106). Here, the superior and inferior borders of the sternotomy may be seen clearly. Note the limited exposure of the pericardium. The superior vena cava and transition of the vein into the pericardial space is clearly visible at the right superior corner. This precise anatomical situation is not often seen in native specimens, because the superior vena cava is usually located behind the ascending aorta. In the presented case, the extrapericardial segment of the vein is positioned more superiorly than the aorta, and consequently the aforementioned transition is clearly exposed. Note that on entering the pericardial space, the course of the superior vena cava is located behind the ascending aorta. The pericardium is then exposed with the aid of an opening inversed “T” incision (Fig. 6.107). The pericardial edges and the sternocostal surface are fixed; consequently, the sternocostal surface of the heart is exposed (Fig. 6.108). text: Aorta Superior vena cava Right atrium Pulmonary trunk Right ventricle Terminal sulcus Area of the sinoatrial node Ascending aorta Coronary sinus Sternum Diaphragm Inferior vena cava Oval fossa Superior vena cava The incision of the right lateral atrial wall is made as described previously, running in a diagonal direction between the uppermost part of the terminal sulcus and the ostium of the inferior vena cava (Figs. 6.109, see dashed line, and 6.110), thus opening the right atrium (Fig. 6.111). The opening of the inferior vena cava is found at the right inferior part of Fig. 6.111. Note that the valve of the inferior vena cava may be also seen; in the literature, this valve is also known as the Eustachian valve. In every case, the Eustachian valve is a very prominent structure. The proximal attachment of the valve reaches to the inferior limb of the oval fossa and continues into the Eustachian ridge. This ridge is a direct continuation of the inferior edge of the oval fossa (also known as the oval fossa limb). This muscular fold is formed by the reflection of the Eustachian valve and the valve of the coronary sinus (also known as the Thebesian valve). The interatrial septum may be found superior to the inferior limb of the oval fossa, and the ostium of the coronary sinus may be found inferior to the leaflet of the inferior vena cava (Fig. 6.111). The left atrium must be opened after opening of the right atrium, by using the inverse “V” incision of the interatrial septum and of the anterior atrial wall. The apex of the “V” incision is at the anterior superior edge of the interatrial septum. Anterior limb of “V” corresponds to the left atrial incision and inferior limb to the septal incision. Pericardial incision The mitral valve is now exposed by inserting a special three-horned retractor into the left atrium (Fig. 6.114). To facilitate the exposure, purse strings may be placed at the area of annulus fibrosus just over the commissural zones. From this viewpoint (Fig. 6.114), the entire annulus and both leaflets may be inspected. In the presented case, the mitral valve is in the closed position. The commissural zones are easily distinguished from the anterior and posterior leaflets. 6.2.2.3 “j” Sternotomy for the Superior Transseptal Approach The operative technique for the “j” sternotomy is described in Chap. 2. The skin incision is performed between the jugulum and fourth intercostal space, after which the subcutaneous fat tissue is dissected down to the anterior sheath of the sternum. The jugulum must be freed from the surrounding tissue, as for a standard median sternotomy. The sternotomy is performed with the aid of an oscillating saw. The retrosternal space is thus exposed and the fat tissue is dissected down to the pericardium. The thymic veins must be ligated if appropriate. The left brachiocephalic vein is exposed and identified, and then the pericardium is incised (see Fig. 6.115; the course of the incision is marked with dashed line). The opening cut of the pericardium is initiated inferior to the brachiocephalic vein, and is extended between the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, toward the inferior part of the exposure. On reaching the most distal part of the exposed pericardium, two horizontal incisions are performed. The pericardial edges are then lifted using purse strings, which are in most cases fixed to the sternal spreader (Fig. 6.116). Note that in this exposure the ascending aorta and the initial part of the aortic arch are visible. The intrapericardial part of the superior vena cava may be observed behind the ascending aorta. 6.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Mitral Valve 349

The skin incision is made over the fourth intercostal space, and the patient is normally in the left supine position. The subcutaneous tissue is dissected away and the intercostal space is opened over the fifth rib. A thorax spreader is then inserted, and the right superior lobe of the lung is retracted, revealing the right lateral sheet of the pericardium (Fig. 6.121). The phrenic nerve initially runs on the lateral side of the superior vena cava, progressing forward on the lateral pericardial sheet, and then turns down toward the pulmonary hill. Subsequently, the pericardial edges are fixed to the thorax spreader with sutures, exposing the entire lateral wall of the right atrium, the superior and inferior vena cavae, and the ascending aorta. In the case presented here (Fig. 6.123), the right atrium is a relatively large structure, with the appendage laying over the ascending aorta. On the specimen presented in Fig. 7.1, the human heart is examined from above and the left posterior view. The walls of the pulmonary and aortic roots have been removed down to the attachment of the leaflets; consequently, only the fibrous skeleton of both structures remains. The left and the right atria have been removed down to their annuli. The pericardial fat tissue and coronary vessels have been removed down to the ventricular musculature, and the mitral and tricuspid valves are open. Note that the right ventricle wraps around the left ventricle to such a degree that the ostium of the infundibulum is positioned at the level of the left ventricular ostium. However, the two ostia are not positioned in the same plane. The plane at the level of the nadirs of the semilunar leaflets in the pulmonary root may be taken as the reference plane; in the future, Fig. 7.1. Relationship between the pulmonary and the aortic root this will also be referred to as the pulmonary root base. This plane is shifted to the left and laterally relative to the left ventricle. The base of the aortic root, which is considered as a reference level for the left ventricle, is shifted anteriorly and to the right. Consequently, the posterior commissure of the pulmonary root will be positioned in front of the anterior aortic root commissure (Fig. 7.1), and the left coronary sinus of the aortic root will be positioned posterior to the left pulmonary sinus. Note that the left pulmonary sinus is superior and to the left relative to the left coronary sinus. The right coronary sinus is positioned even deeper in the left ventricular musculature than the left coronary sinus (Fig. 7.1). 358 7 Pulmonary Valve

The specimen seen on Fig. 7.1 is presented from a posterior superior view, and the pulmonary root is in front of the aortic root. The right coronary sinus is posterior and deep relative to the right pulmonary sinus. On the schematic drawing in Fig. 7.2, the sinuses have been removed and the roots are inspected from the posterior superior view. The leaflets and the intervalvular triangles remain in situ. Both roots are asymmetric in structure, and this asymmetry should determine their direction. The aortic root is oriented to the right and in an anterior direction, in contrast to the pulmonary root, which is oriented in a left posterior direction. Thus, we can see that the roots are oriented in opposite directions (Figs. 7.1 and 7.2). Similar to the aortic root, the pulmonary root is a component of the sinotubular junction, the leaflets, the three commissures, the three sinuses, and the base of the root. The three sinuses are in the same position as for the aortic root, being placed between the attachment of the leaflets and the sinotubular junction. The sinotubular junction is the superior border of the root and is placed between the sinus and the tubular part of the pulmonary artery (Fig. 7.3). According to their position, we may differentiate the anterior, left, and right pulmonary sinuses. The three sinuses have different shapes, and measurements show that the left sinus is the largest, followed by the anterior and right pulmonary sinuses. This asymmetry means that the base of the root and the sinotubular junction are not parallel. These two planes subtend an angle, which is defined as the tilt angle of the pulmonary root. In the presented specimen, the sinuses are viewed from above and the leaflets are closed (Fig. 7.3). The closing attachment of the leaflet shows a typical three-horned pattern. Like the aortic leaflets, the pulmonary leaflets close at their superior Fig. 7.2. Relationship between the pulmonary and the aortic root, schematic drawing Fig. 7.3. Superior view of the pulmonary root edge are also called the lunula (Fig. 7.3). The lunulae are almost translucent and located at the superior edge of the leaflet. They allow the congruent closure of the leaflets at diastole (Fig. 7.3). The anterior sinus is positioned in front of the two posterior sinuses, lying over the anterior wall of the infundibulum. The left and right pulmonary sinuses may be found behind the anterior sinus (Fig. 7.3). Note also that in this view we can confirm that muscle is present between the leaflets and the ostium of the infundibulum; this subvalvular muscle may be seen through the translucent leaflets. The inferior third of the leaflets is attached to the musculature of the infundibulum. This may be well seen on Fig. 7.4. From here on toward the commissure, the leaflet attaches directly to the wall of the root. The aforementioned special morphological relationship is very important for surgeons when performing the Ross procedure, because with dissection and mobilization of the pulmonary root, a rim of the musculature just beneath to the root must be dissected. The muscular rim must be sufficiently wide; the sutures are placed on this edge during implantation into the aortic position. 360 7 Pulmonary Valve

Segments of the right ventricular outflow tract with the anterior wall removed, anterior view, schematic drawing 7.1.2 Topography of the Infundibulum The infundibulum of the right ventricle is defined as a part of the right ventricular outflow tract and is considered to be the terminal part of the outflow tract. It is located just over the sinus of the right ventricle, which also belongs to the outflow segment of the right ventricle. The infundibulum has two segments, superior and inferior, and the border between the two is not always very clearly defined. The superior part is positioned inferior to the pulmonary root and is the only free part of the right ventricle. In some cases, this free segment does not exist. The inferior segment of the infundibulum is located between the free segment and the sinus of the outflow part (see Figs. 7.9 and 7.10). Before discussing the posterior wall of the infundibulum, the arrangement of the right ventricular outflow tract will be discussed. The free infundibulum is positioned between the pulmonary root and the septal margin. The inferior segment is between the septal margin and the moderator band. This segment includes the anterior papillary muscle of the tricuspid valve. The sinus is placed between the inflow segment and the moderator band (Figs. 7.9 and 7.10). The length of the free segment may differ between individuals; in some cases, it is present as a very short structure placed inferior to the opening of the left ventricle, and in others the free part of the infundibulum may even be placed over the left coronary artery. The infundibular walls may be divided into anterior, posterior, left lateral, and right lateral parts. Depressed infundibulum, left lateral view 7.1.3 Morphological Variations of the Infundibulum The topography of the infundibulum is described in Chap. 6. We have noticed that the dimensions of the tubular part of the infundibulum vary. In some specimens, the free part of the outflow tracts was very well defined, as was the posterior wall of the infundibulum. From the surgical point of view, an exhaustive knowledge of the morphology of the infundibulum, including the more frequently occurring variants, is very important for a successful Ross procedure. A low-positioned infundibulum is defined as one where the pulmonary ostium is located below the ostium of the left ventricle. This deep relationship between the two openings may be seen in Fig. 7.18, wherein the left lateral wall of the infundibulum is observed from the left attitudinal view. In this projection, the left lateral wall has a triangular shape. The pulmonary trunk has been dissected over the sinotubular junction, and the left lateral wall of the left ventricle has been removed. The attachment of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve to the left ventricular has also been exposed. This attachment indicates the level of the left ventricular ostium (Fig. 7.18). Note that in this case the opening of the pulmonary ostium is positioned inferior to the attachment of the mitral leaflet, and is thus placed beyond the left ventricular ostium; this is termed a deep-positioned infundibulum. Awareness of this morphological situation is very important when performing dissection of the pulmonary valve. The nadirs of the leaflets are placed inferiorly to the ostium of the infundibular opening; thus in the depressed infundibulum, separation of the entire pulmonary root includes dissection of the posterior infundibular wall, which forms part of the interventricular septum. Splitting of the posterior infundibular wall must also be performed very carefully, as in some cases the superior septal artery may be found in this superior part of the interventricular septum. 7.1 General Anatomy of the Pulmonary Valve 367

text: Sternohyoid muscle Left brachiocephalic vein Thymic vein Thymus rest Pericardium Left brachiocephalic vein Aorta Right atrium Right ventricle Pulmonary trunk 7.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Pulmonary Valve 7.2.1 Median Sternotomy for Pulmonary Valve Exposure The median sternotomy is performed as described in Chap. 2. After completion of the skin incision and splitting of the sternum, a standard sternum spreader is inserted. The retrosternal space is then exposed, as seen in Fig. 7.25. In adults, the thymus rest may be found in the retrosternal space. The thymus veins must be identified within this fat tissue and ligated; note that in most cases two veins may be found. The surgeon should follow the course of the thymus veins toward the innominate vein, which must therefore also be identified. In the next step of the exposure, the anterior sheath of the pericardium is dissected away from the fat tissue (Fig. 7.25). Note that the ascending aorta, the pulmonary trunk, the right auricle, and right ventricle may be identified in this translucent pericardium (Fig. 7.26). The translucent pericardium occurs more frequently among younger adults than in the elderly, in whom the pericardium consists of a thick fibrous layer. The dashed line in Fig. 7.26 indicates the direction of the pericardial incision, which runs in the sulcus between the pulmonary and aortic trunks and then extends down to the diaphragm. The caudal point of the vertical pericardial incision is placed inferior to the innominate vein. After completion of the vertical pericardial incision, left and right horizontal extensions are performed. Fig. 7.25. Topography of the retrosternal space Fig. 7.26. Incision of the pericardium 371

Pulmonary trunk Fig. 7.28. Exposure of the pulmonary trunk. The dashed line indicates the supravalvular incision Purse strings are then placed arround left brachiocepualic vein and the pulmonary artery and infundibulum are exposed, as seen in Fig. 7.27. Note that in the presented specimen, the ascending aorta and the aortic arch have also been brought into view. In its course, the distal part of the pulmonary artery and its bifurcation are located behind the ascending aorta. The infundibulum and pulmonary root are superior to the aortic root and the proximal part of the ascending aorta. Note that the bifurcation of the pulmonary artery is inferior to the highest point of the aortic arch (Fig. 7.27). Prior to the exposure of the pulmonary valve, the ligamentous tissue that connects the pulmonary artery and the ascending aorta must be dissected away. The same must be done at the posterior wall of the pulmonary artery, thus mobilizing the pulmonary artery from the surrounding tissue. In the presented case, the brachiocephalic and left common carotid arteries originate from a common stem at the beginning of the aortic arch. The second vessel that originates from the aortic arch is the left subclavian artery (Fig. 7.27). In the specimen shown in Fig. 7.28, the topography of the pulmonary artery bifurcation is exposed. For this purpose aortic arch was lifted away from pulmonary artery bifurcation. The pulmonary valve may be exposed using two approaches, one of which involves incision of the anterior wall of the infundibulum and is used mostly for the correction of congenital heart disease. However, in adults the most commonly used approach involves incision of the pulmonary artery superior to the sinotubular junction. Both exposures will now be discussed. 372 7 Pulmonary Valve

Supravalvular incision of the pulmonary trunk, schematic drawing Incision of the pulmonary artery is performed in a vertical fashion (see the schematic drawing in Figs. 7.28 and 7.29). The vertical opening cut is performed between the bifurcation of the pulmonary artery and the sinotubular junction of the pulmonary root. The initial stab incision is made superior to the sinotubular junction, following which the opening incision is extended toward the bifurcation of the pulmonary artery (Fig. 7.29). The incision presented herein is used mostly to correct isolated supravalvular or valvular stenosis of the pulmonary valve. In most cases, stenosis of the supravalvular or valvular area of the pulmonary artery is part of a more complex congenital heart disease, such as tetralogy of Fallot. In very rare cases, however, it may be an isolated finding. The opening incision of the pulmonary artery gives the surgeon an opportunity to directly inspect the valvular apparatus of the pulmonary valve, and may be for replacement or reconstruction of the pulmonary valve. In most cases, an adequate dilatation of the pulmonary artery may be achieved for implantation of the patch. The same strategy may be used to correct stenosis of the pulmonary artery. In these cases, the vertical incision is extended between the anterior and right leaflets into the right intervalvular triangle, after which the patch may be implanted to achieve enlargement of pulmonary valve. 7.2 Surgical Anatomy of the Pulmonary Valve 373

text: Pulmonary trunk Aorta Right atrium Right ventricle Superior vena cava Inferior vena cava Anterior pulmonary sinus Left pulmonary sinus Right pulmonary sinus In most cases, stenosis of the outflow tract of the right ventricle is found at the infundibulum, and only rarely in the sinus part. Exposure of the right ventricular outflow tract is performed by incising the anterior wall of the infundibulum (Fig. 7.32). This approach offers the advantage of allowing the surgeon to expose the ventricular septum, wherein he/she may close the ventricular septum defect. The initial stab incision is made at the middle third of the anterior wall and is extended superiorly toward the right commissure. The extension cut is made by insertion of scissors into the stab incision. Purse strings are then inserted and the infundibulum is exposed. The pulmonary valve may be inspected from the inferior aspect; Fig. 7.33 shows the leaflet in a closed position. As for the superior view, the left and right leaflets are also found in inferior of the anterior leaflet in this inferior view. In this approach the posterior wall of the infundibulum and entire subvalvular apparatus of the tricuspid valve may be inspected. The superior papillary muscle, also known as the muscle of Lancisi, is an important landmark, indicating the border between the infundibulum and the interventricular septum. This papillary muscle is a very small structure that arises in most cases as a single band posterior to the limb of the septal band. It is actually positioned at the separation of the posterior infundibular wall into the parietal and septal bands, which are separated by a virtual line between the superior papillary muscle and the posterior leaflet (Figs. 7.34 and 7.35). Vertical incision of the pulmonary trunk As part of the next step of the exposure, the topography of the pulmonary valve bifurcation will be discussed. After mobilization of the ascending aorta and the aortic arch, the aorta may be lifted away. Consequently, the entire course of the pulmonary artery and its bifurcation may be seen (see Fig. 7.38). In the specimen shown in Fig. 7.38, the pulmonary trunk is viewed from the inferior aspect. The incision of the pulmonary artery is performed in a vertical fashion between the bifurcation of the pulmonary artery and the sinotubular junction of the pulmonary root (Fig. 7.39). The initial stab incision is made superior to the sinotubular junction, and is extended toward the bifurcation. This procedure is mostly used for the correction of isolated supravalvular or valvular stenosis of the pulmonary valve. However, the incision may also be extended toward the left or right pulmonary arteries, thus allowing the surgeon adequate space for dilatation of the pulmonary arteries and implantation of the patch. 378 7 Pulmonary Valve

text: Parietal band Right atrium Anterolateral leaflet of tricuspid valve Interventricular septum Anterior papillary muscle Superior papillary muscle Septal band Right pulmonary sinus Left pulmonary sinus Anterior pulmonary sinus Moderate band 8.1 General Anatomy of the Tricuspid Valve 8.1.1 Papillary Muscles of the Tricuspid Valve In this chapter, we will discuss the anatomy of the tricuspid valve. As with the mitral valve, we will begin the structural anatomy of the papillary muscles. The anterior wall of the right ventricle must be removed to expose the outflow tract of the right ventricle (Fig. 8.1). The trabeculae of the sinus segment were dissected to reveal their attachment to the musculature of the right ventricle. The superior papillary (Lancisi) muscle is located beneath the inferior border of the posterior wall of the infundibulum. The line between the nadir of the left pulmonary leaflet and the superior papillary muscle demarcates the parietal and septal bands. This distance may vary, in the highly positioned infundibulum even reaching 2 cm; in the short infundibulum, this distance is shorter. The posterior wall of the infundibulum and its relationship to the superior papillary muscle is clearly visible on Fig. 8.2, in which the anterior and right leaflets of the pulmonary valve have been removed. The left cusp of the pulmonary valve lies straight over the posterior wall of the infundibulum. The parietal band projects over the anterior commissure and the anterior leafFig. 8.1. Right ventricular outflow tract as seen after removal of the anterior wall let of the tricuspid leaflet. At this point, it should be noted that the superior papillary muscle is a very important landmark for the operating surgeon. This muscle is clearly exposed during infundibulotomy (see Sect. 4.2.1) and as thus serves as a landmark, being positioned on the border between the infundibulum and the ventricular septum. The septal band extends from the attachment of the superior papillary muscle anteriorly, to the anterior papillary muscle. The parietal band runs over the superior papillary muscle toward the attachment of the anterior leaflet of the tricuspid leaflet (Figs. 8.1 and 8.2). The lateral edge of the septal band is fragmented; this area serves as a point of attachment for many trabeculae. The septal band extends inferiorly as the moderator band to the anterior wall of right ventricle. The anterior papillary muscle originates from the beginning of the moderator band (Fig. 8.1). Note that the large anterior papillary muscle attaches to the moderator band with a relatively wide base. Finally, the moderator band runs toward the anterior wall of the right ventricle (Fig. 8.1). 384 8 Tricuspid Valve

The transition between the right ventricular inflow and outflow tracts is seen in the frontal aspect. The superior segment of this border is presented by the parietal band, and the inferior border by the moderator band. On the medial side, the transition between the inflow and outflow segments is bordered by the interventricular septum, and lateral wall is determined by the anterior right ventricular wall. Note that on the presented specimen, the wall of the infundibulum remains in situ. In this view, the anterior papillary muscle is behind the ventricular part of the border (Fig. 8.3). Subvalvular apparatus of the tricuspid valve, posterolateral segment An anterior view of a new specimen is shown in Fig. 8.4, in which the entire musculature of the right ventricle has been removed; only the septal part remains in situ. The right atrium was subsequently dissected just over its attachment to the annulus of the tricuspid leaflet. The pulmonary root and the infundibulum remain in situ; from this view, the posterior pulmonary valve may be seen. The right coronary artery was left in situ; note that the artery runs superior to the position of the annulus fibrosus of the tricuspid leaflet (Fig. 8.4). The tricuspid valve is in the open position in Fig. 8.4, as during diastole, and the anterior leaflet is in the frontal projection. The medial part of the anterior leaflet is conjoined to the septal part of the tricuspid leaflet. The anterior commissure may be found between these two leaflets. The chordae tendineae that originate from the superior papillary muscle attach to the medial part of the anterior leaflet. The superior papillary muscle is positioned at the division of the posterior infundibulum to the septal and parietal bands. The chordae tendineae that are anchored to the lateral part of the anterior leaflet originate from the anterior papillary muscle of the right ventricle. The anterior papillary muscle is seen in frontal plane in Fig. 8.4) and is attached to the moderate band. The moderator band is a direct extension of the septal band and runs from the interventricular septum to the anterior wall of the right ventricle. The anterior papillary muscle originates near the connection between the moderator band and the anterior wall of the right ventricle. This relationship between the anterior muscle, the moderator band, and the left ventricular wall is visible in 386 8 Tricuspid Valve

text: Inferior papillary muscle Apex of the right ventricle Anterior papillary muscle Posterolateral leaflet of tricuspid valve Fig. 8.6. Trabecular arrangement of the right ventricular apex Fig. 8.4. The moderator band marks the upper border of the sinus part of the right ventricle. The same specimen as in Fig. 8.4 is inspected from the posterior view in Fig. 8.5. The posterior wall of the right ventricle has been removed. The posterior part of the right coronary artery runs over the annulus fibrosus. On reaching the posterior interventricular sulcus, the artery runs down toward the apex of the heart as a posterior descending branch. The posterior wall of the right ventricle has been removed down to the trabecular part of the inflow tract. The inferior papillary muscle, which is seen in frontal view, has two parts. The lateral part is positioned between the septal wall and the anterior papillary muscle, and the septal part originates from the posterior section of the interventricular septum (Fig. 8.5). Both parts originate from the trabecular net of the right ventricle. The posterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve is open, as during diastole. The division of the chordae tendineae can be investigated in this view. The lateral part of the inferior papillary muscle gives rise to the chordae tendineae, which run to the lateral commissure and the posterior leaflet. From the septal division of the inferior papillary muscle, the chordae tendineae run toward the posterior commissure (Fig. 8.5). A lateral view in which the inferior and apical parts of the right ventricular wall have been removed is shown in Fig. 8.6. After removal of the aforementioned ventricular wall, the trabecular part of the right ventricle is exposed. In this right lateral view, the separation between the anterior and inferior papillary muscles is seen. It is clear that both papillary muscles are attached to the trabecular part. The anterolateral and posterolateral leaflets have been removed and the right atrium dissected at the level of its attachment to the posterior superior process of the left ventricle. Note that the position of the septal leaflet is as if in diastole. The anchoring region of the leaflet may be investigated in this view. On the dry-dissected specimen, it can be seen that the leaflet attachment is located inferior relative to the attachment of the right atrium. The attachment line of the leaflet may be observed as a shallow groove at the superior edge of the leaflet (Fig. 8.10). It follows an oblique direction, running from posterior-inferior to superior-anterior. At the superior end, the attachment exhibits an inverted “U” shape, and is posterior to the posterolateral wall of the right ventricle (dissected in the frontal plane in Fig. 8.10). Note that the origin of the right coronary artery is superior to the posterolateral wall of the right ventricle. The relationship between the septal leaflet attachment and the neighbor structures can be seen in the schematic drawing in Fig. 8.11. The membranous septum and the posterior intervalvular triangle are part of the subvalvular membrane and are colored yellow in this diagram. Note that the attachment of the septal leaflet and the right atrium encloses a triangular area (Fig. 8.11 red line and Fig. 8.12). The attachment of the septal leaflet may be divided into two parts according to its relationship to the membranous and muscular parts of the interventricular septum (Figs. 8.11 and 8.12). muscular and membranous. The majority of leaflet attachments are of the muscular type, while the membranous part corresponds to the aforementioned reverse “U” segment. In some cases, the “U”-shaped attachment does not continue to the anterolateral leaflet of the tricuspid valve. This is very important in tricuspid valve replacement surgery; in cases where the septal part of the leaflet is positioned far posterior, needle injury may result in perforation of the septum and damage to the His bundle. 390 8 Tricuspid Valve

text: Fig. 8.25. Pericardial incision 8.2.2 Inferior “T” Sternotomy for the Tricuspid Valve The tricuspid valve may be also approached by using the inferior “T” sternotomy. This approach is described in detail in Chap. 2. Using this limited sternal incision, the middle and the inferior mediastinum is exposed. Thus, the right atrium and the tricuspid valve are positioned in the middle and inferior mediastinum. This inferior incision of the sternum enables an adequate inspection of the tricuspid valve. The sternum is incised between the xiphoid notch and the third intercostal space. Following the opening incision and insertion of the sternal spreader, the anterior mediastinum is exposed. The residuum of the thymus is presented in most adult patients as fat tissue, which is dissected down to the anterior sheath of the pericardium. The thymic vein should be identified and followed up to the superior edge of the sternal incision (Fig. 8.25). The pericardium is then incised in an inverse “T” fashion. The vertical incision begins inferior to the superior edge of the sternal incision and is extended down to the level of the diaphragm. The left and right horizontal incisions are created from the inferior point of the vertical incision. The pericardial edges are then lifted using purse-string sutures that are fixed to the sternal spreader. Note that a special minimally invasive sternal spreader is used for this approach. 398 8 Tricuspid Valve

Exposure of the right atrium following pericardial incision 8.2.3 Anterolateral Thoracotomy for the Tricuspid Valve The tricuspid valve may be approached using the right lateral thoracotomy procedure. This approach is described in detail in Chap. 2. Using this minimally invasive approach, the heart is exposed from the right lateral side, and is particularly useful for redo operations, in which extended mediastinal adhesions are likely to be experienced. The right lateral approach enables an adequate exposure of the right atrium of the ascending aorta and the great veins without exposure of the mediastinum. After completion of the chestwall incision and insertion of the rib spreader, the right lateral surface of the pericardium is exposed. This exposure may be facilitated by retracting the right lung into the posterior chest compartment (as seen in Fig. 8.34, wherein the right lung has been retracted into the posterior compartment of the right chest cavity). The right phrenic nerve is seen running in front of the right pulmonary ligament. Note that in this case the phrenic nerve holds a very deep positioned (Fig. 8.34). The pericardium is incised using a horizontal opening cut that is positioned approximately two finger-breadths superior to the phrenic nerve. After the pericardium was incised to an appropriate length, the pericardial edges are lifted to expose the right atrium. This is achieved using the pursestring sutures, which in general are fixed to the spreader. The exposed right atrium is seen on (Fig. 8.35). Orientation and morphology of the interventricular septum, inferior view Fig. 9.2. Orientation and morphology of the interventricular septum, inferior view, schematic drawing The interventricular septum is a wall between the left and right ventricles, and a major part of that wall comprises components of the right and left ventricular musculature. A smaller, membranous part of the interventricular septum lies beyond the connection between the aortic root and the tricuspid valve. This characteristic structure will be discussed herein. We will discuss the submacroscopic morphology of both the muscular and membranous parts of the septum. First, a detailed description of the anatomy is presented, and then a description of the blood supply of the septum. A cross section of the muscular septum is viewed from an inferior direction in the specimen presented in Fig. 9.1 and its corresponding schematic drawing (Fig. 9.2). The dissection runs in a horizontal plane at the border between the superior and middle thirds of the left ventricle. Here, one can see clearly that the right ventricle wraps around the left ventricle, extending between the anterior and posterior interventricular sulci (Fig. 9.1). On the schematic drawing (Fig. 9.2), the anterior and posterior descending coronary arteries can be seen in the anterior and posterior grooves. The left ventricle is indicated in red and the right ventricle in blue. It is essential to understand the anatomical regions of the septum in order to discuss in detail the clinical characteristics of the septum and its blood supply. The septum comprises anterior, posterior, and apical areas. The anterior part of the septum wall is directed anterior and superiorly, the inferior part is directed inferiorly and to the right and laterally, and the apical area includes the apex of the septum. This morphological situation is depicted in Fig. 9.4. The dashed line indicates the border between the mentioned segments (Fig. 9.4). 408 9 The Interventricular Septum

Interventricular septum, left lateral aspect, schematic drawing We will now discuss structure of the septum as seen from the left and right sides. In Figs. 9.3 and 9.4, the septum has been isolated from the left and right ventricular musculature, and an incision made on the leftand right-hand sides of the anterior interventricular groove. In this way, the left and right ventricles have been removed, leaving only the septum. In the first instance, we investigated the left side of the interventricular septum, as shown in Figs. 9.3 and its corresponding schematic drawing (Fig. 9.4). The right coronary sinus and the right side of the noncoronary sinus may be seen. The aortic valve leaflets have been removed. The ostium of the right coronary artery is positioned centrally in the right coronary sinus. Beneath and to the left of the right coronary artery, there is also an opening, which corresponds to the origin of the conus artery (Fig. 9.3). On the schematic drawing (Fig. 9.4), the right coronary sinus is marked in blue and the noncoronary sinus in green. In this projection, the right half of the mitral valve ostium is brought into view (Figs. 9.3 and 9.4). In the schematic drawing (Fig. 9.4), the mitral valve is indicated in orange; note that this part of the mitral valve is positioned behind the noncoronary sinus and is presented as a posterior roof of the muscular septum (Figs. 9.3 and 9.4). Here, one can see that the anterior third of the mitral valve ostium is directly connected to the membranous septum, which is indicated in yellow. The posterior two-thirds of the mitral valve are attached to the muscular part of the septum. The muscular part of the septum makes up the majority of the interventricular septum, and the membranous part is located inferior to the right and noncoronary sinuses. Superiorly, the membranous septum continues into the right intervalvular triangle (Figs. 9.3 and 9.4). Note that at the level of the deepest point of the right coronary sinus, the left bundle of the atrioventricular bundle enters the left ventricle. This entry point is seen on the schematic drawing, wherein the bundle is indicated in orange. Note that after its initial unique course, the bundle divides into the anterior and posterior parts (Fig. 9.4). The clinically very important areas of the septum are indicated in Fig. 9.4. the anterior, inferior, and apical parts. The meaning of these parts will be discussed later. 9.1 General Anatomy of the Interventricular Septum 409

Interventricular septum, right lateral aspect, schematic drawing The right side of the same specimen as in Figs. 9.3 and 9.5 is presented in Figs. 9.5 and Fig. 9.6, respectively, in which the interventricular septum is inspected from the right lateral view. The right coronary sinus and the right part of the noncoronary sinus are located at the superior anterior area of the interventricular septum (Figs. 9.5 and 9.6). On the schematic drawing in Fig. 9.6, the right coronary sinus is marked in blue and the noncoronary sinus in green. The opening of the right coronary artery is positioned in the middle of the right coronary sinus. The infundibular part of the right muscular septum may be seen in front of the right coronary sinus. Note that the infundibular part of the septum wraps around the right coronary sinus (Figs. 9.5 and 9.6). The attachment of the lateral wall of the right ventricle to the muscular part of the septum is found inferior to the right coronary sinus (Figs. 9.5 and 9.6). The lateral wall of the right ventricle is attached with its posterior part to the membranous septum (Fig. 9.5), which is indicated in yellow (Fig. 9.6) and is placed between the right and noncoronary sinuses. The right atrium has been dissected just superior to its attachment, which is superior to the septal leaflet (Figs. 9.5 and 9.6). The attachment of the septal leaflet is an inferior curved line with its highest point at the attachment to the membranous septum. This part of the attachment plays a very important role in the division of the membranous septum. Superior to the attachment of the tricuspid valve, the septum belongs to the atrial part, and inferiorly, the part belongs to the ventricular interventricular septum. The size of the atrial part of the membranous septum in the majority of cases depends upon the level of the anterior attachment of the tricuspid valve. The higher the attachment, the smaller will be the part of the atrial septum. It is very important to note that the atrioventricular node and the His bundle are positioned just superior to the septal leaflet. The His bundle and the right fascicle run at the inferior border of the atrial membranous septum; after crossing the attachment of the tricuspid valve, the right bundle enters the ventricular septum. The right interventricular septum is positioned inferior to the attachment of the septal leaflet. The superior and inferior papillary muscles give rise to the chordae tendineae, which are attached to the septal leaflet. The superior papillary muscle is positioned lateral and anterior to the moderator band (Fig. 9.5). 410 9 The Interventricular Septum

Interventricular septum, membranous part, frontal view Fig. 9.8. Interventricular septum, membranous part, frontal view, schematic drawing The anatomy of the membranous septum will now be discussed. The membranous septum is shown in the frontal direction, as seen on the specimen in Fig. 9.7 and its corresponding drawing (Fig. 9.8). The dissection plane runs in the frontal plane through the superior anterior part of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve attachment. The noncoronary and left coronary sinuses are also seen in the frontal plane, although here only the posterior part of both sinuses is identified. The anterior leaflet of the mitral valve is inferior to the aortic root, and is seen in a frontal projection. The noncoronary sinus is green and the left coronary sinus is red, triscupid valve is lateral to the noncoronary sinus. The membranous septum is positioned between the muscular septum and the base of the noncoronary sinus (Figs. 9.7 and 9.8). Note that cartilage tissue may be identified at the attachment of the membranous septum to the noncoronary sinus. This cartilaginous tissue condensation belongs to the right fibrous trigone, which is seen here in the frontal direction (Figs. 9.7 and 9.8). The superior part of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve may be found at the right side of the membranous septum, inferior to the attachment of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve (Figs. 9.7 and 9.8). The part of the septum that is positioned between the mitral valve and the tricuspid valve attachment corresponds to the atrial part. Note that the perforation of this part connects the right atrium to the left ventricle. The ventricular part positioned inferior to the attachment of the tricuspid valve is the effective interventricular septum. From the presented morphological relationships, it is clear that defects of the membranous septum can cause tricuspid valve insufficiency. In larger defects, the noncoronary sinus loses its attachment support at the superior edge of the septum, which may result in protrusion of the noncoronary leaflet into the outflow tract of the left ventricle. 9.1 General Anatomy of the Interventricular Septum 411

As we are gong to see in the following classification, in some cases the septal artery may supply the majority of the muscular septum, and so surgical damage to that artery may result in ischemia of the supplied area. This in turn, depending on the septal area supplied by the septal artery, may lead to postoperative heart failure. Depending on the level of origin from the anterior descending branch, the first septal artery may be termed superior, middle, or inferior. The superior septal artery originates from the superior third of the anterior descending branch, the middle from the middle third, and the inferior from the inferior third. The morphological variants of the interventricular septum blood supply will now be presented. In our investigation series, the described cases were found as frequently repeating cases. For the purposes of investigation, only hearts without pathological alteration were used. Initially, contrast material was injected into the left and right coronary arteries, and subsequently, coronary angiograms were performed. The left and right ventricles were opened lateral to the anterior and posterior interventricular groove to allow optimal coronary angiograms of the interventricular septum. The left ventricle was entered by cutting through the aorta, downward along the left side of the interventricular septum to the apex. The right ventricle was opened through the right atrium at the right side of the septum, downward to the apex. The heart was thus opened like a book; the interventricular septum was exposed in the horizontal plane, and coronary angiograms were then taken (Fig. 9.15). In Fig. 9.15, the left anterior descending branch is located at the anterior edge of the septum, and the posterior descending branch at the posterior edge of the septum. Consequently, the blood supply of the muscular septum is projected in the horizontal plane and may be easily investigated. In addition, schematic drawings were made corresponding to each morphological variant. In these drawings, the free wall of the right ventricle has been removed and the septum and its blood supply are inspected from the right lateral view (Fig. Fig. 9.16. Septal blood supply, type A, schematic drawing 9.16). The septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve is indicated in pink, the attachment of the left atrium in orange, that of the right atrium in green, and the subvalvular membrane is yellow. Sternocostal surface of the heart 9.3 Surgical Anatomy of the Interventricular Septum Knowledge of the surgical anatomy of the interventricular septum becomes relevant in adult cardiac surgery for the operative treatment of postinfarction septal wall ruptures. Postinfarction ventricular septal defects are a complication of acute myocardial infarction, and occur following 1–2% of acute myocardial infarctions. From the morphological point of view, postinfarction septal defects are most commonly located in the anterior and apical parts of the septum (approximately 60% of cases). This is a consequence of occlusion of the anterior descending branch. To be more precise, of occlusion of the inferior part of the anterior descending branch. When the apex is also supplied by the right coronary artery (see also Fig. 9.19), the anastomosis between the left and right coronary arteries prevents an infarction. Furthermore, in the present case, where the posterior descending artery is well developed, occlusion of the anterior descending artery in its middle third results in only anterior myocardial infarction; the apex continues to be perfused due to the blood supply from the posterior descending branch. In about 20–40% of cases, the rupture occurs in the posterobasal part of the septum, which is usually a consequence of infarction in the posterior descending artery supply area. As one can see, a complete understanding of the morphological factors that may play a role in the development of septal defects requires a detailed knowledge of the previously described anatomical variants. To approach the aforementioned septal areas, the heart is exposed by way of a total medial sternotomy. After the sternum is divided, a sternal spreader may be inserted and the retrosternal tissue dissected down to the anterior sheath of the pericardium. The pericardial incision is made in an inverse “T” fashion and the sternocostal surface of the heart exposed as shown in Fig. 9.25. For exposure of the corresponding septal region, left ventricular incisions are required. For anterior defects, the incision is made at the sternocostal surface of the left ventricle, to the left of the anterior interventricular groove. The anterior descending artery and the accompanying vein are the most precise natural indicators of the anterior groove. This is true especially in the case of extensive condensation of the epicardial fat tissue, as presented in Fig. 9.25, wherein although the anterior descending branch is seen clearly, the extensive fat tissue condensation obscures the view of the anterior interventricular groove, which may thus not be identified (see arrows). The left ventricular musculature may be identified to the left of the anterior descending branch. Note that the branches that run toward this part of the left ventricular musculature are conjoined with the venous vessels. The incision of the left ventricle is normally one to two finger-breadths lateral to the anterior descending artery. 421
