In addition, a left ventricular incision should be performed to the left of the posterior interventricular groove. The most accurate indicator of the posterior groove is the posterior cardiac vein (Fig. 9.26), which in most cases is positioned over the posterior interventricular groove. The incision of the left ventricle should thus be performed approximately two finger-breadths lateral to that vein. The schematic drawing in Fig. 9.27 presents a combination of anterior and posterior incisions of the left ventricle. Here, the heart is exposed by way of a median sternotomy, the pericardial edges are lifted with purse-string sutures, and a cardiopulmonary bypass is instigated via aortic and bicaval cannulation. Note that the heart is viewed as seen from the surgeon’s perspective in the operating theater during the procedure (Fig. 9.27). The opening cut of the left ventricle is positioned just lateral to the anterior and posterior grooves; note that both grooves represent the anterior and posterior borders of the interventricular septum. Naturally, the opening cut may be reduced only on the anterior or posterior surfaces of the left ventricle. Basal part of the interventricular septum, left lateral view, schematic drawing We will now describe in more detail the basal part of the septum, which is placed near to the aortic root and the mitral valve opening. The basal part of the septum includes both the anterior and the inferior areas. In Fig. 9.30, the basal part of the septum is inspected from the right lateral view; the corresponding schematic drawing is in Fig. 9.31, wherein the areas of the muscular septum are divided by dashed line. The entry point is beneath the right coronary sinus. After very short course, the left bundle branches into the anterior and posterior fascicles. The anterior fascicle is located in the anterior area of the septum (Figs. 9.30 and 9.31), and the posterior fascicle runs toward the inferior area. text: Superior vena cava Aorta Right atrium Right ventricle Sinoatrial node artery Posterio interatrial sulcus Sinoatrial node Right superior pulmonary vein Sinoatrial node Sinoatrial node artery Right coronary artery 10.1 The Sinoatrial Node The sinoatrial node (SN) is the heart’s natural pacemaker, and it is located at the connection between the superior vena cava and the right atrial appendage in the superior part of the terminal groove. The terminal groove indicates the position of the attachment of the right appendage and the sinus venosus of the right atrium. In most cases, the SN is found at the lateral anterior surface of the superior vena cava; however, it occasionally extends over the crest of the right appendage. In such cases, the SN exhibits a horseshoe form. In the first part of this chapter, we will discuss the morphology of the SN, including the microscopic anatomy, followed by a description of the morphological variants of the SN artery (SNA). The topographical relationships between the SN and its neighboring structures are shown in the dry-dissected specimen in Fig. 10.1 and its corresponding schematic drawing (Fig. 10.2). In all of the schematic drawings in this chapter, the SN is marked as a yellow, oval structure. On the dry-dissected specimen (Fig. 10.1), the SN is posiFig. 10.1. Topography of the sinoatrial node, right lateral view Fig. 10.2. Topography of the sinoatrial node, schematic drawing tioned at the right lateral side of the superior vena cava, and is a white, oval structure that is approximately 2×1 cm in size. The right atrium and the SN are inspected from the right lateral direction in this figure. The SN may be relatively easily dissected because of its harder consistency as compared to the surrounding tissue. However, tracing the SNA during the dissection makes identification of the SN much easier; the artery runs though the center of the SN (Figs. 10.1 and 10.2), dividing within the SN into smaller branches. In the presented dry dissected specimen (Fig. 10.1) before entering the SN, the SNA bifurcates, the right branch running into the SN and the left toward the left atrium. Here the SNA originates from the posterior part of the right coronary artery, and that from its branching area, the artery runs along the posterior wall of the right atrium, directly toward the SN (Figs. 10.1 and 10.2). To further investigate the submacroscopic anatomy of the SN, histological specimens were prepared, an example of which is presented, with a corresponding drawing, in Figs. 10.3 and 10.4, respectively. Tissue for this purpose was taken from the area of the connection between the superior vena cava and the right atrium. This tissue was prepared according to standard procedures for histological specimens, with sections made parallel to the long axis of the superior vena cava. The sections were stained using Orcein to emphasize the fibrous component (stains dark red) and the hematoxylin-eosin to highlight the cellular structures (stains orange). In the presented histological specimen, the SN tissue may be easily distinguished from the surrounding structures (Fig. 10.3). The schematic drawing in Fig. 10.4 was made to allow a better understanding of the topo graphical relationships. The pericardial fat tissue is found anterior to the SN, and the right atrial musculature is located posteriorly to the SN, toward the axis of the superior vena cava (Figs. 10.3 and 10.4). The histological staining that we performed allows the SN to be easily distinguished from the atrial musculature (stained orange; Figs. 10.3 and 10.4). 10.1 The Sinoatrial Node 429

Note that the border between the SN and the atrial musculature is continuous, especially at the lateral areas of the SN. The most important morphological feature in these figures is the position of the SNA, which as stated earlier, runs through the center of the SN. Note that the endocardium and the pericardium are both stained darkly with Orcein; this is a consequence of the very high content of elastic fibers. The fat tissue may be found inferior to the epicardial layer, which lies directly over the SN. We will now discuss the morphological variants of the SNA. We investigated 50 human hearts in which the coronary arteries were filled with contrast material. Coronary angiograms were made to identify the origin of the SNA. Subsequently, dry-dissected specimens were made to follow the course of the artery and to verify the position of the SN. A corresponding schematic drawing was made for each morphological variant. The SNA was found to originate from the right coronary artery in 33 of the cases (66%) and from the left coronary artery in the remaining 17 (about 34% Table 10.1). Angiogram of a type G sinoatrial node artery Finally, a coronary angiogram of the left SNA is seen in Fig. 10.24. Here, we have a right-dominated coronary circulation. The SNA artery branches off from the initial part of the circumflex artery (it only very rarely arises from the left main branch; in our series we did not find a single case exhibiting this phenomenon). Note that at the area of the anterior wall of the left atrium, the SNA bifurcates; the right branch is the effective left SNA, and the left corresponds to the anterior atrial branch. A good exposure of the mitral valve plays a key role in the success of mitral valve surgery. Visualization of the mitral valve in difficult situations, such as a small left atrium, redo operations, or in patients with a deep chest, can be critical. Several alternative surgical techniques have been described to overcome this problem, one of which is use of the superior transseptal approach. Although the efficacy of this approach is widely accepted, its safety with regard to the preservation of SN function remains controversial, since the SNA may be injured. We found that the superior border of interatrial septum was crossed in all 17 cases (34%) of left SNA in our series (Figs. 10.21 and 10.22). In the case of the right SNA, the interatrial septum was crossed by those arteries that arose prior to the right marginal branch (Figs. 10.5 and 10.8). These arteries, after reaching the dome of the right atrium, pass along the left side of the superior vena cava; the superior border of the septum is crossed before the SNA reaches the SN. Based on our results of 27 cases in our series, the SNA crosses the operating area that is developed in the superior transseptal approach to the mitral valve. Consequently, postoperative dysfunction of the SN is likely in these cases. 10.1 The Sinoatrial Node 439

The anatomy of the left superior process (LSP) is described in Sect. 6.1). Briefly, the LSP is a part of the left ventricle and as such reaches to the right fibrous trigone and the posterior part of the membranous septum. The AVN is positioned at the tip of the LSP, posterior and inferior to the right fibrous trigone, as demonstrated in Fig. 10.25. The position and topography of the node are inspected from the posterior view; the corresponding schematic drawing is seen in Fig. 10.26. In the dissected specimen (Fig. 10.25), the right ventricle and right atrium have been removed, and the left atrium dissected at the level of the oval fossa. The aorta has also been dissected at the level of the sinotubular junction, and from this viewpoint, the noncoronary sinus is placed in an inferior position so that only its right side may be seen. The right coronary sinus is seen in profile, and the right intervalvular triangle is located between the two sinuses. The origin of the right coronary artery has been left in situ. The tricuspid valve has also been removed; however, the line of attachment at the LSP remains to allow investigation of the relationship between the AVN and the tricuspid valve. Note that the right fibrous trigone is located inferior to the anterior inferior border of the interatrial septum. The anterior wall of the left atrium meets the anterior wall of the right atrium anterior to the fibrous trigone. The right fibrous trigone has been dissected and is presented as a white trigone-like structure positioned just behind the nadir of the noncoronary sinus (Fig. 10.25). The AVN and its artery are found inferior and posterior to the right fibrous trigone. In Fig. 10.25, the AVN artery, which arises from the right coronary artery and runs in a coiled fashion toward the tip of the superior posterior process of the left ventricle, has been filled with white contrast material. At first inspection, this tissue island exhibits the same morphological structure as the muscular part of the interventricular septum (i.e., they stain histologically for muscular components). This isolated tissue, which is surrounded by a fibrous coat, is the penetrating segment of the His bundle (Figs. 10.33 and 10.34). The membranous septum is positioned inferior to the septal leaflet. Defects at this level may result in a left-to-right interventricular shunt. During surgical correction of the membranous septum at the level of the anterior commissure of the tricuspid valve, injury may occur to the His bundle as a result of its relative proximity to this structure, resulting in damage to the heart’s conduction system. This may manifest as varying grades of postoperative atrioventricular block. The left and right coronary ostia were separately cannulated and radiopaque material was injected into the coronary arteries. At the time of the investigation, the hearts were without any pathological alterations. The injected hearts were then placed into 4% of formalin solution for 1 month, followed by a solution comprising 25% isopropyl alcohol, 20% propylene glycol, 0.5% glutaraldehyde, and 5% benzyl alconium chloride. After completion of the preserving procedure, dry-dissection of the AVN artery and the left and right coronary arteries was performed. The course of the AVN artery was dissected from its origin up to the AVN. 10.3.1 Left AVN Artery Of the 55 hearts, 13 (23.6%) had a left AVN artery that vascularized the AVN. The anterior arch of the septal leaflet is attached to the membranous septum, and the AVN is positioned behind this anterior arch. It is also very important to know that the AVN artery branches off into smaller branches in the center of the AVN (see Fig. 10.39). The AVN artery originates from the right coronary artery and runs along the LSP toward the AVN. In our series, the right AVN artery originated from the right dominant coronary artery in 37 cases and from the left dominant artery in 3 cases, and 2 of the cases exhibited the intermediate vascularization type (Table 10.2). In the schematic drawing presented in Fig. 10.40, the artery runs in the middle of the LSP; however, cases were also identified wherein the AVN artery ran near to the mitral valve or near to the tricuspid valve. In 13 of the 55 cases in our series (23%), the artery passed along the left lateral margin of the LSP near to the annulus fibrosus of the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve. In 27 cases (40%), the artery ran in the middle of the space between the mitral and tricuspid valves, and in 15 cases (18%), the artery passed adjacent to the annulus of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve. These morphological data show that the AVN artery frequently passes near to the mitral valve annulus. Therefore, damage to the AVN blood supply may become highly likely during mitral valve ring annuloplasty or prosthesis implantation. There appears to be no direct correlation between the type of blood supply dominance and the origin of the artery. This finding is supported by the following two specimens. In the first case (Fig. 10.41), we have a left-dominant coronary vascularization in which the AVN artery originates from the right coronary artery (the AVN artery is viewed from a superior view). text: Superior lobe of right lung Right brachiocephalic vein Internal thoracic artery Right superior pulmonary vein Phrenic nerve Pulmonary trunk Superior vena cava Right auricle Ascending aorta Superior lobe of left lung Left pulmonary artery Phrenic nerve Internal thoracic artery Right brachiocephalic vein Left subclavian artery Left internal jugular vein Left vagal nerve Left subclavian artery Brachiocephalic trunk Right common carotid artery Right subclavian artery Trachea Left superior pulmonary vein Vagal nerve Right internal jugular vein 11.1 The Aortic Arch 11.1.1 General Anatomy of the Ascending Aorta and the Aortic Arch Surgery of the aorta is one of the most challenging areas of cardiac and vascular surgery, from the management of emergency situations to the treatment of degenerative diseases. To achieve an optimal surgical result, it is essential not only to have an exhaustive knowledge of the pathological mechanisms involved, but also to be familiar with the anatomy of the aorta. Hence, we are dedicating an entire chapter to this great vessel of the human body. In this chapter, we will focus on the anatomy of the aorta, but not including the aortic root. In the past, the aortic root (also known as the bulb of the aorta) was considered to be an integral part of the ascending aorta. However, since the introduction of reconstructive procedures of the aortic root, this part of the ascending aorta is now regarded as an independent morphological and functional unit. The detailed morphology of the aortic root has been discussed elsewhere (Chap. 5), and so only the segments of the aorta positioned superior to the aortic root are discussed herein. A morphological description of the ascending aorta, aortic arch, thoracic aorta, and supraceliac part of the aorta will be provided. A discussion of the abdominal part of the aorta is outside the scope of this book. The human aorta commences at the upper part of the aortic root at the level of the sinotubular junction, where it is about 3 cm in diameter, and after ascending for a short distance, it arches backward and to the left side, over the root of the left lung. It then descends within the thorax on the left side of the vertebral column, passes into the abdominal cavity through the aortic hiatus in the diaphragm, and ends by dividing into the right and left common iliac arteries. Thus, the aorta can be described as having several portions: the ascending part, the arch, and the descending part, the latter of which is again divided into the thoracic and abdominal aortae. The anterior chest wall has been removed and the pericardium opened to secure adequate exposure of the anterior surface of the heart. In the presented case, the entire anterior sheath of the pericardium has been removed, sparing the left and right phrenic nerves on the lateral surfaces of the pericardium. The superior lobes of the right and left lungs have been retracted. The initial part of the ascending aorta is positioned behind the infundibulum (Figs. 11.1 and 11.2). This initial part is viewed from the posterior aspect and is surrounded by the left and right atria. Here, the ascending aorta causes a furrow on the surfaces of both atria. The incisure on the right medial wall of the right atrium is particularly prominent and is seen clearly on the cross section of the mediastinum presented in Fig. 11.3 and the corresponding drawing (Fig. 11.4). Note here that the ascending aorta is inspected from the superior aspect. The same situation is seen on Figs. 12.4 and 12.5, wherein the ascending aorta is seen from an inferior view. The part of the ascending aorta positioned inferior to the pulmonary artery is covered by the epicardial fat tissue. The presence of this condensation of fat is characteristic and is found in every heart, independent of the habitus. At this level, the ascending aorta is joined on the right to the superior vena cava and on the left to the pulmonary trunk. Anteriorly, the ascending aorta is covered by the appendage of the right atrium, from the left by the pulmonary trunk, and from the right by the superior vena cave. The aforementioned fat-tissue condensation elevates the epicardium from the anterior wall of the aorta, forming a semicircular plica, as seen clearly on Fig. 11.1. The fold of the transition between the pericardium and the epicardium may be found on the superior part of the ascending aorta, just before the junction with the aortic arch. Note that the ascending aorta is contained within the pericardium and is enclosed in a tube of serous pericardium, which it shares with the pulmonary artery. On the presented specimen, this is seen as oblique line running along the anterior wall of the ascending aorta, from right to left, from inferior to the brachiocephalic artery, inferior toward the pulmonary trunk (Figs. 11.1 and 11.2). 11.1 The Aortic Arch 457

Here, only the ascending aorta and the aortic arch are viewed from the left superior lateral view. To expose the entire course of the aortic arch and its topography relative to the neighboring structures, the left lung has been removed and the left brachiocephalic vein has been resected in order to expose the branches of the aortic arch (Figs. 11.7 and 11.8). The aortic arch begins at the level of the upper border of the second sternocostal articulation of the right side, and runs at first upward, backward, and to the left in front of the trachea (Fig. 11.7). It is then directed backward on the left side of the trachea, and finally passes downward on the left side of the body of the fourth thoracic vertebra, at the lower border of which it becomes continuous with the descending aorta. It thus forms two curvatures: one with its convexity upward, the other with its convexity forward and to the left. Note that the upper border of the aortic arch is usually about 2.5 cm below the superior border of the manubrium of the sternum; this is a very important feature that must always be considered, especially when performing a median sternotomy. To clarify the topography of the aortic arch, the vessel was divided into three parts: right, central, and left. These are indicated on the schematic drawing in Fig. 11.8 by full lines. The junction between the aortic arch and the ascending aorta is indicated by the fold of the pericardial sac (see Fig. 11.5 arrows). This circular fold is positioned just beyond the origin of the brachiocephalic artery, and indicates the transition between the pericardium and the epicardium (Figs. 11.7 and 11.8). Note that the right part of the aortic arch, which corresponds to the initial part, is positioned between the pericardial fold and the origin of the brachiocephalic artery. From this anatomical situation, it is clear that the ascending aorta is covered with pericardium throughout its length. The anterior surface of the arch is covered by the pleura and the anterior margins of the right lung. This part is positioned to the left of the junction between the superior vena cava and the brachiocephalic vein (Figs. 11.7 and 11.8). This topographical situation may be seen on the cross section of the thorax in Fig. 11.9 and its corresponding schematic drawing (Fig. 11.10), wherein the aortic arch is seen from the superior view. The transition between the right side of the aortic arch and the central segment is covered anteriorly by the retrosternal tissue, which corresponds to the remnant of the thymus. At this position, the right side of the aortic arch is very short; however, it may be extended in aneurysms or as a result of chronic dissection. In these situations, the distance between the sternum and the aortic arch is reduced to a minimum. There are described cases wherein the posterior wall of the sternum was destroyed by large aneurysms of the aorta. The central part of the aortic arch is actually the convexity of the aortic arch. The part of the aortic arch that is positioned between the origin of the left subclavian artery and the attachment of the ligamentum arteriosum is on the left or terminal part of the arch. In the literature, this part of the aorta has been labeled the isthmus of the aorta. In the fetal stage, this part of the aorta is considerably narrowed, forming what is termed the aortic isthmus, while immediately beyond the origin of the ductus arteriosus, the vessel present a fusiform dilatation; His named this dilatation the aortic spindle. These conditions persist, to some extent, in the adult, where His found that the average diameter of the spindle exceeded that of the isthmus by 3 mm. As described previously, the esophagus runs behind the thoracic part of the subclavian artery; at this level, the aortic arch is in front of the esophagus. However, the aortic arch passes downward, to the left lateral side of the vertebral column, finally passing down on the left side of the vertebral column. The aortic isthmus is the area where the transition from the aortic arch to the aforementioned posterior position is completed. From this topographical relationship, it is clear that the isthmus is initially in front of the esophagus, but on running toward the posterior position, the arch wraps around the esophagus. Morphological variants of the aortic arch sixth thoracic vertebrae. This morphological variation should be borne in mind, especially when performing a median sternotomy; with a high-positioned aortic arch, efforts must be made to avoid damage to the vessel. The aortic arch and its branches may exhibit numerous variations, which are result of disturbances in the intricate process of development. Some of this dimorphism may be silent with regard to clinical manifestation; however, the anomaly may be accompanied by pathological changes. The differentiation of these may be very difficult. In general, the aortic arch can exhibit different morphological aspects, with normal or anomalous numbers and places of the origin of the great vessels. However, it is clear that a normally positioned aortic arch may also present anomalous numbers and branching positions. These will now be discussed; the corresponding schematic drawings are seen in Fig. 11.16. Under normal morphological conditions, the branches of the aortic arch are positioned as follows. The brachiocephalic trunk arises from the right convexity, followed by the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery, which arise at the left convexity (Fig. 11.16a). This “normal” variation is found in 83– 85% of cases. Deviations from this norm may present as an increase or decrease in the number of branches (Ad 1–Ad 9): ) Ad 1: The double brachiocephalic trunk (Fig. 11.16b). The four main vessels arise from the left and right brachiocephalic trunks. ) Ad 2: The left bicaroticosubclavian trunk (Fig. 11.16c). The right subclavian artery arises as an independent artery from the aortic arch. The right and left common subclavian arteries arise together with left subclavian artery from one common branch. ) Ad 3: Right bicaroticosubclavian trunk (Fig. 11.16d). The brachiocephalic trunk and left common carotid artery have a common origin. The left vertebral artery arises between the aforementioned trunk and the left subclavian artery, directly from the aortic arch. The incidence of this variant may be as high as 10%. ) Ad 4: Bicarotic trunk (Fig. 11.16e). The left and right common carotid arteries arise from one common artery, from the middle of the aortic arch. The left and right subclavian arteries arise independently from the aortic arch. ) Ad 5: Separate origin of all four branches (Fig. 11.16f). Here, there is no brachiocephalic trunk. The right common carotid artery and the right subclavian artery each originate separately from the aortic arch. 11.1 The Aortic Arch 467

The specimen is viewed from inferior; note the position of the fundus of the stomach, the spleen, and the liver. In some instances, we focus on the transition of the aorta and the esophagus through the aorta. The aortic hiatus is in some instances positioned deeper, at the level of the 12th thoracic vertebra. Here, the aorta is still positioned in the posterior mediastinum in front of the tenth thoracic vertebra, where the converging muscular fibers of the left and right crura create the esohageal hiatus (Fig. 11.38). Note that the aortic hiatus it is not an aperture in the diaphragm, but rather an osseoaponeurotic opening between the diaphragm and the vertebral column. Occasionally, some tendinous fibers extend across the bodies of the vertebrae from the medial parts of the lower ends of the crura and pass behind the aorta, thus converting the hiatus into a fibrous ring. The hiatus is situated slightly to the left of the midline, the aorta, the azygos vein, and the thoracic duct pass through it (Fig. 11.38). The esophageal hiatus is situated in the muscular part of the diaphragm at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra, and is elliptical in shape. It is placed above, in front, and a little to the left of the aortic hiatus, and transmits the esophagus, the vagus nerves, and some small esophageal arteries. The following branches of the thoracic aorta may be identified: pericardial, bronchial, esophageal, mediastinal, intercostal, subcostal, and phrenic. We will discuss all of these in brief, but the bronchial and segmental branches will be discussed in more detail. The pericardial branches are small vessels that are distributed to the posterior surface of the pericardium. The bronchial arteries will be discussed later. The esophageal arteries number four or five. They arise from the ventral surface of the aorta and pass obliquely downward to the esophagus, forming a chain of anastomoses along that tube. These arteries are connected to the esophageal branches of the inferior thyroid arteries above, and with ascending branches from the left inferior phrenic and left gastric arteries below. The mediastinal branches are numerous small vessels that supply the lymph glands and loose areolar tissue in the posterior mediastinum. Morphological variants of the bronchial arteries The bronchial arteries are highly variable in their number and origin. In general though (about 40.6% of cases), there are two left and one right bronchial arteries (Fig. 11.39a). The two left bronchial arteries arise from the ventral aspect of the descending aorta at the height of the fourth to sixth thoracic vertebrae. They reach the lung by traveling along the anterior surface of the corresponding bronchi. The right bronchial artery exhibits a larger number of morphological variations. The most common is where it originates with the first intercostal artery or directly from the dorsal wall of the aorta (Fig. 11.39a). After the origin, the bronchial branches pursue a spiral course in the loose connective tissue around the bronchi. Along their course, they adhere to the wall of the bronchi and follow their ramifications. The bronchial arteries usually communicate with a branch of the pericardiacophrenic artery, although communication between the tracheal vessels and the coronary vessels has also been described. According to Cauldwell, who carried out an anatomical investigation on 150 human specimens, several bronchial artery variants can be identified: ) Variants with only one left and one right bronchial artery were described in 21.3% of cases (Fig. 11.39b). ) Two left and two rights arteries were found in 20.6% of cases, wherein the second right bronchial artery also originates from the ventral aspect of the aorta (Fig. 11.39c). ) Variants with a single left bronchial artery and two right bronchial arteries were identified in 9.7% of cases (Fig. 11.39d). ) Cases with one right and three left bronchial arteries were mentioned (4% of cases; Fig. 11.39e). ) Other combinations of three or four left bronchial arteries combined with one, two, or three right bronchial arteries were also identified (Fig. 11.39f–i). A large number of morphological variants has also been recorded with respect to the origin of the right bronchial artery. For surgeons, it is perhaps important to know that this artery may take also its origin from the right subclavian artery (Fig. 11.39i), the internal thoracic artery, or even from the brachiocephalic trunk. 11.2 The Thoracic Aorta 481

It either crosses the body of the eighth thoracic vertebra to join the azygos vein, or ends in the hemiazygos vein. When this vein is small, or altogether lacking, the left highest intercostal vein may extend as low as the fifth or sixth intercostal space. Note that in the case of obstruction of the superior vena cava, the azygos and hemi-azygos veins are the principal means by which the venous circulation is continued, connecting as they do, the superior and inferior vena cavae, and communicating with the common iliac veins via the ascending lumbar veins and with many of the tributaries of the inferior vena cava. 490 11 Surgical Anatomy of the Aorta

After removal of the liver and the lesser omentum, the soft tissue of the retroperitoneal space between the lesser curvature of the stomach and the first segment of the liver has been dissected. At the very superficial level, we find the left and right gastric veins, which represent the two major venous drainage vessels of the lesser curvature. Both veins commence the veinous drainage from the small coronary veins on the anterior and posterior surfaces of the lesser curvature. The left gastric vein may be found at the level of the cardia in the gastropancreatic fold, running inferiorly to the celiac trunk and parallel to the proper hepatic artery, and drains into the portal vein from its dorsal side. This vein is seen clearly on the specimen in Fig. 11.57. The right gastric vein is found at the inferior part of the hepatoduodenal ligament, crossing the gastroduodenal artery and finally opening into the portal vein (Fig. 11.58). At the lesser curvature, the left gastric vein is seen running toward the antrum, where it joins with the right gastric vein. The celiac trunk is found behind the aforementioned venous arborization. Note that the anterior gastric plexus may be found at the lesser curvature, being positioned just inferior to the cardia. The same topographical situation as presented previously, but with the inferior vena cava lifted away to facilitate exposure of the celiac plexus and the ganglia, is shown in Figs. 11.59 and 11.60. The celiac plexus is the largest of the three sympathetic plexuses. It is situated at the level of the upper part of the first lumbar vertebra and comprises two large ganglia, the left and right celiac ganglia. However, the very dense network of nerve fibers uniting these two ganglia is also a part of the plexus. The two ganglia are presented on the schematic drawing in Fig. 11.60. On the dry-dissected specimen (Fig. 11.59), the right celiac ganglion is positioned behind the inferior vena cava. The positions of both ganglia are indicated by a dashed line. Note that the left ganglia are positioned to the left of the celiac trunk (Fig. 11.59). The left ganglion also surrounds the root of the superior mesenteric artery. Both ganglia have the appearance of lymph glands and are placed on either side of the midline in front of the crura of the diaphragm, close to the suprarenal glands. The upper part of each ganglion is joined by the greater splanchnic nerve, while the lower part, which is segmented off and named the aorticorenal ganglion, receives the lesser splanchnic nerve and gives off the greater part of the renal plexus (Figs. 11.59 and 11.60). The plexus and the ganglia receive the greater and lesser splanchnic nerves of both sides and some filaments from the right vagus, and give off numerous secondary plexuses along the neighboring arteries. 492 11 Surgical Anatomy of the Aorta

Morphological variants of the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery The morphological variants of the celiac trunk are shown in Fig. 11.66. Normally (i.e., 73–90% of cases), the celiac trunk is formed by the common hepatic, left gastric, and splenic arteries (Fig. 11.66a). If the left gastric artery arises as an independent vessel that branches off from the abdominal aorta; the celiac trunk gives off only the hepatic and splenic arteries (Fig. 11.66b). In some cases, the superior mesenteric artery also arises from the celiac trunk (Fig. 11.66c), in which case the left gastric artery is also an independent branch arising from the aorta. Finally, the condition wherein the vessel is formed by the standard celiac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery is known as the truncus celiacomesentericus (Fig. 11.66d). According to Adachi’s data, the splenic and left gastric arteries originate as a common artery arising from the abdominal aorta in 0.4% of cases. Furthermore, in this morphological variant, the common hepatic and superior mesenteric arteries also arise from the common trunk (Fig. 11.66d). The gastrosplenic trunk is presented in Fig. 11.66e, wherein the left gastric and splenic arteries arise together. In this case, the common hepatic artery is absent and is replaced by either the left or right accessory hepatic artery, which arise from the large superior mesenteric artery. 11.3 The Celiac Trunk 497

Transition between the thoracic and abdominal aortae, schematic drawing At this point of the surgery, it is very important to consider the local morphological situation when performing proximal cross clamping. Furthermore, it is also suggested that the course of the esophagus should be identified at this stage. This is easier when a nasogastric tube or transesophageal echo probe has been introduced. Note that the position of the esophagus may be altered by an extensive aneurysmatic extension of the aorta. In the next step, the diaphragm is divided, as described in Chap. 2. In most cases, the diaphragm is opened in a circular fashion to protect the phrenic nerve and to preserve as much of the diaphragm as possible. A 3- to 4-cm rim of diaphragmatic tissue is left laterally and posteriorly to facilitate closure when the operation is complete. The abdominal aortic segment is then exposed via a retroperitoneal approach; the retroperitoneum is entered laterally to the left colon. A dissection plane is developed in the retroperitoneum, anterior to the psoas muscle and posterior to the left kidney. This situation (i.e., entering the abdominal cavity in front of the left psoas musculature and behind the peritoneum) is presented in Fig. 11.80, in which the transition between the thoracic and abdominal aortae has been exposed. The esophagus is positioned in front of the abdominal aorta (Figs. 11.80 and 11.81). A cross section of the left crus may be seen left and inferior to the transition between the thoracic and abdominal aortae. After circular dissection of the diaphragm, the left crus must be transected, thus exposing the retroperitoneal part of the abdominal aorta (Figs. 11.80 and 11.81). 11.4 The Thoracoabdominal Aorta 505

Topography of the aortic isthmus, schematic drawing The aortic arch and the transition toward the descending aorta is dissected from the surrounding tissue, exposing the left vagal, left recurrent, and left phrenic nerves (Figs. 11.84 and 11.85). Knowledge of the anatomy of the distal aortic arch is very important, otherwise damage may be incurred during cross clamping of all three of the aforementioned nerves. Note that the phrenic nerve runs superficially relative to the accessory azygos vein; the vagal nerve is positioned inferior to the vein, which is a very important landmark for identification of both of these nerves. Damage to the recurrent nerve must be avoided in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and reduced pulmonary function. To facilitate its identification, the vagal nerve may be dissected below the level of the recurrent nerve, this maneuver providing additional mobility of the nerve, thereby protecting it from injury (see Figs. 11.84 and 11.85). In most cases, cross clamping is preformed distal to the left subclavian artery; however, if clamping proximal to the left subclavian artery is anticipated, this vessel must be separately and circumferentially mobilized to enable placement of a bulldog clamp (see Figs. 11.84 and 11.85, where the branches of the aortic arch have also been isolated from the surrounding tissue). 11.4 The Thoracoabdominal Aorta 507

The branches of the abdominal aorta Fig. 11.93. The branches of the abdominal aorta, schematic drawing The abdominal aorta has then dissected in order to identify the most important visceral branches. In Figs. 11.92 and 1.93, the first branch of the celiac trunk, which is positioned inferior to the diaphragm, has been identified and its entire circumference dissected and isolated with a single purse-string suture. In the presented case, the superior mesenteric artery is an independent artery whose origin was also identified. In the cross section of the abdominal cavity shown in Fig. 12.9, the superior mesenteric artery is seen as a vessel positioned in the fat tissue behind the pancreas and in front of the abdominal aorta. Further dissection of the abdominal aorta allows identification of the left renal artery, and on the right side, the right renal and inferior mesenteric arteries (Figs. 11.92 and 11.93). The aorta has been liberated down to its bifurcation, which is in most cases found between the fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae. The left common iliac artery has also been exposed. 11.4 The Thoracoabdominal Aorta 511

Relationship between the thoracoabdominal aorta and the inferior vena cava, schematic drawing In Fig. 11.94, the aorta has been elevated from the lumbar column and the segmental lumbar branches exposed; these branches correspond to the segmental intercostal arteries (Figs. 11.94 and 11.95). Elevation of the aorta in this way exposes the inferior vena cava. It is essential to take note of the relationship between the two large vessels; aneurysmatic dilatation of the aorta may shift the inferior vena cava anteriorly. When manipulating the artery, care must be taken not to lesion the inferior vena cava, as this may prove fatal. The relationship between the inferior vena cava and the abdominal aorta is also seen on cross section in Figs. 12.9, 12.10, 12.11, 12.12, and 12.13.
